Appendix: Master Miaofeng
[Dream-Wanderings Collection]
Also called The Dream-Wanderings Collection of the Old Man Hanshan. It is a great gathering of Master Hanshan's Dharma words, letters, and verses, in fifty-five fascicles. It was written by
Hanshan Deqing of the Ming dynasty, recorded by his attendant Fushan, edited by his disciple Tongjiong, and re-collated by his student Liu Qixiang.
[The Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan] Of these, the annals were recorded by Master Hanshan's attendant Fushan, and the expansive commentary was composed by his disciple Fuzheng.
[Fushan] The Authentic Record of the Chronicle of the Old Man Hanshan records:
“In the fifteenth year of Wanli
in the year of Dinghai, I was forty-two.
In the eighth month of autumn, the Censor-in-Chief Hu
(Hu Shun'an; censor-in-chief: a regional inspector)
asked leave to return to his estate, and thereupon brought his own son to send him forth to take the tonsure as an attendant, naming him Fushan.”
The Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan says:
(I, Fuzheng)
when the Venerable Hanshan journeyed east, I happened to meet the scribe-attendant, the master known as Zhiwei. Already at the Mirror-of-Essence Hall
(Jingci Temple)
of Jingci, morning and evening we met face to face, and together we studied the profound Dharma
(together studying the Buddha's Dharma)

. The Master assisted with the brush-and-ink affairs of the abbot's quarters and at last completed the Dream-Wanderings Collection. Among the Venerable Hanshan's outstanding disciples of that time, none surpassed Master Zhiwei. In hardship and peril he never failed to attend; the complete record of the collection came forth from his hand. Later he was entrusted with the abbot's quarters at Wuru, presided over the Cloud of Dharma Temple on Mount Kuang, and at seventy passed away seated in meditation
(passing away while seated)
Again it says:

“The foremost disciple whom the Master most approved was none other than Master Zhiwei, named Fushan. At first he shared both fortune and misfortune, appearing six times in the chronicle of the Master's final transformation
(appearing six times in the autobiographical annals of the Old Man Hanshan, written in the year before his nirvana)
; at last he hurried about to bear the funerary bier and recorded in detail the karmic circumstances of the Master's passing; he was indeed the filial son of Wuru.”
[Fuzheng] Tan Zhenmo

, with the style Liangsheng and also the style Fuzheng, the sobriquet Saowei, also called Saowei Nunnery, and by another name the Bearded Daoist, a native of Jiaxing. At twenty-seven (the forty-fourth year of Wanli,
) he took refuge with Master Hanshan; at sixty-one (the seventh year of Shunzhi,

) he obtained the autobiographical annals of Master Hanshan and composed the expansive commentary. A Ming scholar, he passed the examinations as a metropolitan graduate in the first year of Chongzhen (

). He successively held the posts of Director of the Bureau of Works' Weighing Section, Assistant of the Court of Judicial Review, Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud, and Director of Studies and Chancellor of the Imperial Academy. In the early Qing he was recommended to act as Director of Studies, but declined and returned home, ending his days in his native place. He read broadly and was said to be “one who reads everything,” maintaining deep friendships with Qian Qianyi, Chen Zilong and others. He wrote many books, but because of the severe literary inquisition under the Qianlong reign, only the Tanzi Diaochong (The Insect Carvings of Mr. Tan), the Saowei Collection, and the Three Scriptures Seen as Sacred, among others, survive. Of these, the Tanzi Diaochong is the first monograph on insects in our country, recording close to a hundred kinds. His mother was of the Yan clan. According to the Records of Virtuous Women

Biography of the Mother of Tan Zhenmo, Madam Yan”: “Madam Yan was the mother of Tan Zhenmo, Director of the Bureau of Works. Her family was prosperous and honored, yet she wore plain clothes and ate simple fare, taking the Diamond and Lotus Sutras as her daily practice. In her later years she also upheld the Avatamsaka, reading one scroll each day, and would explain its gist to her daughters-in-law. In the fifth year of Chongzhen she fell ill, and knew her end was near. In the height of summer, rising at dawn, she changed clothes and bathed, then prayed before the Buddha, saying: 'I have served the Buddha all my life. If there is truly a karmic bond with the Buddha, may my body not give off any foul odor.' Then she sat upright in the lotus posture and passed away. Seven days after her death, her color was still as in life, a rare fragrance wafted about, and flies fled far away. All who came to mourn could not but sigh in admiration.”

blocks.text: 1. Avalokiteshvara Bestows a Son

inline.s: Master Hanshan (—

) was named Deqing, with the style Chengyin and the sobriquet Hanshan, a native of Quanjiao County in Jinling (now part of Anhui). His father's surname was Cai, taboo-name Yansheng, and his mother was of the Hong clan.

[Style] The courteous name, an alternate name for a person. In addressing oneself one uses the given name, to show modesty; in addressing others one uses the style, to show respect. [Sobriquet] The style-name, another designation beyond the given name and the style.

His mother piously venerated the Great Being Avalokiteshvara. One night she dreamed that Avalokiteshvara led a child through the door, and in her joy she took the child in her arms; from that time she was with child. In the twenty-fifth year of the Jinsheng era of Emperor Shizong of the Ming (

), at midnight on the twelfth day of the tenth month, a child was born wrapped in a double, white caul. When the caul was peeled away and the child bathed, an extraordinary fragrance filled the whole room, seeming to herald that a great teacher would come into the world to revive the Dharma of the Buddhist schools.
The biography of the Master's disciple, the Dull and Foolish One, in the Chronicle of the Reviver of Caoxi, Venerable Han, says:
(Master Hanshan)

after leaving home at the Temple of Requital of Kindness, one day before the stupa of the relics met an Indian monk, who said: 'This young one will in days to come turn the great Wheel of Dharma; his mouth will be like the upturned moon, the very mouth of a Buddha.' Again, beneath the corridor of the temple he met a man who said: 'Yao's brows bore eight colors; your brows bear five, and you carry the burden of the three teachings
(Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism)
.' Later, on Mount Wutai, passing the Great Pagoda Temple, then an ascetic pilgrim
(a wandering mendicant monk)
, he met a monk of great stature
(a tall and imposing figure)
, who, grasping his hand, said: 'The Master is a great being returned; his whole head of hair is of dark-violet hue, and in time he shall surely do great Buddha works.”
Master Ouyi, in his later years, wrote in his autobiography:
“At twenty-three,
I resolved to leave home and investigate the Great Matter. At twenty-four I dreamed of bowing to Master Hanshan, weeping that our karmic bond was so thin and that we had met too late.

In the course of one month I dreamed of the Master three times. The Master had gone to Caoxi, and I could not follow him afar. So I took the tonsure under Master Xueling, who named me Zhixu. Master Xueling was a disciple of the Venerable Han.”
(From the Collected Essays of Lingfeng)

His parents named this extraordinary infant Damei. But good fortune is often beset by hardship, and the child's arrival in the world was not smooth. The next year, when Damei was a full year old, he fell gravely ill with a wind-disease and nearly died. His loving mother, seeing that medicines were of no avail, prayed with utmost sincerity before Avalokiteshvara and made a vow: 'O Great Being Avalokiteshvara, if you can heal my son Damei of this grave illness, I will let him grow up to leave home and become a monk, to uphold the true Dharma and repay the Great Being's boundless kindness!' After several days the illness truly healed. To make Damei's life go well, his mother likewise entrusted his name to the Temple of Longevity in the village, changed his milk-name Damei, and called him “monk.”

As a child the Master was of a quiet disposition, often preferring to sit alone in stillness and reflection, and disinclined to play with the village children. His grandfather, seeing the boy sit alone all day, often said to others: “This grandson is like a wooden stake.”

His uncle, who usually doted on him, suddenly died one day. Coming in from outside, the boy saw his uncle lying in bed. His mother came to coax him: “Your uncle has fallen asleep; you can call him to get up.” So he called out to his uncle several times, but got no reply; he only heard his aunt weeping bitterly, “Heavens! Where have you gone?” Finding it very strange, he asked his mother, full of doubt, “Uncle's body is plainly right here; where has he gone?” His mother answered, “Your uncle is dead!” He asked again, “Where has he gone in death?” His mother did not tell him, but the question of “where does one go in death” grew ever more doubtful in him, and from then on he often pondered it.

Before long his aunt bore a son, and his mother took him to see. Seeing the child was so big, he asked his mother in curiosity, “How did this infant get into aunt's belly?” His mother, finding the question odd, tapped him and said, “Fool! How did you get into your mother's belly?” Hearing this he was all the more puzzled. Where does a person come from after all? From that time on, the two questions “where does one go in death” and “where does life come from” occupied his young mind, just as with many great scientists the sparks of inquiring after truth were already kindled in childhood.
(Under his mother's guidance the Master first began to investigate the gong'an of birth and death.)

When he was seven, his mother sent him to the village school to study. The next year he transferred to a school across the river, and because the back-and-forth was inconvenient, he lodged with relatives. His mother allowed him to come home only once a month; at other times he was not permitted to return.

One day he came home to visit, and, feeling so attached to his mother, he refused to cross the river to study. His mother, angry, drove him to the riverbank, and when he still would not board the boat, in a fit of anger she seized his hair-bun and threw him into the river, then walked away without a backward glance. His grandmother, seeing him struggling in the water, hurriedly had someone rescue him and bring him back home. His mother, seeing that someone had saved and returned him, still said angrily, “This worthless son — if he isn't drowned, what use is there in keeping him!” She drove him out again at once, with not the least tenderness. The young Master Hanshan, seeing his mother so hard-hearted toward him, no longer thought of home, and studied earnestly. After he left home, his mother would often stand on the far side of the river gazing across, shedding tears. His grandmother scolded her: “Since you are so hard-hearted, why do you still weep?” His mother replied, “It is not that I am hard-hearted. I must cut off his clinging attachment, so that he can study with real earnestness!”
(With such a great mother, how could he not succeed! A mother's grace is as weighty as a mountain.)
At nine, the Master studied at a temple, where he heard a monk say that reciting the Avalokiteshvara Sutra
(the Universal Gate Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara)

could save one from all the world's suffering and calamity. Overjoyed, he asked the monk for a copy, studied it with deep attention, and could recite it from memory. His mother often burned incense and bowed before Avalokiteshvara; when he was home he would always join her in worship. One day he said to his mother, “The Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara has a scripture.” His mother had never heard of it, so he immediately recited it for her. His mother, greatly pleased, said, “Where did you get this? The sound of your recitation is truly like the old monk's in the temple!” He then told his mother the whole story.
When he was ten, because his mother supervised his studies very strictly, he found reading both exhausting and arduous, and began to feel disheartened. One day he asked his mother:
What is the purpose of study?”
To become an official,” his mother answered.
What kind of official?”
Starting from a minor post, you could rise, if capable, to be prime minister.”
And after becoming prime minister?”
In the end it comes to nothing.”
Hearing this he sighed and said, “What a pity that a life of toil should come at last to nothing. What use is it for me to study? I only want to be one who does not come to nothing!”

His mother, angered, rebuked him: “A worthless son like you can only be a roaming mendicant monk!” Hearing the words “roaming mendicant monk,” he asked in curiosity, “What is a roaming mendicant monk? And what good is there in being one?”

His mother explained to him: “Monks are disciples of the Buddha. Their footsteps reach the whole world; they are free and unconstrained, the field of blessedness for gods and men, and so people everywhere give them offerings.” Hearing that roaming monks were so transcendent and free, he said to his mother, “In the future I too will become a roaming mendicant monk, all right?” “All right, all right,” she said, “but I fear you may not have that share of blessedness.”
Why does one need blessedness?” He still did not understand.
In the world one often sees those who become top graduates and high officials; but where are those who leave home to become a Buddha and patriarch?” his mother explained.
I have this share of blessedness; I only fear that Mother will not approve of my leaving home!” Fearing his mother might object, he said this quickly.

If you have this share of blessedness, then I will agree to your leaving home.” His mother had long been sincere in her Buddhist faith, and seeing her son delighted to leave home, she consented. From that day onward, the young Master planted in his heart the seed of leaving home to become a monk.
(What exquisite repartee between mother and son!)

One noon the next year, he saw at the door several itinerant monks, with gourd and almsbowl shouldered, coming from afar, and ran to ask his mother: “Who are they?” “They are traveling mendicant monks.” He was secretly pleased, and went out to the door to look again. He saw the monks come to a tree, lay down their loads beside it, and then ask alms of his mother for the meal. His mother at once bustled about steeping tea and cooking rice, being very respectful to the monks. After the monks had eaten, they shouldered their loads and raised a hand to thank his mother; seeing this, she hurriedly stepped aside and said respectfully, “Please do not thank us!” The monks then went straight on their way.

When the monks had gone far off, he asked his mother, puzzled: “Why were the monks so ill-mannered as to eat their meal without a single word of thanks?” “If the monks thanked us,” his mother explained, “we would not receive the blessing.”

Hearing his mother's words, he thought to himself: “Seen this way, monks are indeed the noblest and greatest people in the world!” From then on he constantly aspired to leave home and cultivate, only that he had no convenient way to do so.

blocks.text: 2. Buddha-Recitation and Seeing the Buddha

inline.s: In the thirty-sixth year of Wanli (

), the Master was twelve. With the growth of his years, his understanding also rose year by year, and he gained a certain awareness of what the world of human life was. Because his latent faculties were deep, there increasingly showed forth a detached, non-active nature. He did not delight in the world's sensual pleasures, nor yearn for the affections between man and woman; so when his father made ready to arrange a marriage for him, he at once objected strongly, and his father, unable to sway him, had to give it up.

One day he heard a monk of Jinling say, “The abbot of the Temple of Requital of Kindness in Jinling, Master Xilin, has practiced all his life and is a renowned great virtuous one.” So he resolved to follow Master Xilin to study the Dharma. He told his father of his wish to leave home and study Buddhism, but his father refused, so he could only go again to beg his mother. His mother said to his father, “The purpose of raising a child is to hope he attains genuine accomplishment. Since he has such a noble aspiration, we as parents should let him go!” So one day in the tenth month, they sent him to the Temple of Requital of Kindness.
[We as parents should let him go] Fuzheng, the disciple, in his
Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan, comments:

“When one considers that the Venerable Hanshan, had he not had this mother, could not have left home, and could not have remained a lifelong virgin youth to become Buddha and patriarch — she is truly a Buddha-mother!”

When he came to the Temple of Requital of Kindness, many who cast a glance at him marveled, thinking he would surely accomplish great things. Master Xilin met him in the abbot's quarters, and, much pleased, said, “This child has an extraordinary bone-spirit; if he were to remain merely a worldly monk, that would be a great pity!”

At that time the celebrated Chan master Wuji was preaching the sutras in the Tripitaka Hall, and Master Xilin took him to pay his respects. When they met, the Grand Secretary Zhao Dazhou was also present; seeing him he too was delighted, and said, “This child will in the future be a teacher of gods and men!” Then he stroked his head and said, “Do you love to be an official, or do you love to be a Buddha?” He answered at once, “I love to be a Buddha!” Zhao Dazhou said to the two masters, “This child must not be slighted; he should be well nurtured, and will surely achieve great things.” Thus, under the care and esteem of many elder masters, he began to set foot on the most meaningful path of life. His first lesson was to join the Dharma assembly where Master Wuji preached; although he could not fully understand what was being said, in his heart he felt as if he knew something, only he could not put it into words.

After this session of sutra-lecturing ended, Master Xilin at once chose the most learned among his dharma-grandsons to teach him specifically. First he studied the Lotus Sutra, and in only three months could recite it fluently. He then studied earnestly for two years, and could recite from memory all the commonly circulated sutras and treatises.

Seeing his rapid progress, Master Xilin said joyfully, “This child can be taught; we must not waste his time.” So he engaged a teacher thoroughly versed in the Four Books and Five Classics. The teacher first had him study the Four Books and Five Classics, the required course for passing the examinations, and afterward he studied the doctrines of the Hundred Schools, historical classics such as the Zuo Commentary and the Records of the Grand Historian, as well as ancient prose, poetry, verse, and song, in truth learning everything and reading everything. After studying with the teacher for three years he could compose poetry and essays. At that time he even wrote a poetic essay on “The River-scene Chapter,” which had considerable influence among his fellow students. Seeing how swiftly his learning advanced, they all showed him great respect. But he felt the literary occupation burdened his own heart, and so had no great interest in taking the examinations.

[The Four Books and Five Classics] The Four Books: the Great Learning, the Doctrine of the Mean, the Analects of Confucius, and the Mencius; the Five Classics: the Book of Songs, the Book of History, the Book of Rites, the Book of Changes, and the Spring and Autumn Annals.
In the forty-second year of Wanli (

), the Master was nineteen. Because many of his fellow students had achieved excellent results in the examinations, someone urged him to sit for them also. Just at that time Master Yungu of Mount Qixia was also staying at the temple, and hearing that someone had urged him to take the examinations, he feared the young man might be swayed, and so earnestly instructed him on how important and how subtle are the matters of transcendence and liberation and of seeing the mind and realizing the nature; he also cited the auspicious karmic circumstances of the patriarchs recorded in the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp and the Biographies of Eminent Monks, and told him to go read the bequeathed works of the ancients himself. Master Yungu was the true Dharma-eye of the Chan school, and Master Hanshan had always held him in deep respect. Now, following his guidance, he went to the Sutra Repository, and from a book chest picked up a copy of the Collected Works of Zhongfeng, and read it earnestly. Before he had reached the end of the volume, he felt within himself great comfort, thinking: “This method of investigating, which can escape the sea of bitter birth and death, is exactly what I delight to cultivate.” From that time on he resolved to leave the world in cultivation, in order to escape the sea of bitter birth and death, and no longer had any heart for the examinations.

Thereupon he respectfully asked Master Xilin to shave his head and formally leave home. Then he burned all his former writings, to cut off all clinging, and devoted himself exclusively to investigating the matter that leads upward.

[Having his head shaved] Donning the monk's robe and shaving the head, i.e., first leaving home to become a monk or nun. [The matter that leads upward] The great matter of the one road that leads upward. The ultimate point of the Chan school is called ‘the one road that leads upward.’

Having cultivated in this way for a time, he felt he had not yet understood the essentials of investigating, so he tried the method of single-mindedly upholding the Name of Amitabha Buddha. When, day and night without cease, he had been reciting for several days, suddenly one night he dreamed he saw Amitabha Buddha appear in the sky, exactly in the place where the sun sets. The Buddha seen in the dream had a majestic countenance and a halo, all perfectly clear. The Master reverently performed the rite of touching the feet, his heart filled with longing. He prayed also to see the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, and the two bodhisattvas immediately revealed half their forms. After this dream, the three Holy Ones of the West frequently appeared shining brightly before his eyes, and his body and mind were immersed in the joy of Dharma. He thought, full of confidence, “Cultivation will surely succeed.”

When winter came, the Temple of Requital of Kindness held a sutra-lecture assembly and invited Master Wuji to preach the National Teacher Qingliang's Commentarial Essay on the Avatamsaka. Master Hanshan at this time received the full precepts, and joined the assembly to listen to the Master's explanation.

[The full precepts] The complete and perfect precepts, such as the 250 precepts of a bhikshu and the 348 precepts of a bhikshuni. [National Teacher Qingliang] That is, Master Chengguan, the Fourth Patriarch of the Avatamsaka school. He dwelt on Mount Wutai and wrote commentaries on the Avatamsaka Sutra. Later he lived in the capital; Emperor Dezong of the Tang welcomed him into the palace and conferred upon him the title National Teacher Qingliang. His life spanned nine dynasties, and he was teacher of seven emperors.

When he heard the phrase of the Ten Mysterious Gates, “The ocean-seal of the Dharma-realm, the dense and pervasive, ever-present,” he suddenly awakened to the principle of the perfect, interpenetrating, inexhaustible Dharma-realm. From the subtle, profound text he thought of its author, and his admiration for Master Qingliang's spiritual bearing grew all the more. Taking “Qingliang” as his meaning, he also adopted the style “Chengyin,” and asked Master Wuji to correct both his thought and his style.

Master Wuji asked him, “Do you have the aspiration to enter this Dharma gate?” He answered, “Yes!” The Master approved his aspiration, and made known to him the cool, wonderous scenery of Mount Wutai, where the ice grows hard in winter and snow still falls in summer, and where there is never sultry heat.

From then onward, whether coming or going, in all things, the scene of ice and snow would appear before his eyes. Therefore his longing to dwell on Mount Qingliang grew all the more firm, and he vowed to live there and cultivate. At this time he was utterly free of attachment to the world's fame and profit, and the thought of being weary of the world's five desires never left his mind for a moment.

On the last day of the year, Master Xilin gathered everyone together and said, “I am already eighty-three; sooner or later the day will come when I must go! In my life I have shaved more than eighty disciples, and not one has been able to shoulder my great cause of spreading the Dharma.” He paused, then stroked Master Hanshan's back and said, “This young man's latent faculties are deep. I hope he may become a dragon-elephant of the Buddha's house, but it is a pity I shall not see his accomplishment! Though he is still young, he already has a mature understanding. After my death, all matters, great and small, of the halls, the rooms, and the doors, you must all defer to his arrangements; do not think him young and employ others instead!” Through tearful sighs, the assembly accepted Master Xilin's entrustment.

On the seventh day of the new year, Master Xilin donned the precepts-robe, made a circuit of all the monks' quarters in the temple, and bade the assembly farewell. Seeing that Master Xilin's body was still quite healthy, the assembly was greatly surprised.

Three days later, Master Xilin instructed his disciples to arrange the matters of his passing, and his body showed slight signs of illness. His disciples offered him medicine, but he said to them, “I am about to go; what use is medicine to me?” Then he gathered the assembly and recited the Buddha's name for five days and nights. On the sixteenth day of the first month, Master Xilin, holding his prayer beads, sat cross-legged in the lotus posture and passed away peacefully. Thus Master Hanshan's first guiding teacher left the world most freely; and this was indeed the abundant fruit borne by the flower of his boundless merit in a single life!

blocks.text: 3. Investigating Buddha-Recitation

inline.s: After Master Xilin passed into nirvana, his dharma-brother, the young Master, took up the abbotship of the Temple of Requital of Kindness. In that very year (when Master Hanshan was twenty), Master Yungu held a great meditation period at the Temple of Heaven and Earth, gathering fifty-three celebrated virtuous monks from across the land to propagate the Chan school's method of investigating and awakening.

On hearing this news, Master Hanshan was extraordinarily happy; and to be able to sit in meditation together with many celebrated virtuous monks — how fast would his progress be! Master Yungu had always held Master Hanshan in high regard, and on this occasion earnestly encouraged him to go participate. Master Hanshan sought the abbotship of the young Master, and, having obtained consent, went to the Temple of Heaven and Earth.

When the Master began to apply effort in the meditation hall, not knowing the method of effort, his mind could not settle and he felt very distressed. To clarify the foundational practice of Chan investigation, he humbly came before Master Yungu, burned incense and bowed, then requested instruction on the method of Chan investigation. Master Yungu taught him the gong'an of examining reality through Buddha-recitation (investigating Buddha-recitation), that is, taking a single Buddha-name (Amitabha Buddha) as the head-topic, to investigate who is reciting the Buddha's name. Hearing Master Yungu's instruction, he investigated with a focused mind, single-mindedly unshaken. In these three months, it was as if he were in a dream; he entirely did not see the fellow cultivators gathered together, nor knew of everyday affairs. His fellow cultivators all praised his aspiration.

Applying effort too urgently can also bring illness. Since the Master's effort had found power, he grew ever more valiant and vigorous. Because he pushed too hard, a boil broke out on his back, swelling into a large red area and causing extraordinary pain. Master Yungu, seeing it, also found it hard to manage. At this time Master Hanshan put on his kashaya and sincerely prayed before the Bodhisattva Weito, saying: “That I have developed this boil on my back is surely due to the karma of past enmity calling for its debt of life. I vow to recite the Avatamsaka Sutra ten times to dissolve my past karma. I beg the Bodhisattva to bless me, so that in the last three months of this meditation retreat I may not suffer the affliction of illness, so as to complete the merit of this cultivation; afterward I will recite the sutra to fulfill the vow and dissolve the karma.” After praying before the Bodhisattva, at midnight he felt exceedingly weary, and as soon as he lay down on the meditation couch, fell fast asleep. When the morning bell and board sounded, he was still deep in sleep. When he woke, the daylight was already bright; he felt his boil, and it had already healed. Master Yungu, seeing him, asked, “How is your illness?” He replied cheerfully, “The boil is already healed.” Master Yungu lifted his clothes and looked, and indeed it was healed to its original state. All those present were astonished and marveled.

The last three months of the meditation period passed quickly in stillness. When it ended, the Master stepped out of the meditation hall; his mental state was utterly calm. Eating rice and dressing, or laboring in chores, or walking through the market streets, it was as pure as if he were still in the meditation hall, entirely undisturbed by the environment. Those who knew him at the time all found it extraordinary.

The Chan practice grounds south of the Yangtze, only after Master Yungu's advocacy, began to flourish. But among the monks few practiced Chan investigation, and those who advocated and carried it forward were even fewer. Only Master Hanshan, receiving Master Yungu's directive, investigated the matter leading upward with great effort. Moreover, at that time the monks' robes in the monasteries mostly followed the customs of the world, favoring brilliant colors. The Master, not pandering to common views, and in accordance with the requirements of the precepts and the exhortations of the ancients, simply found a patched robe and put it on. When people saw him they said this monk was somewhat eccentric.

blocks.text: 4. The Great Fire at the Monastery

inline.s: The next year the Master was twenty-one. On the twenty-eighth day of the second month, at noon, a torrential rain fell. Suddenly a great peal of thunder came down from the top of the pagoda, and within the pagoda hall a blazing fire at once broke out; in a matter of moments it burned away the Great Hero Hall. The fire burned until dusk, and over a hundred and forty halls and galleries of the Temple of Requital of Kindness were nearly all reduced to ashes. The young Master reported this to the court, and the emperor held that, since the fire had not been extinguished in time, the monastery must bear the responsibility. So punishment descended: the young Master and seventeen others were arrested. Monks dwelling in the temple, fearing implication, departed one after another, and the remaining dharma-functionaries no longer had anyone to deliberate with. At this critical moment when the great fabric was about to topple, Master Hanshan stepped forward, resolutely assuming all affairs of the monastery and doing all he could to extricate the situation from calamity. He himself shouldered food and provisions to carry to the prison for those arrested. To rescue them from prison, though the way from the monastery to the Ministry of Punishments was some twenty li, he rushed back and forth for three months, and only then were they spared the death sentence.

At that time there was a Dharma Master Xuelang, named Hong'en, who at thirteen followed his father to the Temple of Requital of Kindness to hear Master Wuji preach the Lotus Sutra's Rules of Practice. For more than ten consecutive days he listened attentively, and then cut off his own hair, begging his father to let him leave home to become Master Wuji's young novice. At that time Master Hanshan, aged twelve, had also left home at the Temple of Requital of Kindness; the two young novices were of similar age, both relying on Master Wuji, and were of one mind and heart, as close as siblings born of the same womb. Their deep friendship never wavered throughout their lives.

One day Master Hanshan, speaking with him about reviving the monastery, said: “To revive this great and expansive monastery, if one does not possess great merit, blessing, and wisdom, it will not be easy to succeed. We should press on with all our might in cultivation, accumulating moral virtue, and await the arrival of the right moment.” Master Xuelang agreed wholeheartedly, and also vowed to revive the monastery.

Before long the Junior Master-ancestor also passed away, and from that time on there was no one left to sustain the legacy of Monk Xilin. Because Xilin had been in the habit of keeping no savings, every expense of the funeral had to be borrowed, and so a great many debts were incurred. If the temple's property were taken to repay them, this famous monastery south of the Yangtze would be ruined in a single morning. At this point the Master recalled Xilin's charge and resolved to protect the temple's property. He found ways to repay every loan, and what remained he used to maintain the life of the monastery; only thus was the Temple of Requital of Kindness preserved.

That winter Master Hanshan went to Tianjie Temple to hear Master Wuji expound the Lotus Sutra. Because he had set his heart on a pilgrimage of study, he kept watching during the lectures for one among the monks whose precepts and practice were both excellent, to be his companion on the road; but a long time passed, and he never found a fellow traveler after his heart.
One day the Master went to the latrine
(the privy)
, and found it spotlessly clean. He thought: this latrine keeper
(the monk in charge of cleaning the latrines)
must be no ordinary man. So he went to the guest quarters to call on him. When he saw him, he was a man jaundiced and swollen, which made him all the more puzzled.

Every morning when the Master rose and went to the latrine, he always found it already swept spotlessly clean, and never knew when the cleaning had been done. Wishing to find out, one evening after the day's practice had ended he walked up and down the corridor, secretly watching the latrine keeper. He saw that by the time the assembly was dismissed, the man had already finished tidying the latrine. Several days later the Master noticed that the latrine was no longer clean and that the keeper did not appear; on inquiring of the monastic officers, he learned that the latrine keeper had fallen ill in the guest quarters. The Master went at once to visit him, and seeing that the illness was grave, asked with concern: “Master, how does your body feel? Are body and mind still at peace?” The latrine keeper answered: “This body is so bound by karmic obstruction that I can scarcely hold up, and the thought of craving food is even harder to bear.” The Master asked him why. He said: “When I see everyone taking their meal, my mind can never let go of the thought of eating.” The Master laughed and said: “That is the hunger of long illness.” From this encounter the Master knew that the man was a genuine practitioner; so he went back and prepared some fruit and cakes to bring to him, and asked him his Dharma name. The latrine keeper replied: “My secular surname is Xu; I am a descendant of Xu Juju of the Spring and Autumn period. My home is in Puzhou, and my Dharma name is now Miaofeng.” The Master at once proposed that they join company and travel on pilgrimage, and Miaofeng gladly agreed, saying to the Master: “If you have this resolve, then on the road I will carry your straw sandals for you, and when we settle on a mountain I will supply you with firewood and water.” Before long Miaofeng recovered; but when the Master went to see him again, he had long since vanished. The Master understood that, his great matter of investigation still unfinished, he feared to be encumbered, and so had slipped quietly away.
[Miaofeng]
The Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan records:
“Master Miaofeng of Puzhou, whose name was Fudeng, went to Nanhai to offer incense on behalf of the Prince of Shanyin. On his way back he passed through Jianye
(Nanjing)
, and as a northerner newly come to the south he was afflicted by dampness and broke out in sores; so he asked at the Tianjie monastery for the post of latrine keeper, as a way to rest.”
, the Master was twenty-two. That year the education authorities issued a proclamation establishing a charity school at the Temple of Requital of Kindness
(a charity school, where poor children studied free of charge)

, for the express training of monks. Master Hanshan was invited to serve as the teacher, and two hundred young monks came to study under him. The Master therefore went back over the writings of the various masters and the hundred schools, the Zuo Commentary, the Records of the Grand Historian, and other works, devoting himself to the work of education. The following year Gaozuo Temple also invited the Master to teach there, and for the two years after that he was engaged to lecture at Jinshan Temple. In all, the four years from his twenty-second to his twenty-fifth year were spent in the bustle of educating monks.

blocks.text: 5. Wandering Afar in Search of Learning

inline.s: In the fifth year of Longqing (

), Master Hanshan was twenty-six. He set out with Dharma Master Xuelang on a study journey to Mount Lu. When they reached Nankang the local people told them that tigers were causing trouble in the mountains and that it was unsafe to climb, so braving wind and snow they made their way to Ji'an and paid their respects at Qingyuan Temple.

The Master saw that Qingyuan Temple had fallen into such decay that it was painful to look at: the monastic rules had long been lost, and the monks had all grown their hair and beards. He was filled with deep lament and resolved to restore the temple. He therefore advised those in charge to select men under forty who were willing to leave home and cultivate, and to ordain them as monks; more than forty were obtained. At the same time he reorganized the monks already in the temple. From then on Qingyuan Temple regained its former state, and a pure and clean Sangha was established.

When summer came, the Master returned from Qingyuan Temple to the Temple of Requital of Kindness to attend to its affairs. By the time he had set everything in order it was already the eleventh month, and only then did he begin preparing to fulfill his vow of traveling far with a single bowl. Dharma Master Xuelang objected, fearing that he could not endure the hardship and cold of a long journey, and urged him first to travel in Zhejiang and Jiangsu, where the climate was mild and there were many beautiful mountains and waters and lovely scenery to enjoy. But the Master held: “The habitual tendencies of us living beings all cling to softness and ease, and delight in scenery that pleases the eye and gladdens the heart. If one wants to end birth and death and cut off afflictions, one must train hard and go where the habits have no room to run wild; only there is it easy to subdue the afflictions and habits. If I merely linger in the regions of Jiangsu and Zhejiang, is that not as close as the mat and pillow? What meaning would that have for cultivation?” Xuelang, however, insisted that he must not go, and pressed him to stay. But Master Hanshan's resolve was fixed, so he deceived Xuelang by saying that he was going into the city, and set out in heavy snow. When Xuelang discovered that the Master had gone and would not return, he wept bitterly for a long time.

The next year the Master came on foot, alone, to Yangzhou. Held up by heavy snow and stricken with illness, he could only stay there for a time. After some days, feeling that his illness had improved, he took up his bowl and went to beg in the marketplace. But when he came to people's doors he could only pace back and forth, unable to call out for alms. The Master wondered what the reason could be. Feeling in his purse, he found that he still had two qian of silver, and he at once examined himself: “So there is still this silver to lean on — that is why I cannot let go.” Just then he saw some monks in the snow begging and getting no food; without hesitation he invited them to an inn, took out all his silver, and ate his fill with them.

The next day the Master went out to beg again. Coming to the door of one or two households, he called out for alms quite naturally, and so received food. He thought to himself with secret joy: “My strength is enough to make light of a minister's stipend of ten thousand bushels.” He therefore had engraved on his bowl the inscription “An Instrument That Makes Light of Ten Thousand Bushels,” and called his patched robe “The Thing That Makes Light of All Under Heaven,” composing an inscription for it as well: “Your form you lend to me, my mind I lend to you; by you this single body is made whole and true, and by you all ten thousand things are counted few. Soon I shall trail these sleeves that catch the long wind's flight, and wear a collar of white cloud light. I rise as soars the swan upon its wing; I rest as hides the dragon in its spring. At ease through all the universe I roam, in mountains and in forests make my home. Why flaunt the scarlet and the purple's glow? I prize alone what frost and snow can never invade.” In this inscription the Master fully expressed his indifferent temper and his lofty, pure aspiration.
In the seventh month of that year the Master arrived in the capital
(Yanjing, present-day Beijing)

, and having nowhere to lodge, he could only beg in the streets from morning to night; yet by dusk he had not obtained a morsel of food. As darkness fell he came to the tea shed at West Taipingcang, and only there received one meal. That night he slept at Yijiao Temple by the river nearby.

Wang Boyu, elder brother of the Master's youthful schoolmate Wang Zhongyan, was at this time Left Vice Minister of War. Hearing that the Master had come to the capital, he invited him to stay at his house for ten days. Afterwards the Master paid his respects to Chan Master Mohe Zhong, and followed Master Zhong to the Western Hills to hear the Miaozong Chao. When the lecture period ended, Master Zhong kept him for the winter, and he received instruction in the Lotus Sutra and the Cheng Weishi Lun; and he asked Dharma Master An to explain hetuvidyā
(one of the five sciences, namely logic)
and its three-membered syllogism.
One day in the eleventh month there came to the Western Hills a man with long hair, wearing a brown robe
(coarse cloth garments, such as the poor and lowly wore in ancient times)

. He stood before the Master's door and first called out loudly: “A salt merchant has come to visit!” Then he walked straight in. As soon as he saw the Master he asked: “Do you still recognize me?” The Master looked him over carefully for a while, and when he saw those bright, piercing eyes he suddenly recalled the monk Miaofeng who had been latrine keeper at Tianjie Temple, and said: “I recognize you.” Miaofeng said wittily: “I have changed my head and face!” The Master answered with humor too: “The original face is still there, at ease as ever!” The two looked at each other and smiled.

The next day Master Miaofeng came to pay his respects. At night the two sat cross-legged and talked heart to heart, and the Master asked him why he was dressed in that way. Master Miaofeng answered: “I am now living at Longhua Temple in Shanyin. Because I have long dwelt among the mountains, my hair and beard have grown and I have no way to cut them. Not long ago the patron Prince of Shanyin was building a temple, and he asked me to obtain a set of the canon; that is why I have come here. What brings you here too?” Master Hanshan said: “First, I came north to look for you; second, I wished to see the capital and call upon the good and wise teachers of the realm, so as to cut off the delusive hope of regretting in days to come that I had not met them.” Master Miaofeng said: “Since we parted, there has not been a moment when I did not think of you, and sometimes I thought we should never meet again. How fortunate that you have come here, and that we have this one meeting,” and so they talked the whole night through. The next morning they parted with a smile.

Master Hanshan then went alone to pay his respects to Master Bianrong. Having entered and made prostration, he respectfully asked Master Bianrong to point out the practice of the one step beyond. Master Bianrong said not a word, only fixing both eyes on him. Then the Master went to pay his respects to Chan Master Xiaoyan. The Chan master asked: “Where have you come from?” The Master answered: “From the south.” The Chan master asked again: “Do you remember the road by which you came?” The Master said: “Once I have passed it, I pay it no more heed!” The Chan master praised him: “Yet your place of coming is clear!” The Master then bowed his head to the feet of Chan Master Xiaoyan
(touching one's head to the feet of a venerable one — the highest gesture of respect in Buddhism)
, and then stood at his side to ask for instruction. Chan Master Xiaoyan gave him a few words of Dharma on the one step beyond.
Wanli
(the reign title of Emperor Shenzong of the Ming, who came to the throne at the age of ten,
— the era name was changed, and the Master was twenty-eight. At this time he thought of going to Mount Wutai to study, and so first sought out a copy of the Record of the Cool and Clear Mountain
(one of the nine gazetteers of Mount Wutai)

, and by the events and locations recorded in it he decided the direction of his ascent. It was the season when the breath of spring first stirred, and the Master climbed the North Terrace first. Because he knew that the surroundings of Hanshan were quiet and secluded, he asked along the way about the route to Hanshan. Guided by the monks' directions he came to Hanshan, and seeing the strangely beautiful colors of the mountain he was overjoyed, and secretly took “Hanshan” as his own style name. The style name “Hanshan,” by which later generations commonly knew him, dates from this. At this time the Master also wrote a poem expressing his resolve to cultivate on Mount Wutai. Two lines of it run: “Zhemo
(that is, do not)
follow others away; here let me still the workings of the mind.”
[Changing the Era Name]
When a sovereign or a dynasty changes the reign title, the first year of each new title is called the ‘prime year.’

The mountain scenery of Hanshan was wonderfully beautiful, but the climate there was bitterly cold, and for the time being he could not settle there to practice; so the Master had to turn back to the capital and set out eastward to study.

blocks.text: 6. First Awakening to Form and Emptiness

inline.s: One day the Master came in his travels to Mount Pan
(northwest of Jixian in Tianjin, an outlying range of the Yan Mountains; a famous mountain east of Beijing, praised as “the first mountain east of the capital”)

, Qianxiang Peak. When he reached the summit of Mount Pan he saw a recluse living beside a rock at the side of the peak, with gray hair and an earth-colored face. The Master went in and bowed to him, but the man did not raise his head, only sitting upright with his mind collected; and when asked anything he did not utter a sound. The Master realized that this recluse was no ordinary man, and so sat down in meditation beside him.

After a while the recluse rose and boiled tea. When the water had boiled he poured himself a cup and drank; seeing this, the Master also poured a cup and drank. When the tea was finished the recluse put the tea things back in their place and, still silent, sat down in meditation again, and the Master did the same. After another while the recluse rose and cooked a meal; when it was ready he filled a bowl and ate by himself, and the Master also filled a bowl and ate with him. After the meal the recluse sat upright as before, and the Master also sat upright. When night came the recluse rose and went outside the rock to walk in meditation, and the Master followed him out and walked too.

The next day the recluse no longer stirred. Following the recluse's times for tea and meals, the Master boiled tea and cooked rice punctually; after the two had eaten they sat in silent investigation as before, and at nightfall they walked together again. Thus they passed seven days in utter silence, until at last the recluse opened his mouth and asked the Master:
Where have you come from?”
From the south.”
What have you come here to do?”
I came especially to visit the recluse.”
The recluse's face is utterly ordinary — what is there that is special?”
I saw through it the moment I stepped in!”
Hearing this the recluse laughed and said: “I have lived here for more than thirty years, and only today have I met a man of the same wind
(a man of like style)
!” So he asked the Master to stay, and the Master, feeling that he had met a man of high attainment from whom he might well learn, stayed on.

One night the Master, as usual, went out before the rock to walk in meditation. In the midst of his walking, suddenly a crash like thunder sounded at the crown of his head. In an instant mountains, rivers, and the great earth, body, mind, and world, were utterly empty. This emptiness was not the “emptiness” of the eye-faculty set over against empty dust, but the state of empty samādhi corresponding to the mind. In this empty samādhi about the time of five inches of incense passed before he slowly became aware of the existence of his body, and slowly felt the solidity of the ground beneath his feet, and opening his eyes slowly saw the mountains and rivers and the great earth again. All the physiological functions of his body returned to what they had been before. His body seemed to be borne up by a wind, light and joyful, and the inner bliss he tasted could not be put into words.

When the Master returned to the cave, the recluse asked him: “You walked in meditation tonight — why did it last so long?” The Master told him one by one the states he had experienced. The recluse gravely warned him: “You are still within the realm of the aggregate of form; that is not your original mind-nature. I have lived here more than thirty years, and except in rain, snow, and wind, every night's walking brings such a state. If you do not dwell upon that state, it will not delude you out of your original mind-nature!” Hearing this, the Master deeply trusted his teaching and bowed in gratitude with great reverence.

Now Master Miaofeng had already obtained the canon, and he asked Wang Boyu where Master Hanshan had gone; Wang Boyu at once sent men up Mount Pan to search. They searched until they came to the cave, and relayed to the Master how urgently Master Miaofeng longed to see him. The Master reflected that he had already stayed long in the cave on Mount Pan, and that he had a prior agreement with Master Miaofeng, so he could not but go. When the Master took his leave of the recluse, neither could bear the parting. The recluse saw him out of the mountain, tears glistening on his face, and accompanied him all the way to the middle of the slope before turning back.

When the Master returned to the capital, Master Miaofeng and Wang Boyu both came out to welcome him. They said to Master Hanshan with a laugh: “Why did you stay so long in the mountains?” The Master then told them the whole story of meeting the recluse in the cave on Mount Pan. When Wang Boyu heard it he said: “Since you have already reached such a state, the matter of dwelling in the mountains may be considered settled!” The Master said: “That is no more than scenery by the roadside; I am still far from the jeweled city!” At this the two looked at each other and burst out laughing.

At that time the capital gathered many eminent men, who were outstanding in virtue and talent and all believers in Buddhism. Such men as the two brothers Wang Fengzhou and Wang Linzhou, the two brothers Wang Boyu and Wang Zhongyan, and Ou Zhenbo of Nanhai were all very famous, and the Master had long admired their virtue and talent.

One day the Master went to visit Wang Fengzhou, who, thinking him young, did not pay him much attention. Seeing how self-important Wang was, the Master too put on a very proud air. Wang instructed him in the method of composing poetry, but the Master merely stared at him with both eyes, and without saying a word got up and left. Wang felt quite put out, and told his younger brother about it. The next day Wang Linzhou came to visit the Master, and the moment they met he said: “Last night my elder brother lost an eye!” The Master said: “Have you an eye, then?” Linzhou clasped his hands in salute and said: “The young fellow has met you face to face!” The two looked at each other and laughed heartily. When Linzhou got home he said to his brother: “Elder brother, you have been worsted by Vimalakīrti.” Later Linzhou wrote a poem to present to the Master, two lines of which read: “We know that Wang Yishao
(Wang Xizhi, whose courtesy name was Yishao)
yielded in metaphysical discourse to Master Zhi
(the eminent Jin-dynasty monk Zhi Dun)

Once, when the Master was together with Wang Zhongyan, who was reading the Zuo Commentary, Wang said to the Master: “You are naturally quick and have great literary talent, and my elder brother is the master craftsman of letters of our day — why do you not study under him, and seek to make a name for yourself as a writer?” The Master laughed and spat, saying: “Keep your elder brother's knees; one day he will bow to this old monk and receive the meaning of the coming from the West
(the essential teaching transmitted by Bodhidharma when he came from the West)

.” Hearing this, Zhongyan was greatly displeased, and when he went back and told Wang Boyu, Boyu said: “I have great faith in him. Looking at his bones of the Way, in time he will enter the inner chambers of Chan Master Dahui and Chan Master Zhongfeng — how could he be willing to be fettered by mere literature? I only fear that his present drifting, superficial wandering in study will ruin the great matter of cultivating the Way!” One day Boyu saw a poem the Master had inscribed on the head of a fan for Zhongyan, and pointing to the two lines “This body and world, a cicada's two wings
tiáo
, the cicada in the ancient books)
, heaven and earth, a horse's single hair,” he said: “Zhongyan, look — how could such a poem have been written by a monk of letters!”

Not long afterwards Wang Boyu prepared a special vegetarian feast to make offerings to Master Hanshan and Master Miaofeng. As they ate they talked, and Boyu said: “The Chan gate is now desolate, with no one to succeed it; this truly deserves our concern, and it is precisely this that weighs on my mind.” Then he said to Master Hanshan: “From your bearing I judge that your future attainment will not be small. Why do you not treasure your time and strive to revive the Chan gate, instead of wandering all over the world?” The Master replied: “This poor monk has come on foot through the world solely for the great matter of birth and death, to call upon good and wise teachers. The reason I now wish to call upon the many great virtuous ones of our time is to cut off the delusive hope of regretting in other days that I had not met them!” Then he added: “I am not wandering idly; I have a purpose, and before long I shall be leaving.” Boyu approved, saying: “I have great faith in what you do. Look at the monks who have left home today — there is not one fit to be your teacher. And but for Master Miaofeng, you would not have found a fellow cultivator to be your Dharma companion.” The Master said: “In the past, amid the assembly at the Dharma gathering, I singled out Master Miaofeng, and at that time we swore an oath to be fellow students; and so I came looking for him, never thinking I should chance upon him here.” Boyu was delighted, and said: “Excellent! If the two of you go to dwell in the mountains and cultivate, I will provide the traveling expenses.”
By this time Master Miaofeng had obtained the canon, and Wang Boyu presented him with the two Kanhe passes; he also wrote an essay and gave it to Master Hanshan.

One day Wang Boyu sent someone to ask the Master to come quickly; the moment they met he said: “Master Miaofeng has already left — why are you still here?” The Master answered: “I thought I would stay a few more days before going.” Boyu was greatly displeased and said: “I know you are unwilling to follow at another's heels, but that is not necessarily right. The ancients were not ashamed of small matters, but ashamed that their merit and name should not be manifest in the world. I hope that in the future you will accomplish a glorious work in the Dharma gate — why, then, weigh such a trifling thing as whether or not to go with another?” The Master was much enlightened by this, thanked him for his good intent, and decided to travel together with Miaofeng. He set out at once to catch up with Miaofeng, and found him already seated in the carriage. Miaofeng asked him: “Brother, are you coming too?” The Master answered: “I am coming too!” and at once climbed into Miaofeng's carriage and departed without taking leave of anyone else.

blocks.text: 7. Harmonizing All Dharmas

inline.s: In the eighth month of autumn, when the sky was high and the air clear, the Master and Miaofeng crossed at Mengjin and viewed the place where King Wu reviewed his troops. Here the Master wrote a poem lamenting the past:
A broken stele and a lonely stone lean on the riverbank; here once he mustered all the lords in ranked array.
The kingly law he established
(the sovereign's guiding order)
should stand as long as heaven and earth, and flow with the Yellow River, unbroken, on and on.
Traveling on to the place where Bo Yi and Shu Qi reined in the horses, the Master wrote another poem lamenting the past:
They cast off throne and glory, their purpose deep and true; only the ancient temple remains, its cypress gloom to view.
So clear the colors of Shouyang Mountain still appear — the very heart that reined the horses in, in that old year.
[Bo Yi and Shu Qi Reining In the Horses]

In the last years of the Shang dynasty, Bo Yi and Shu Qi were sons of the ruler of Guzhu. After the lord of Guzhu died, the two yielded to each other, unwilling to take the throne, and went to King Wen of Zhou. After King Wen died, King Wu sent out his troops to punish the tyrant King Zhou of Shang, carrying King Wen's tablet in the war chariot as he marched. Bo Yi and Shu Qi laid hold of the horses' bridles and remonstrated: “Your father is dead and unburied, yet you take up shields and spears (that is, go to war) — can this be called filial? As a subject you would slay your sovereign — can this be called loyal?” The guards wished to kill them, but Jiang Taigong said: “These are men of righteousness.” So the guards did them no harm, but drove them away. King Wu assembled eight hundred feudal lords at Mengjin, and after crossing the river joined battle with King Zhou's army at Muye. King Zhou was defeated because his troops turned their weapons about in the front ranks, and he burned himself on the Deer Terrace, and the Shang dynasty perished. Bo Yi and Shu Qi, ashamed to eat the grain of Zhou, withdrew to Mount Shouyang, where they gathered wild vetch to eat. A woman said: “You, sirs, in your righteousness will not eat the grain of Zhou — yet this vetch too is a plant of Zhou.” The two, shamed and indignant, refused all food and died, and were buried on Mount Shouyang.

They entered Shaolin Temple on Mount Song and paid homage to the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma. Reaching Luoyang, they saw the Sutra-Burning Terrace, the White Horse Temple, and other sights of the ancient capital.

The two of them reached Hedong in the ninth month. When the Prince of Shanyin heard that the canon was about to arrive, he led the various princes of the imperial clan, with banners, canopies, music, incense, and flowers, to welcome the scriptures into his palace. Miaofeng told the Prince of Shanyin: “The Master Chengyin whom you have been speaking of all this while
(Chengyin was the courtesy name of Master Hanshan)

has now come here as well.” The Prince of Shanyin was overjoyed, and at once asked to see the Master first, and only afterwards attended to the housing of the canon. The Prince kept the Master for the winter, asking him to stay within the prince's residence, where they sat facing each other at all hours, investigating the essential purport of the Surangama Sutra.
At that time the prefect of Shanyin, Lord Chen, was preparing to print the Zhongwu Collected Explanations of the Zhaolun and asked Master Hanshan to collate it. In former days, in the Zhaolun

On the Immutability of Things, the Master had not understood the essential meaning of “a whirlwind topples the mountains”; his doubt about this principle had lasted a long time, and now, reading it again, he still felt bewildered.

[The Whirlwind Topples the Mountains] The passage in the treatise reads: “The whirlwind topples the mountains, yet all is ever still; the rivers race and pour, yet they do not flow; the wild horses toss and drum, yet they do not move; the sun and moon traverse the sky, yet they do not go round.” (Translation: a fierce wind fells the mountains, yet all is ever still; the rivers race and pour, yet they do not flow; the dust tosses and drums, yet it does not move; the sun and moon march through the sky, yet they neither rise nor set.) The phrases in it — “the whirlwind topples the mountains,” “the rivers race and pour,” “the wild horses toss and drum,” “the sun and moon traverse the sky” — are surface appearances (appearances of the world). Yet seen from the true reality of all dharmas, the whirlwind, the rivers, the wild horses, and the sun and moon do not exist at all (originally there is not a single thing); where then could there be any toppling of mountains, racing and pouring, tossing and drumming, or traversing the sky? Therefore it is said: ever still, never flowing, never moving, never going round. (See in full
The True Reality of All Dharmas

, the article.) [Whirlwind] Also called the Pilan wind, rendered as: a great fierce wind. This is the great fierce wind that arises at the time of the kalpa-disaster. [Kalpa-disaster] The three disasters of fire, water, and wind that arise at the end of the kalpa of destruction; these three disasters sweep away the entire world. [The whirlwind topples the mountains] The great fierce wind of the kalpa-disaster blows down Mount Sumeru. [Wild horses] A metaphor for dust. It means that in the season of spring, when the yang energy stirs, one gazes far off at the dust in the marshes and grassy wilds and it seems like galloping horses; hence it is called “wild horses.”

Later, when he read: “The brahmacārin left home to cultivate, and only returned when his hair had turned white. The neighbors saw him and asked: ‘Is the brahmacārin of former days still here?’ The brahmacārin answered: ‘I look like the brahmacārin of former days, but I am not the brahmacārin of former days!’” — he suddenly awakened to the immutability of all dharmas
(all dharmas are from the first neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going)

, and he at once exclaimed with feeling: “This is a truth worthy of deep faith! All things whatsoever, in their essential nature, are from the first without birth or death, without coming or going, but forever abide.” He got down from the meditation couch to pay homage to the Buddha, and though he bowed up and down, no mark of rising or falling could be grasped. He lifted the bamboo blind and stepped out to stand on the terrace, when suddenly a cool wind blew through the leaves of the trees in the courtyard; it was the golden season of autumn, and flying leaves filled the sky, yet in the Master's mind no mark of movement could be grasped either. The Master thought: “This is precisely the state of ‘the whirlwind topples the mountains, yet all is ever still!’” Later, when he urinated and saw no mark of flowing, he thought: “This is like ‘the rivers race and pour, yet they do not flow!’” Thus the mass of doubt about birth and death melted away like ice, and he wrote a verse to express what his mind had understood: “Birth and death, day and night, water runs and flowers fall; today at last I know — the nostrils turn downward, after all”
(it has always been so, and never changed. Chan Master Fanyuan Cong said: “From the first the nostrils hang downward.” The Complete Five Lamps Record)
The next day Master Miaofeng came to see him and asked with delight: “Brother! Have you gained anything in your practice of late?” The Master answered: “In the night I saw two iron oxen by the river
(existence and nonexistence, coming and going, movement and stillness, birth and death)
fighting each other
, and both went into the water
(the two opposites are both extinguished)
, and to this day there is no news of them
(entering the gate of non-duality)
.” Master Miaofeng laughed and said: “Now you have the capital to dwell in the mountains!”
Not long afterwards the Prince of Shanyin invited Chan Master Faguang of Mount Funiu. The Master had long admired Master Faguang by reputation, and the moment they met their conversation

was wholly in accord. The Master then sought his instruction, and Chan Master Faguang expounded the Chan method of investigation — “investigate apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness; study beyond the paths of ordinary and sage” — and the Master grasped its subtle purport deeply. Only then did the Master understand that one who has awakened and clarified the mind-ground speaks words utterly different from ordinary people's, and he admired Chan Master Faguang all the more.

One day Chan Master Faguang found a few poems in the Master's bag, and after reading them said with feeling: “Such subtle and excellent lines — how did you come to write them?” Then he laughed and said: “Good they are, but the one step beyond is still not penetrated!” The Master asked: “Has the Master penetrated that step?” Chan Master Faguang said: “For thirty years I caught dragons and seized tigers; today a rabbit runs out of the grass and gives me a fright.” The Master said: “The Master is no dragon-catching, tiger-seizing hand.” Hearing this, Chan Master Faguang lifted his staff to strike the Master; the Master at once caught hold of the staff, and with his other hand stroked the master's beard, saying: “You speak of a rabbit, but it is a toad
(Master Hanshan's jest, meaning that he himself talks big)
.” The Chan master heard this and went off with a laugh.

Once Chan Master Faguang said to the Master: “You need not go elsewhere; shall we cultivate together on Mount Funiu?” The Master said: “In Dharma and in dialectic I see no gap between you and Chan Master Dahui; but in your daily behavior there seems to be something of the madman — reciting poems and matching couplets, your hand and mouth never resting. What is this about?” The Chan master answered: “This is my Chan sickness. When I first awakened, verses poured from me like a stream, day and night without cease, and I could not control them; afterwards it became this morbid state.” The Master asked again: “How is the Chan sickness to be treated when it first arises?” The Chan master said: “When the Chan sickness first arises, if you cannot see through it yourself, you must find a man of great eye and great skill to give you a sound beating, and then sleep soundly once; when you wake, the Chan sickness is gone. I regret that in those years, when my Chan sickness first arose, I had no clear-eyed expert to point the way, and so it came to this.”

In the first month of the new year the Master was to go to Mount Wutai. When the Chan master learned of it he wrote a poem to present to him, in which were the two lines “The lion in the snow — I ride it here to see you; the hidden dragon in the cave — let it go free.” He asked the Master: “Do you know what they mean?” The Master said: “No.” The Chan master explained: “What the poem means is that you should not clutch a dead snake.” The Master nodded in agreement. For a long time the Chan gate had lacked masters, and only after meeting Chan Master Faguang did the Master come to know what the methods of the school really were.

blocks.text: 8. Realizing the Way at Mount Wutai

inline.s: In the third year of Wanli (

), the Master was thirty. In the first month of that new year he set out from Hedong with Master Miaofeng for Mount Wutai, and only on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, at the year's end, did they climb Mount Wutai. Dharma Master Dafang of the Great Pagoda Temple asked the two masters to choose a place to live at Longmen on the North Terrace; it was the most secluded and precipitous of spots. On the third day of the third month of the following year the Master cleared several old rooms out of the snowdrifts, and he and Master Miaofeng settled there.

Here the Master beheld the ice and snow of ten thousand mountains, cool and radiant, a scene that seemed exactly the realm he had once longed for, and he felt body and mind swept clean, as though he had entered the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Before long, Master Miaofeng set out alone for Yetai, while the Master stayed on at Longmen to continue his practice. Amid the ice and snow he raised a single thought and held it; when people came he did not speak with them, but only glanced at them. As time went on, he saw people as so many wooden stakes, and in the end he could not even recognize written characters.

By early summer, great winds roared and every crevice howled; the ice slowly melted away, and the floodwaters battered the mountain ravines, their racing torrents like crashing thunder. Heard in the stillness, it was as though a thousand armies and ten thousand horses were marching forth. The Master was disturbed by these sounds, and his practice suffered for it. He went to ask Master Miaofeng how one might be undisturbed by surroundings, and Master Miaofeng told him: “States arise from the mind; they do not come from outside. The ancients said: ‘Hear the sound of water for thirty years without turning the root of the mind, and you will realize Avalokiteshvara's perfect penetration.’” When the Master returned, he sat every day on a single-log bridge over a rushing torrent, training himself to “hear the sound of water without turning the root of the mind.” At first, as he sat, the sound of the water was plainly there; after a long while, when a thought stirred he heard the water, and when no thought stirred he did not hear it at all.

One day, as the Master sat in stillness on the single-log bridge, suddenly his body vanished from his awareness and every sound ceased at once. From then on, though the din rolled like thunder, it could never again disturb the stillness of the Master's mind.

The Master's daily food was no more than wheat bran and wild greens boiled into gruel with a little rice. At first someone gave him three pecks of rice, and half a year later there was still some left.

That day, having eaten his gruel, the Master was walking in meditation on a flat stretch of rock when, gathering his mind into oneness, he suddenly stood still: body and mind were gone, and there was only one great treasury of radiant light, perfect, still, and serene, like a great perfect mirror, in which mountains, rivers, and the whole earth all appeared reflected. When he emerged from that samadhi, his wisdom was bright and clear, and he felt that body and mind were utterly ungraspable. At this the Master composed a verse:
One sudden glimpse — the mad mind is stilled; / Within and without, the roots and dust shine clear.
He turns, and shatters the vast void; then, filled / With myriad forms, they rise and disappear.
From then on, body, mind, and world were utterly still and silent, no longer obstructed by sound or form, and the mass of doubt that had gathered before melted away in that instant.
Returning to his hut, he saw that the rice pot was already thick with dust; since he lived alone with no companion and had no one to ask, he did not know how many days had passed.

Dharma Master Xuelang, wishing to find Master Hanshan, visited Shaolin, crossed Funiu, and climbed Longmen on Mount Wutai, where at last he found the Master amid the heaps of ice and snow. He meant to cultivate the Way together with the Master and vowed to share life and death with him. But the Master said to him: “Each person has his own aspiration, and each has his own karmic conditions. Your karmic bond, Dharma-brother, lies in spreading the Buddha Dharma and continuing the Buddha's wisdom-life; you should not end your days in this bleak solitude. In the regions south of the Yangtze, the true Chan method has long lain buried; you ought to succeed to Master Wuji's Dharma seat, shoulder the entrustment, and transform beings below, becoming the eye for gods and men — only then will you not betray the great causal occasion of your leaving the world!” Hearing this, Dharma Master Xuelang found it wholly reasonable, and took his solemn leave of the Master. Later Dharma Master Xuelang took up his staff in the various commanderies of the Three Wu, where for thirty years he spread the Buddha Dharma, surrounded by great assemblies, and from this the lecture seats of the Southeast flourished greatly.
[Found the Master amid heaps of ice and snow] The Chronicle of the Reviver of Caoxi, Venerable Han, says:

“That year the great snow lasted more than ten days, and the snow of every peak was blown and gathered at Longmen, burying the meditation hut more than ten zhang deep. The Master and Master Che sat bolt upright behind closed doors, once a day kindling a fire to warm tea and food. Two or three hundred people from the assemblies of the North Peak, White Horse Temple, and the Central Peak, moved by the aspiration to take up hoes, mattocks, baskets, and brooms, probed with poles down from the peak to find the road to Longmen. Probing as they went and digging as they went, going forward and back again, the great assembly pressed on with courage, and only after two full days of probing with poles did they reach the meditation hut, entering with cheers. They all said: ‘After such a time in the mountains, there is great hardship in getting a fire; this is the protection of the Buddhas and the gods.’ The Master and Master Che thanked them, and then said: ‘Even so, one has to go through it oneself.’ Then they melted snow for soup and joyfully drank with the assembly. The next day, when the other mountains heard that the two Masters were unharmed, those who came bringing rice, flour, fruit, and cakes were so many that there was scarcely room to set foot.”

After his awakening, since there was no one to consult for confirmation, the Master opened the Surangama Sutra to verify it. He had never before heard this sutra expounded, and its meaning was not yet fully clear to him. Now he illumined the text with the state of direct perception; the moment a subtle movement of consciousness arose, he at once became aware of it, and did not let it fall into discriminating thought. Thus eight months passed, and the whole purport of the sutra became utterly clear, free of doubt.
In the third month of spring, Master Lianchi came to Mount Wutai and visited Master Hanshan, staying for more than ten days; night after night they talked heart to heart, in deep accord.

In the seventh month of summer, Hu Shun'an, prefect of Pingyang, who had been transferred to the post of military defense commissioner of Yanping, entered the mountains to visit Master Hanshan. In the meditation hut they ate gruel made of oats and pounded wild greens. At that time the country below the mountain was in fierce heat, and Lord Hu's attendants went to the mountain stream to break off ice and chew it. Seeing this, Lord Hu said: “This is truly another world! Now that I have come here, worldly thoughts in me have grown as cold as this ice.”

In the tenth month of that winter, Master Dafang of the Great Pagoda Temple was falsely accused by a villainous merchant, and it was proposed to sentence him to exile and return to lay life. To save him, Master Hanshan went alone through the heavy mountain snow to Lord Hu Shun'an's residence. Seeing the Master arrive, Lord Hu said with unusual delight: “I was just thinking of going into the mountains, but the heavy snow and bitter cold were too much to bear; I had already written a letter and was about to send someone to fetch you, and here you have come just at the right time — truly the response of sincerity!” The Master then told him of Master Dafang's false accusation, and Hu at once asked that Master Dafang be released; thus the Dharma ground of the Great Pagoda Temple was preserved.

Hu Shun'an kept the Master through the winter, inquiring after the Way morning and evening with great earnestness. The Master instructed him, saying: “He who is meticulous in affairs keeps his mind at a distance; he who is meticulous in mind brings affairs to accomplishment. Hence the more meticulous the affairs, the more distant the mind; the more meticulous the mind, the more accomplished the affairs. One who does not wash his mind has no means of being meticulous; therefore the sage prizes washing the mind and withdrawing to hide in secret.” He further instructed: “The eye contains heaven and earth, yet a speck of dust can rob it of its clarity; the mind encompasses the vast void, yet a single thought can block its breadth. Know therefore that a single thought is the root of birth and death and the source of calamity and misfortune; hence one who knows the subtle and perceives the incipient — in him the sage keeps watch.” And again he instructed: “When a thought has an object, objects exist; when the mind is empty, dharmas are empty. Therefore if a thought is melted into emptiness, one is at ease in every circumstance; if the mind is like a perfect mirror, coming and going are ever at leisure. One who excels in this need not leave the ordinary, yet dwells upright in the wondrous realm.” Thus the Master spoke as it came from his mouth, and after a month Hu Shun'an had recorded it into a volume, calling it the Introductory Words of Hanshan, and at once had it printed and circulated.

At that time there was a Lord Gao, who held the title of kaifu and had moved to reside in the Zhen-Dai commandery. Hearing that Master Hanshan was staying at Lord Hu's residence, he went to Lord Hu and said: “My family's garden pavilions, though already celebrated in many poems, would now have one more verse from a man of high attainment; would you ask Master Hanshan to inscribe one?” Lord Hu agreed to ask the Master.
