But when he relayed Lord Gao's request for a poem, the Master refused, saying: “There is not a single word in my breast — how could I compose poetry?” Lord Gao pressed Lord Hu again and again, and Hu, unable to decline, could only beg the Master earnestly, even bringing out many collections of famous ancient poems and laying them on the Master's desk, hoping thereby to stir his literary thought. The Master happened to open a poetry collection, and just as he was about to ponder, a sudden inspiration came and verses arrived swiftly. By the time Lord Hu returned from the hall, he had already written out twenty or thirty poems. The Master suddenly realized: “This is nothing but the habit-demon of letters and words!” He at once stopped his brush, casually took one poem to satisfy Lord Hu, and thought no more of poetry. Yet now his literary thought could not be controlled at all; unwittingly, all the poetry, books, lyrics, and rhapsodies he had studied in the past, whatever had ever passed before his eyes, came surging up together, pressing and filling the whole vast void, so that even with a mouth on every part of his body he could not recite it all — he did not even know what body and mind were. The Master silently looked within and examined himself, and it seemed to him that he was about to float upward, and he did not know how he would pass through this barrier.

The next day, after Lord Hu had seen Lord Gao off, the Master sat in stillness alone, thinking: “What has now arisen in me is precisely the Chan sickness that Chan Master Faguang spoke of — but who is there to cure it for me?” Then he thought again: “There is no other way; I must rely on sleep to dispel this Chan sickness. If I can sleep soundly, that will be a great blessing!” The Master shut his door and forced himself to sleep. At first he could not sleep at all; after persevering for a time, he suddenly sat in self-forgetfulness, as though asleep.
At the meal hour, the boy came and knocked at the door, but could not get it open no matter how he knocked; he struck it with a wooden mallet, and still there was no answer from within.

After Lord Hu returned, he asked why the Master had still not come out, and the boy told him that the Master had been in his room for five days. Hu had the window broken open and went in, and saw the Master sitting upright on the bed in his patched robe; he did not answer when called, nor could he be moved when pushed. Lord Hu suddenly recalled a past matter: there was a Buddha hall in his study, and on the offering table lay a striker; he had once raised the striker and asked the Master, “What use is this thing?” The Master had said, “When a monk of the Western Regions enters samadhi and cannot come out, one strike of this brings him out.” Lord Hu now thought: “The Master has perhaps entered samadhi.” He at once took the striker and sounded it by the Master's ear several dozen times, and only then did the Master slowly wake; he opened his eyes and did not know where he was. Lord Hu said: “After I went out to see off my guest, you closed the door and sat, and it is five days now; how have you passed these five days?” The Master said: “I do not know; it seemed only a moment.” Having said this, he again silently contemplated with close attention, and to his astonishment did not know what place this was, nor from where he had come; and looking back on those years of dwelling in the mountains, and on all his former journeys on pilgrimage, they were as unreal and insubstantial as a dream, ungraspable when sought. The mind that had formerly been disturbed by the one-sided view of emptiness and the notion of self now dispersed like rain ceasing and clouds scattering; the vast sky was as if washed clean, and every shadow was swept away without trace. Mind empty and surroundings still — the wonder of it truly cannot be described. The Master then thought: “The Surangama Sutra says: ‘When purity is complete, light shines through; still and illumining, it embraces the void. Then one turns to look upon the world, and it is like things seen in a dream.’ The Buddha's words truly do not deceive!”

The Master prepared to return to Mount Wutai in the first month of the new year, and said to Lord Hu: “The forests of Mount Wutai have been greatly felled by villainous merchants; the Dharma ground of Bodhisattva Manjushri is about to become a barren mountain.” Hu accordingly wrote out a memorial and petitioned his superiors for a strict ban on felling. From then on, whenever monasteries and Dharma temples were built at Mount Wutai, they all relied on the timber preserved by this great ban; otherwise there would have been no wood to be had.

blocks.text: 9. Writing the Sutras in Blood

inline.s: In the fifth year of Wanli (

), the Master was thirty-two. Winter departed and spring came, a hundred flowers vied in beauty; the Master left Lord Hu's residence, and all along the way, treading the tender green grass, returned to Longmen on Mount Wutai. As he stood on the stone cliff at Longmen and looked around at the towering mountain scene still locked in ice, a vast expanse of white snow, it seemed that the world of men was to be sealed forever in bitter cold. The Master gazed and gazed, and his heart could not but turn from that thoroughly awakened mind-nature back to his dreamlike yet strangely vivid childhood, reliving the days and nights spent with his parents; and gratitude rose in his heart: “Had it not been for my parents' deliberate nurturing, and above all my mother's shaping influence, how could I have awakened the mind-nature as I have today? My honored parents! How are you now? How I long to repay your boundless kindness!”

Even as the Master yearned over his parents' kindness, he looked back on all that had befallen him since leaving home, and saw that although he had awakened, there still lay before him, on the road toward the treasure city, countless hardships and perils; where should he begin to walk from here?

One day, having read Master Huisi of Nanyue's vow-text, whose lofty aspiration and earnest words plucked the bodhi-string in the Master's heart, he thought: Yes! After awakening, one should perform Buddha-work far and wide, benefit all beings, and complete the great enterprise of the Dharma — awakening oneself and awakening others! The Master decided that the first step would be to prick his own blood, mix it with gold, and write out one copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra, thus forming above a supreme karmic bond with prajna, and below repaying the profound kindness and great virtue of his parents and all sentient beings.

[Writing out one copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood mixed with gold] He drew the fresh blood from his tongue, mixed it with gold powder, and wrote out one copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra. Master Yinguang said: “When Master Hanshan wrote out sutras, it was the Empress Dowager who supplied the paper and the gold. For writing in gold, the paper must be blue for the characters to show; on white paper they do not appear.
Thus Hanshan, at Miaode Hermitage on Mount Wutai, pricked blood from his tongue, ground it with gold, and wrote the Avatamsaka Sutra.” (From Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
Reply to Master Hongyi, Letter One)

The Empress Dowager Cisheng, principal mother of Emperor Shenzong of the Ming, was a most devout Buddhist. She delighted in good works and generosity, and the people of the capital called her the Old Buddha Lady. One day she selected eminent monks from all over the realm and convened a sutra-chanting assembly to pray for the peace of the nation and the happiness of the people. The Master was among them. When the Empress Dowager learned that the Master intended to prick his blood, mix it with gold, and write out a copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra, she graciously bestowed gold and paper upon him.

In the fourth month of the following year, the Master began to write the sutra. However large or small the dots and strokes, with every stroke he set down he recited the Buddha's name once. Monks and laypeople who came to the mountain and reached Miaode Hermitage on Mount Wutai all insisted on seeing the Master and asking him to instruct them in the Dharma. And though the Master's hand never ceased copying, he still did not fail in his responses. Everyone who came to ask for instruction, he would speak a few words with. As for men of high attainment and old friends, the Master respectfully invited them to sit on the meditation couch and discussed the Dharma with them, while never hindering the copying in his hand. Day after day the Master wrote in this way, and though people came and went, in his mind not the slightest trace of movement could be found.

When the elders of the neighboring literary circles heard of the Master's state, they were all astonished and could hardly believe it. One day the elders brought many of their disciples to the Master's meditation hut, wanting to confirm just what was going on. Beside the Master they deliberately used every means to disturb him; then, when he had finished a section, they compared it with the original text, and truly there was not the slightest error. Only then were they convinced that the Master's attainment was far from ordinary. Yet they were greatly puzzled, and went to ask Master Miaofeng: “How can Master Hanshan use his mind for many things at once?” Master Miaofeng answered: “My Dharma-brother's Buddha-recitation samadhi has reached a wondrous realm!” At that time Master Miaofeng too was at the North Peak, pricking his blood and mixing it with gold to write out the Avatamsaka Sutra.
[Editor's Note] The relevant original text is transcribed below:
Master Hanshan's Dream-Wanderings Collection
, Autobiographical Chronicle, says:
“In the sixth year
(the sixth year of Wanli)
, wuyin, I was thirty-three. I applied my mind with single purpose
(with undivided attention)

to writing out the sutras. No matter how large or small the dots and strokes, with every stroke I set down I recited the Buddha's name once. When monks and laypeople came from their wanderings in the mountains, I always had an attendant announce and explain. Though my hand never stopped writing, I never failed to respond. To all who came to inquire, I always spoke a few words. Men of high attainment and old friends I would invite to sit on the meditation couch; as we talked I did not fail them, nor did it hinder my writing. Copying against the original, I made no errors or omissions either. Each day was as usual, without the slightest appearance of disturbance or stillness. The elders of the neighboring places secretly thought it strange, and led a number of their followers to test me, deliberately creating disturbances. When I had finished writing, they read it, and were fully convinced. Then they asked Master Miaofeng: ‘How can Master Yin do such a thing?’ Master Miaofeng said: ‘My friend has entered this samadhi’
(Buddha-recitation samadhi)
and is utterly proficient in it.’”
Master Hanshan's Dream-Wanderings Collection
, A Letter to the Chan Monk Xingchu Yuan on Sutra-Writing, says:
“This old man
(Master Hanshan's self-reference)

once dwelt at Mount Wutai, where I pricked my blood and mixed it with gold to write out the great sutra Avatamsaka. In all my writing, regardless of the dots and strokes of the characters, their size and length, at every stroke I set down I recited the Buddha's name once. Thus dot after dot, stroke after stroke, the light of mind streamed forth, thought after thought unbroken and unforgotten, without error or omission. After a long time, it no longer mattered whether I was writing or not writing; even in dreams and sleep it all became one piece. From this, through all states, however tumultuous and clamorous, the mind remained utterly still, and I attained the gate of liberation, sovereign and unobstructed in every state; until all that is seen and heard was nothing but the true sutra appearing before me.”

blocks.text: 10. Three Extraordinary Dreams

inline.s: During the whole period from when the Master first dwelt at Longmen on Mount Wutai until he finished writing out the Avatamsaka Sutra, he had three extraordinary dreams. They are of great help in understanding the Master's stage of practice and realization during this period.

The first: he dreamed he entered the Vajra Grotto. Beside the Great Prajna Temple there were two stone doors; the Master walked through them and looked: within, it was vast and boundless, with tier upon tier of halls, towers, and pavilions, majestic beyond all description. In the center of the main hall was set a great couch, on which National Teacher Qingliang reclined, while Master Miaofeng stood in attendance on the left. At the sight of the National Teacher, Master Hanshan hastened forward to bow, then stood in attendance on the right, listening as National Teacher Qingliang expounded the state of the perfect and interfused contemplation of the Dharma-realm at first entry: the mutual entry of Buddha-lands, the interplay of host and companion, the mark of coming and going without movement. As the National Teacher expounded, the corresponding states appeared before the Master's eyes, and he felt body and mind interflow and merge. When the National Teacher had finished, Miaofeng asked: “What state is this?” The National Teacher smiled and said: “The state of no state.” When Master Hanshan awoke, he saw for himself that mind and state were fused and transparent, and he had no doubt or obstruction left.

The second: the Master dreamed that he rose into the sky; when he had risen to the boundless heights, he gradually drifted down again, and saw all around him only emptiness, hollow and void, without a single thing. Below the void lay the earth, round and smooth and bright like a mirror, as clear and translucent as crystal glass. Gazing far off, in the infinite sky there appeared a tower and pavilion of incomparable vastness, spreading over heaven and covering the earth, majestic and magnificent. Within the tower and pavilion appeared all the comings and goings of human affairs in the world, and even the meanest and most sordid doings of the marketplace were contained within it. In the center of the tower and pavilion was set a jeweled throne of purple-gold flame color. The Master thought: “This must be the Vajra Throne.” The Master delighted greatly in this majestic, wondrous, inconceivable tower and pavilion, and wished to draw near; but in the blink of an eye he thought again: “Why, in this cool and pure world, should there be such foul things?” No sooner had the thought arisen than the tower and pavilion receded far away. The Master thought again: “All states, pure and impure alike, arise from my own mind.” Pondering the principle that the ten thousand dharmas arise from the mind, the tower and pavilion drew near again. In a moment he saw before the Vajra Throne many monks of tall stature and incomparably dignified appearance standing in attendance. Then suddenly a bhikshu came out from behind the Vajra Throne, holding a scroll of scripture in both hands, and walked straight up to the Master, saying: “The Master sends me to give you this scroll of scripture.” The Master took it and looked: it was entirely in golden Sanskrit letters, and he could not recognize a single one. Having put the scripture away, he asked the bhikshu: “Who is the Master?” The bhikshu replied: “He is Bodhisattva Maitreya.” Hearing this the Master was overjoyed and at once followed the bhikshu to the foot of the steps, where he closed his eyes and gathered his thoughts and stood.

After a moment he suddenly heard the sound of a chime being struck; the Master opened his eyes and saw that Bodhisattva Maitreya had already ascended the seat. The Master then reverently gazed up and bowed before the Bodhisattva, and saw that Maitreya's countenance shone with the radiance of true purple-gold, more magnificent than anything in the world. After bowing, the Master thought: “Today the Bodhisattva has ascended the seat especially to speak the Dharma for me, so I must be the one who fits the occasion.” Then the Master knelt long with palms joined and took out the scroll of scripture and opened it. The Bodhisattva Maitreya then taught: “Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Depending on consciousness, one is defiled; depending on wisdom, one is pure. Defilement has birth and death; purity has no Buddhas.” When the Master heard this, body and mind suddenly became utterly empty, and he felt only that the sound came distinctly out of emptiness. When the Master woke, the sound of the Bodhisattva's teaching was still echoing by his ear. From then on the difference between “consciousness” and “wisdom” was completely clear to him. And he knew that the place he had reached in the dream was Bodhisattva Maitreya's inner court of Tushita Heaven.

The third: the Master dreamed that a monk came and told him: “Bodhisattva Manjushri has set up a bathhouse on the summit of the North Peak; he asks you to come and bathe.” The Master followed him to the North Peak summit and entered a vast, pure hall, within which a rare fragrance drifted. The attendants here were all monks from India, and they led the Master to the bathing pool. As the Master was about to undo his clothes and enter the water, he saw that a woman was already bathing in the pool, and a sudden disgust rose in his mind, and he no longer wished to enter. Then the person in the pool, seeing the Master's disgust and his refusal to enter, deliberately exposed her body, and only then did the Master realize that the bather was in fact a man. The Master then entered the pool and bathed with him. The person in the pool used his hand
to scoop
hù
water

and washed the Master; the water poured down over his head and soaked straight into his five viscera, as though he were washing a barrel of meat. Each of the five viscera was washed through, and only a single skin remained, like a crystal cage, utterly transparent.

After a while, the person in the pool told him to drink tea. A monk from India raised aloft half a skull, like a watermelon cut in two; the Master looked closely and saw that it was filled with human brains, with fresh blood dripping. The Master felt great disgust at the skull, but the Indian monk dug out a piece of the brains with his finger and asked the Master: “Is this impure?” Then he put it in his mouth and ate it. Thus, eating and digging it out at the same time, he ate with keen relish. When the brains were all eaten, only some blood and water remained inside. Then the person in the pool said: “He may be allowed to drink it.” The Indian monk handed the skull to the Master, and the Master drank a mouthful; it tasted truly like sweet dew, and the blood and water he swallowed ran out crosswise from every pore of his body. When the blood and water were finished, the Indian monk came and rubbed the Master's back, and gave a great slap on his back, and the Master woke at once. His whole body was streaming with sweat like water, his five viscera were transparent, with no obstruction. After this dream, his body and mind were bright and pure, light and at ease beyond all description.

Besides these three extraordinary dreams, the Master had many auspicious dreams during this period, all of them dealings with Buddhas and bodhisattvas. So he said with deep feeling: “The Buddha said, ‘Such good dreams are common’ — how truly so!”
[Such good dreams are common] The Buddha said:
“All Buddhas' bodies are golden of hue, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings. Hearing the Dharma and speaking it for others, such good dreams are common.”
(Lotus Sutra)

blocks.text: 11. The Unrestricted Assembly

inline.s: In the ninth year of Wanli (

), Master Hanshan was thirty-six. He and Master Miaofeng, having completed the writing of the sutras, took counsel together to establish a perfect Dharma ground to be called the Unrestricted Assembly. Master Miaofeng set about soliciting funds and grain, and prepared to go to the capital to invite five hundred greatly virtuous and renowned monks to take part. Just as the arrangements for the assembly were initially complete, it happened that Emperor Shenzong issued an edict to pray for an imperial heir, sending eunuch envoys to Mount Wudang to seek Daoist priests, while the Empress Dowager Li sent eunuch envoys to Mount Wutai to seek monks.
[The Unrestricted Assembly]

This kind of assembly offered universal and equal support: like the present-day meal offering to a thousand monks, forming a bond with ten thousand people, anyone at all might take part, with no restriction or exclusion.

In this matter Master Hanshan held that all Buddha-works performed by monks are nothing other than for the peace of the nation and the happiness of the people. Now the Empress Dowager was praying to Buddhism for an imperial heir — a matter concerning the future of the nation and its people, and therefore of the utmost importance as well. The Master wished all the arrangements of the Unrestricted Assembly to be merged into the single purpose of praying for an imperial heir, and that no thought be given to mere personal reputation. Master Miaofeng and the eunuch envoys both objected, and the Master insisted on contending with them; by this he offended the eunuch envoys, and some also wished to seize the chance to slander him and ruin the Dharma ground. Yet the Master's resolve to pray for an heir to the throne on the nation's behalf left him unharmed throughout.

[Master Miaofeng and the eunuch envoys both objected] Master Miaofeng objected because he held that the perfect Dharma ground of writing sutras in blood and the praying for an imperial heir were two different matters and should not be jumbled together. The eunuch envoys, however, knew the inside story of the prayer for an heir: the Emperor (Shenzong), a devout Daoist, sent eunuch envoys to Mount Wudang to ask Daoist priests to pray for an heir, so that his beloved Consort Zheng might bear a son; while the Empress Dowager Li, a devout Buddhist, sent eunuch envoys to Mount Wutai to ask monks to pray for an heir, so that Consort Wang the Talented might bear a son. The eunuch envoys sent by the Empress Dowager Li had spied out the imperial will and wished secretly to sabotage the prayer for an heir at Mount Wutai, and therefore firmly opposed praying for an heir at the Unrestricted Assembly. Master Hanshan fought for it and succeeded in praying for an imperial heir at the Unrestricted Assembly, which not only enraged the eunuch envoys, conspicuous in power, but also planted the seed of disaster that later drew him into the “contention over the imperial heir.”
[The contention over the imperial heir]

In the reign of Emperor Shenzong of the Ming, the “contention over the imperial heir” was the greatest affair of the age, and Patriarch Hanshan and Master Daguan were both implicated in it. The matter may be briefly told as follows: the birth mother of Zhu Changluo, Shenzong's eldest son, was Consort Wang the Respectful, originally an ordinary palace maid who served the Empress Dowager Cisheng (Shenzong's birth mother) in the Palace of Compassionate Tranquility. One day Shenzong came to the Palace of Compassionate Tranquility to pay his respects to his mother; the Empress Dowager happened to be absent, and Shenzong noticed the fresh and lovely Wang, and privately favored her, and Wang conceived. The Empress Dowager Cisheng was herself of palace-maid origin, and when she learned of this she not only did not make things hard for Wang, but summoned Shenzong in great delight and questioned him about it. Yet Shenzong flatly denied ever having favored Wang. But the emperor's daily life was recorded by special attendants, and Shenzong's favoring of Wang had long since been entered in the Inner Diary of Daily Life. In the end Shenzong had no way to deny it, and blushing, tacitly admitted it. In the eighth month of the tenth year of Wanli (

), Consort Wang the Respectful gave birth to Shenzong's first son, Zhu Changluo. Although the palace woman Wang was established as Consort the Respectful, the eldest imperial son Zhu Changluo was never established as heir apparent. Four years later, in the first month of the fourteenth year of Wanli, Consort Zheng, whose favor eclipsed the whole palace, gave birth to a son, named Zhu Changxun. Consort Zheng was clever and quick-witted, and Shenzong's affection for her was deep and true, lasting all his life. Because the emperor followed her every word, for a very long time she was the figure on whom court and country fixed their eyes, and she drew the curses of nearly everyone. Since Shenzong's empress had no son, and Consort Zheng was the emperor's favorite, as soon as she bore a son Shenzong at once elevated her to the rank of Imperial Consort. The Grand Secretary Shen Shixing and others held that the eldest imperial son Zhu Changluo was already five years old, that his birth mother Consort Wang the Respectful had never been granted any promotion, and that Consort Zheng, having just borne a prince, had at once been raised and enfeoffed — plainly showing that Consort Zheng monopolized the emperor's favor. The ministers feared that in time the elder might be set aside and the younger established, and so submitted memorials requesting the installation of the Eastern Palace. But Shenzong, urged on by Consort Zheng, wished always to seize the occasion to establish Zhu Changxun as heir apparent, and so devised every kind of means to delay, and met with the strongest opposition from the ministers. At that time the heir apparent was also called the foundation of the state, and therefore this struggle between emperor and ministers was also called the “dispute over the foundation of the state.” The ministers strove with all their might to have Zhu Changluo established as heir apparent, while Shenzong delayed again and again; so the ministers contended again and again, and this went on for fifteen years, stirring up a storm throughout the city and making the palace struggle intricate and tangled. Only in the twenty-ninth year of Wanli (
), when Shenzong had no choice, did he establish the eldest imperial son Zhu Changluo, then already twenty by nominal age, as heir apparent. In the eleventh month of the thirty-first year of Wanli (

), someone wrote a piece entitled A Continued Discussion of Anxiety and Danger, which was spread widely in the capital as a handbill, so that overnight it was everywhere from the palace gates above to the streets and lanes below. The piece said that Shenzong had been forced to establish Changluo as heir apparent, that the position of heir apparent was in peril, and it roundly criticized the chief grand secretary Shen Yiguan and the Grand Secretary Zhu Geng. When Shenzong learned of it he was greatly enraged and ordered the Eastern Depot, the Embroidered-Uniform Guard, and the patrol offices of the five wards to arrest the culprits at once, “and to be sure to get the name of the one who wrote the book”; thus began the “Seditions Book case.” Thereupon Shen Yiguan, of the Zhejiang faction, seized the chance to falsely accuse Guo Zhengyu, Shen Li, and other members of the Donglin faction. Master Daguan was likewise falsely implicated in connection with the seditious book and was arrested and imprisoned, and after severe torture was sentenced to death.

Not long before, the Empress Dowager Li, wishing to offer sacrifice to the former emperors and to protect the reigning emperor, had sent eunuch envoys with three thousand workmen to Mount Wutai to build pagodas and temples. The Master feared that, on the court's first undertaking of Buddha-works at Mount Wutai, the construction might not be completed, to the detriment of the Dharma gate, and so he did all he could to assist in coordinating it, until the following year when the pagoda court was completed. The Master placed the Avatamsaka Sutra written in blood and gold upon the pagoda, and wrote a vow-text to be enshrined in the pagoda.

By this time Master Miaofeng had already gone to the capital, and Master Hanshan solicited funds alone. First he had made a revolving sutra repository of the Avatamsaka Dharma-realm, for the use of the Dharma ground, and prepared offering implements, vegetarian provisions, and everything else required. For ninety days and nights the Master hurried to and fro, and at last completed all the affairs of the Dharma ground. When the tenth month drew near, Master Miaofeng led the more than five hundred greatly virtuous and eminent monks he had invited, and they all assembled in the mountains; with the people of the mountain itself, the number came to a thousand. The bedding and covers and offering implements, the tea and food for these thousand people at their retreat, were under the Master's direction orderly and complete, everything ready to hand. The assembly was astonished at the Master's ability.

In the first seven days and nights of the assembly, affairs were extraordinarily busy, yet the Master ate not a grain of rice, taking only a little boiled water, and still attended to every kind of business as usual.

In the Buddha hall, five hundred tables of vegetarian food were offered daily to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, day after day without fail, in perfect order; the assembly did not know where so many offerings came from. Some thought they were transported by divine power, but only the Master knew that this was the blessing of Buddha-power.
When the seven days and nights of the Unrestricted Assembly had ended and its merit was complete, the Master, in the following year (the tenth year of Wanli,

), again expounded the Huayan Xuantan at the Great Pagoda Temple on Mount Wutai. During the hundred days of the lecture period, the monks and laypeople of the ten directions who gathered daily at the Great Pagoda Temple numbered no fewer than ten thousand; yet under the Master's direction they ate their one vegetarian meal as though sitting a single period of meditation, in perfect order and utter quiet, with not the least sound of summoning or knocking to be heard.

After the assembly ended, an inventory was made of the money and grain remaining in the storehouse, amounting to some ten thousand in all; the Master sealed it all up and handed it over entirely to the Great Pagoda Temple, then departed lightly with Master Miaofeng.
In the eighth month of that year, Consort Wang the Talented gave birth to the eldest imperial son.

The Master had spent his energies to excess on these two great assemblies, and when the lecture period ended he fell ill. Master Miaofeng went alone to Mount Luya. Because his body was ailing, the Master went to Zhangshiyan in Zhending to recuperate. There he wrote a poem, of which two lines read: “Sheer cliffs propped against the sky must balk the stone; / A broken crag, no road — only a flying ladder.”

After the Master had somewhat recovered, he went again to Zhongfeng Temple in the west of the capital, where he composed a preface, the “Preface to the Engraving of the Zhongfeng Record.” In the winter he closed himself in a stone room and took a water-fasting retreat.

blocks.text: 12. Taking Refuge at Mount Lao

inline.s: Having passed through these two great Dharma assemblies at Mount Wutai, together with the timely birth of the eldest imperial son, Master Hanshan's fame filled the world; and his uprightness and unyielding courage in daring to offend the powerful eunuch envoys and strive against them was also known far and near, and spread into the capital and the palace. The ancients said: “Beneath a great name it is hard to dwell long.” Therefore the Master resolved to avoid the empty reputation of Mount Wutai and to take the path of dwelling in seclusion and practicing in secret.
[Master Hanshan's fame filled the world] With the timely birth of the eldest imperial son, the people called the Master the “imperial maternal uncle.” The Collection of Dream Wanderings
in the Autobiographical Chronological Account records:
“In the thirty-fourth year of the Wanli era
, bingwu, when I was sixty-one.
The Grand Minister Zhang, Lord Hongyang,
gathered together his sons and prepared a feast
(a feast of welcome for Master Hanshan)

at the Idle Cloud Tower by the river. In the midst of the gathering the Lord said: “Everyone knows that Master Han is a great good teacher; they do not know how great is the hidden merit he has done for the altars of state.” Those present were startled and asked the Lord about it, and the Lord told its outline
(the same as “outline”)
, and the whole gathering changed countenance
(those present were all deeply moved)
[Beneath a great name it is hard to dwell long]
The Chronicle of Master Hanshan's Life says:
“Knowing the cause of his great fame at Mount Tai
(Mount Wutai)

: because at that time the unhindered Way-place had been too grand, and the fame of having prayed for an heir and obtained an heir for the imperial household was too conspicuous, and the words that had offended the eunuch envoys had reached within the court; the matter was all the greater and the name all the more unendurable. Therefore he could not return to Mount Tai, and could not settle on another mountain, and so went far off to the Eastern Sea and hid his traces at Mount Lao.”
Previously the Master had read the Avatamsaka Commentary

in the “Chapter on the Abodes of the Bodhisattvas,” which says: “In the Eastern Sea there is a place called the Naluoyan grotto, where from ancient times the hosts of bodhisattvas have dwelt.” The National Master Qingliang explained: “The Sanskrit word naluoyan means firm and strong, and that is Mount Lao in the Eastern Sea.” From that time on the Master had always admired Mount Lao. Now the Master began to realize his wish to go to Mount Lao; he crossed the Eastern Sea to seek out Mount Lao, and began to use the name “Hanshan,” the style-name he had long since chosen.
In the spring of the eleventh year of the Wanli era

, the Master was thirty-eight. Having ended the water-fasting (a dwelling by the water) life, he left Mount Wutai and went to Mount Lao. There he found the Naluoyan grotto, but as it could not be inhabited, he went on to search for a more deeply hidden place. On the south face of the mountain he found a quiet and lovely spot that leaned upon a hundred ranges behind and faced the great ocean before. The scenery here was magnificent and wondrous beyond compare, giving the feeling of a fairy realm far from the smoke of the human world.

Here there had originally been a Avalokiteshvara chapel, but having suffered the calamities of history it had long since become a ruin. The Master spread a mat beneath a tree and sat in the open air for seven months. Later a local man
(a person whose family had lived here for generations)

, the layman Zhang Daxin, seeing the Master practicing diligently and hard in the open air, built him a thatched hut. After the Master settled in, no one came and went anymore, and so he felt very content.

In the autumn of the following year, because the Empress Dowager Li had obtained the eldest imperial son through the unhindered Way-place at Mount Wutai where she had prayed for an heir, she sought out the three masters who had presided over the matter. Master Dafang and Master Miaofeng had both already received the imperial benefaction
(the bestowal of the emperor's favor)

, but Master Hanshan alone could not be found. The Empress Dowager was determined to find the Master, so she ordered the abbot of Longhua Temple, Master Duan'an, to seek him. Master Duan'an, knowing already that the Master was at Mount Lao, took a boat to call on him. When he found the Master and, in the thatched hut, told him of the Empress Dowager's regard, the Master declined with thanks, saying: “If I could but enjoy the gracious kindness of the Empress Dowager and be allowed to dwell quietly here amidst these seas and mountains, that would already be a great bestowal — why need there be any other gift?” Hearing this, Master Duan'an could only return to report.

Hearing Master Duan'an's words, the Empress Dowager was still uneasy at heart, so she built a temple in the Western Hills of the capital and sent a eunuch envoy to insist that the Master come; but the Master was resolved to dwell in the mountains. Having no way to make him, and knowing of his thatched hut, the Empress Dowager took out three thousand pieces of gold and sent a eunuch envoy to have a house built. The Master did his utmost to stop it, saying: “With these few rooms of thatch I am already happy enough; why should I build other houses?” The Master would not accept a single coin, putting the eunuch envoy in a very difficult position, for he feared he could not report back when he returned. Seeing his difficulty, the Master thought: “The ancients had the case of forging an edict to relieve famine. Now the eastern quarter of Mount Lao is exactly in a year of scarcity; why should I not spread the loving-kindness of the Holy Mother and rescue the starving people?” So he had the eunuch envoy distribute the three thousand pieces of gold widely among the monks, the solitary and elderly, and the prisoners of the various prefectures, to relieve the famine. The responsible offices of each place recorded every bit of the distributed gold in a register, and the eunuch envoy brought these back to the palace to report to the Empress Dowager. Hearing that the Master had used this three thousand pieces of gold to relieve those in distress, the Empress Dowager was delighted and sighed with approval again and again.

The people near Mount Lao had never known of the jewel of the Sangha or of the right Dharma of Buddhism. Among the places the Master dwelt, the Huang clan was the most populous; seeing the Master's diligent and vigorous practice, they admired him greatly at heart, and gradually drew near to him. Through the Master's earnest effort in gathering and transforming them, the followers of Luo Qing there and the teachers of the heterodox sects all in turn led their disciples to take refuge in the Master, and gradually they came to understand the meaning of genuine Buddhist practice.
[Luo Qing (

)] Style name Menghong, sobriquets Sifu and Wuwei, a man of Jimo in Shandong, leader of a religious movement in the Ming dynasty. His later disciples called him the Patriarch Luo, also called “the Old Ancestor of Non-Action.” The religion he founded was commonly called the Luo religion, also known as the Luo Dao religion, the Luo Patriarch religion, and the Non-Action religion. Once the Luo religion appeared, almost all the folk religions were influenced by it, including the famous Vegetarian religion and the White Lotus religion; and later folk societies such as the Green Gang also honored him as their patriarch.
In the fourteenth year of the Wanli era

, the Master was forty-one. The Shenzong emperor issued an edict bestowing fifteen sets of the canon, to be distributed to the famous mountains of the world. First, four sets were placed at the four border regions, namely Mount Lao of the Eastern Sea, Mount Putuo of the Southern Sea, Mount Emei of the Western Shu, and Mount Luya on the northern frontier
(in the depths of Mount Guancen, thirty

kilometers southwest of the county seat of Ningwu in Shanxi province; there a hundred mountains stand in ranks and layered peaks rise one on another, with sheer cliffs and precipices, blue waters and the roar of pines — its main peak above all being of singular beauty, with jagged strange stones, tall and towering, dominating the northern regions)

. The Empress Dowager Li sent people to carry the canon to Mount Lao in the Eastern Sea. Because the Master had not known of it beforehand, when the canon arrived there was no place to house it. Seeing this, the local officials such as the provincial governors had no choice but to have it enshrined temporarily in the government offices. The Master, seeing that there was an imperial decree, had no choice but to go to the capital to give thanks. The Empress Dowager and the palace ladies each contributed silver to support the Master, having him build a temple at Mount Lao to house the canon, and the Empress Dowager named it the Haiyin Temple.

While in the capital the Master heard that Master Daguan had gone to Mount Lao to call on him, and immediately hurried back by forced marches. No sooner had he returned to the foot of Mount Lao than he met Master Daguan coming down the mountain, and at once invited him to return together to the meditation room. The two talked of Chan and discussed the Way, full of the savor of the Dharma, and in this way Master Daguan lingered there over twenty days before returning. When he left, he presented a poem to the Master, in which were the lines: “At leisure I dwell upon the sea, my name by error cast into the east of the mountain”
(because of the error of his great fame, cast into Shandong)

When winter came, ice and snow covered the land, and fine was the sea-and-sky scenery. One night, after sitting in meditation, the Master rose and took a walk; he saw the deep blue sea and the clear, transparent night sky, and clearly realized the great treasury of illumination, wholly without a single thing. At once he composed a verse:
The sea is still, the sky is clear, moonlight upon the snow; within this realm, ordinary and sage alike have no trace of coming or going.
The diamond eye suddenly opens and the flowers of emptiness fall; the whole earth returns to the field of extinction.

After the Master returned to his quiet room, he saw a copy of the Shurangama Sutra on the desk. When he opened the scroll, he came upon the words: “Your mind and your body, reaching out to the mountains, rivers, the void and the great earth — these are all things in the wonderfully bright true mind.” The whole contemplative scope of the sutra was suddenly clear to his mind and eyes. He took up his brush and wrote rapidly; within a short while he had written out everything he had realized, and titled it the Shurangama Suspended Mirror. When he looked, only half a candle had burned. Then the Master called in the rector and had him read it aloud. As he listened, the Master too felt as though he were listening to words spoken in a dream.

One day, recalling the koan in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch about a man coming at midnight to cut off his head, the Master wished to learn the Sixth Patriarch's power of concentration. Each night the Master opened his door and practiced this contemplation: “If someone comes to borrow my head, I will gladly give it to him.” After a long time in this way, he felt his power of concentration deepen. One night someone suddenly shouted: “A robber is coming!” The Master said calmly, “Call the robber in!” He lit the candle and sat upright and composed, without the slightest fear. When the tall, big robber reached the Master's door and saw the Master's imposing dignity, his arrogance vanished at once, and he crouched low, not daring to enter. The Master said to him: “There is nothing here of value.” He then had his attendant take two hundred coins from the storehouse and gave them to the robber, and the robber left the Haiyin Temple with a feeling of admiration.

The next year, when the hall of Mount Lao was completed, the Master then opened the hall and preached the precepts to the assembly. From this time monks from all directions came to the Haiyin Temple in ever growing numbers. Then the Master also expounded the Heart Sutra for the laypeople, and a disciple recorded it, entitling it the Direct Explanation of the Heart Sutra. In the autumn, the governor Hu Shun'an retired and returned to his native village, and sent his son to the Haiyin Temple to renounce as the Master's attendant, with the Dharma-name Fushan. From then on, whether in fortune or misfortune, he never left the Master's side, becoming the disciple who rendered the greatest service and attained the highest accomplishment among the Master's followers.
[Fushan]
The Chronicle of Master Hanshan's Life says:
(I, Fuzheng)
when the Patriarch Han traveled east, I was fortunate enough to meet the scribe and attendant, the Venerable Gong Zhiwei. Later at the Mirror-of-the-Ancestors Hall of Jingci
(Jingci Temple)
we met morning and evening, and together entered the profound stream of the Dharma
(jointly studying the Buddhist teaching)

. The master assisted the abbot with the affairs of brush and inkstone, and in the end the Collection of Dream Wanderings was completed. The outstanding disciples of the Patriarch Han for a time, none surpassed the Venerable Zhiwei. Through hardship and danger he followed without exception, and the records of the whole collection came from his hand. Later he was entrusted with the abbot's seat of Wuru and presided over the Fayun Temple of Kuangshan; at seventy he sat out
(passed away seated in meditation)
It also says:

“Among the foremost disciples whom my Master most approved, none equaled the Venerable Zhiwei, named Fushan. At first he shared fortune and misfortune alike, and saw six times the chronological accounts of my Master's approaching transformation; in the end he hurried about to prop the bier and recorded in detail the circumstances of my Master's latter affairs — he was the devoted son of Wuru
(Wuru Temple on Mount Lu)

blocks.text: 13. The Mother and Son Are Reunited

inline.s: In the seventeenth year of the Wanli era
, the Master was forty-four. That year the Master began to read through the canon, and for the monks and assembly expounded the Lotus Sutra and the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana.
After the Master left Mount Wutai, he often had the thought of paying his respects to his parents; but fearing he would fall into worldly views, he had never gone.

Before long the Master wished to request a great canon for the Bao'en Temple, and in the tenth month arrived at the capital, where the Empress Dowager at once had a set bestowed upon him. The Master, carrying the canon, reached Longjiang; at this time the Bao'en Temple's pagoda emitted light day after day, revealing auspicious signs. When the Master reached the Bao'en Temple of Jinling, on the day of the sutra-reception the light of the pagoda was like a bridge, extending in a semicircle toward the north, and the monks who went to receive the canon all passed through the light. Even after the canon was installed and the Way-place established, the light continued without a break day after day.

This rare and wonderful light drew thousands upon thousands of people to gaze upon and pay homage to it; facing such an auspicious sign, there was no one who did not exclaim that it was something rare indeed.

The news that the Master had brought the canon to the Bao'en Temple spread without legs, all the way to the ears of his old mother. Overjoyed, the old mother first sent someone to ask on what day the Master would come home. The Master said: “This time I have come on business for the court, not for the family. If my old mother, when we meet, is as joyful as in the days before I left, then at most I may stay at home two nights; otherwise I will not return!” When the old mother heard him say this, she sent someone again to say: “To be able to meet again now — I cannot be more delighted. How could there be any sorrow? To see one another once is enough, and how much more two nights?”

When the Master returned home, the old mother, seeing her son, laughed heartily and unceasingly, with not the least trace of sorrow. In the evening, as everyone gathered in the room to talk, an elder of the clan asked: “Did you come by boat or by carriage?” The old mother said: “Why ask whether by boat or by carriage!” The elder asked again: “Then from where did you come?” The old mother said: “I came through the sky!” The Master marveled and thought: “No wonder my old mother was able to let me leave home back then!” Then he asked his mother: “After I left home, did you miss me?” The old mother said: “How could I not miss you!” The Master asked again: “How did you dispel this longing?” The old mother said: “At first I did not know what to do; later I knew you were at Mount Wutai, so I asked a master where Mount Wutai was. The master said: ‘Beneath the Northern Dipper is where your son dwells.’ From that time on, every night I bowed in the direction of the Northern Dipper and recited the name of the Bodhisattva, and gradually I no longer missed you. If you had died, I would not have bowed anymore, nor missed you anymore. Today when I see you, you have come as a transformation
(From “came through the sky” and “come as a transformation,” one can see that the old mother was a person who had seen the nature, and so in meeting there was absolutely no trace of sorrow)

The next day the Master accompanied his parents to sacrifice at the ancestral graves, and also went to choose a burial site for them. By this time his old father was eighty. The Master joked: “Today let us bury the old man alive, so as not to have to come again!” And he drove the spade into the ground. Seeing this, the old mother snatched the spade away and said: “Let this old woman bury herself — why trouble others to come!” And she chopped down several dozen times. On the third day the Master took leave of his parents. The old mother was joyful as before, not once furrowing her brow. The Master knew that his old mother was by no means an ordinary person.
There was a certain Huang Ziguang, the younger brother of the Grand Marshal of the time
(the Minister of War)

. Not long after the Master came to Mount Lao, when Huang was only nineteen, he had already taken refuge in the Master and asked his instruction. The Master gave him the Shurangama Sutra, and in two months he could recite it by heart. From then on he ate only pure food and practiced diligently. Though his parents opposed him, he never changed his resolve to cultivate. In his daily practice he was bent upon investigating to illuminate the mind, often with his side never touching the mat, sitting in meditation until dawn. Once, when the Master had gone south, Huang Ziguang thought to himself: “I was born in a border region and for a long time have not heard the name of the Three Jewels; today by good fortune I have met a great good teacher. If the Master should not return, we would lose our reliance!” So he pierced his arm and burned a lamp as an offering to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, praying that the Bodhisattva would bless the Master to return safely soon. After the lamp had been burned, the wounds inflamed and hurt; yet he still sat upright day and night, holding to and reciting the holy name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara. After three months in this way, the burn wounds healed. But on the scar of the wound there had formed the figure of a Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, its brows, eyes, body and robes vivid as a painting. When the Master returned, his resolve to leave home was very strong; but because his parents opposed him, the Master never agreed. The next year Huang Ziguang sat out and passed away.

Throughout these several decades of his cultivation, the Master never once forgot to revive the Bao'en Temple. When he had earlier dwelt at Longmen on Mount Wutai, though there had been opportunity, the cost was too great and he could not act. When he came to Mount Lao in the Eastern Sea, he was ever waiting for the moment. Now the Master judged that the conditions were ripe, and so, taking the occasion of delivering the canon, he went to the capital and memorialized the Empress Dowager on the whole story of the Bao'en Temple, saying: “The project is vast and needs very great funds, so it is hard to undertake lightly. I beg that the Holy Mother would each day reduce her meals and daily expenses by a hundred taels; accumulating thus for three years, the project can begin, and accumulating for ten years, the project can be completed.” The Empress Dowager was delighted, and in the twelfth month of that year began to set aside funds.

blocks.text: 14. The Disturbance of the Daoist Practitioners

inline.s: In the eighteenth year of the Wanli era

, the Master was forty-five. In the spring of that year the Master wrote out the Lotus Sutra, to express gratitude for the Empress Dowager's gracious regard. During this period a group of men wanted to seize the Haiyin Temple Way-place. They bribed the yellow-capped Daoist priests outside the tradition, falsely claiming that the Master had occupied their cloister. They also gathered many people to bring a suit to the provincial court. The governor of the time, Lord Li, after learning the truth of the matter, deeply detested this band of ruffians and sent them to the Laizhou prefecture for punishment. The Master also went to Laizhou to hear the case, and tried his best to save them. But those several hundred ruffians, not knowing the Master's compassion, still made a clamor in the prefectural city and surrounded the Master, refusing to go. Seeing this, the Master had the attendants beside him go elsewhere, and walked off slowly alone.

When he reached outside the city, the leader of the ruffians brandished a knife before the Master, wanting to kill him. The Master looked at him calmly and said with a smile: “If you kill me, how will you deal with yourself?” Hearing the Master's words, the leader felt ashamed at heart, and at once put away his knife, and accompanied the Master two li outside the city. When they were about to go their separate ways, the ruffians, thinking their leader had turned traitor, wanted to strike him. The Master thought to himself: “If they are stirred up, this leader will be in danger. What should be done?” The Master simply took the leader by the hand back to his lodging, closed the door, took off his outer robe, and set out melons and fruit to entertain him. As the two ate and talked together, the leader was completely transformed by the Master. Meanwhile the whole market resounded with cries of “The Daoist has killed a monk!” When the prefect heard this news, he sent his men to arrest the gang of ruffians, and the ruffians, in panic, knocked their heads on the ground begging for mercy. The Master said to the ruffians: “Do not be afraid; let me go and speak for you.” The Master went before the prefect, and the prefect asked: “Did the madmen want to kill you?” The Master said: “No; when the constables came in pursuit, I was eating melons with their leader!” The prefect asked again: “Then why did they raise the disturbance?” The Master replied: “They were only making the usual market-place clamor.” The prefect wanted to detain them, and the Master said: “You should let them go. If you shackle and imprison them, it is the same as keeping evildoers constantly by your side, which does no good.” Hearing this, the prefect was suddenly enlightened, and at once ordered the local troops to disperse them. Within three days the madmen had all scattered, and so the disturbance of the madmen was settled peacefully.

That year the Master also wrote a book titled On the Influences of Laozi and Zhuangzi, in eight chapters; of these, the chapter “On the Mind-Dharma,” though shortest in text, had already summed up the central thought of the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism. In “On the Mind-Dharma” he says: “In my youth I studied the Confucian teaching, yet did not know the source and stream of the Confucian teaching; later I studied the doctrines of Laozi and Zhuangzi, yet did not reach the purport of those doctrines. So I withdrew from worldly affairs, entered the deep mountains and great marshes, and devoted myself to cultivating stillness in order to observe the mind. Because I cultivated stillness to observe the mind, I understood the profound and wondrous principle that “the three realms are only the mind and the ten thousand dharmas are only consciousness.” Since the three realms and the ten thousand dharmas are all illusory manifestations of mind and consciousness, then all things with form and mark are shadows of the mind; all sounds and words are echoes of the mind. And the bodies of all sages are the most majestic forms revealed within the shadows of the mind, and the words of the sages are the sounds within the echoes of the mind that accord most with truth. Precisely because the ten thousand dharmas are only mind, therefore the politics, law, literature, and art of governing the world, and all the enterprises that support human life, if they are good and beneficial to the multitude of people, are likewise in accord with the right Dharma. This is because outside the mind there is not a single thing that exists independently, and so it is said that all things are manifested by the true mind. Those deluded to the true mind, attached to these shadows and echoes as real existents, are unable to penetrate to the wondrous function inherent in the true mind; but if one awakens to the wonderfully true mind that one inherently possesses, still yet ever shining, shining yet ever still, then all the phenomena of the world and of life are at once the inconceivable wonderful existence. Yet to awaken to this unified source of all things, and to produce its inconceivable wonderful function — only a sage can attain this!”

blocks.text: 15. Meeting with Disaster While Spreading the Dharma

inline.s: In the twentieth year of the Wanli era

, the Master was forty-seven. In the seventh month of that year he went to the capital to call on Master Daguan, and the two met in a garden in the western suburbs of the capital gate. Master Daguan was overjoyed at the Master's coming; the two sat facing each other in still concentration for forty days and nights without once closing their eyes, discussing how to write the transmission-lamp record of the Ming dynasty, and agreed to meet again at Caoxi, there to open together a line of the Chan teaching for a generation.

Later he went together with the Master up Mount Shijing and viewed the Stone Sutra Cave. The canon engraved on stone slabs within the cave had been made by a Master Jingwan of the Jin dynasty, who, concerned that in the calamity of the three disasters there would be no Dharma and thus no Buddhism, had cut stone slabs in Fangshan county and engraved an entire collection of the Buddhist scriptures, storing them in the mountain cave and sealing it with a stone door. By the Ming dynasty, the stupa-court of this cave had been sold off by a monk, and Master Daguan resolved to buy it back. Thus the treasures of the stone canon were preserved. At this time Master Hanshan composed the “Record of the Stupa-Court of Master Wan” and the “Record of the Reburied Relics,” which were engraved in the stupa-court.

The next year a famine struck the eastern quarter of Mount Lao, and many people died of hunger. Master Hanshan distributed all the vegetarian provisions stored in the mountains among the nearby residents. Still not enough, the Master took a boat to Liaodong and bought several hundred bushels of beans, so that of the residents near the mountain not one starved to death.
In the twenty-second year of the Wanli era

, the Master was forty-nine. At the winter solstice in the tenth month, the Master went to the capital to offer congratulations to the Empress Dowager. The Empress Dowager kept the Master for the winter, and asked him to preach the precepts at the Cishou Temple, with rites and gifts of extraordinary solemnity, a spectacle without precedent. Within the abbot's hall, the ground was spread with felt and brocade. The fruits and offerings set before the Buddha were all rare treasures from the four quarters. The clothing, food, and utensils the abbot's hall required — the Empress Dowager had the Grand Rites Commissioner present them daily morning and evening, in an endless stream along the way, and those who crowded to watch were often like a wall. The meritorious nobility
(imperial relatives of merit)
and

the eunuchs of the inner palace made offerings beyond counting — gold, coins, cloth, and grain filling the baskets and overflowing the granaries. Every day thousands attended the Dharma assembly, and the vegetarian meals were exceedingly sumptuous. Yet Master Hanshan accepted not a jot of the money and grain bestowed from the inner treasury.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month of that year
(the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month)

, the Holy Mother specially ordered the close attendant Chen Ru to bestow a Vairocana hat, a brocade purple kasaya, a Zhigong's shoes, and undergarments, the whole outfit of fine wool. Master Hanshan declined and would not accept, so the Empress Dowager bestowed them three times before the Master would accept them; and having accepted, he still did not wear them.

On the day of the gift of robes, the Empress Dowager ordered a eunuch to convey her command, asking the Master to enter the palace that she might in person request a Dharma-name from him. The Master knew that this was not the emperor's decree, so he firmly declined, for by the ancestral law, monks could not enter the palace. Thereupon the Empress Dowager sent a eunuch to have someone paint a portrait of Master Hanshan, and had it brought into the palace. She hung the portrait in the inner hall, had the emperor stand in attendance, and after making obeisance herself, respectfully received the Dharma-name that Master Hanshan had bestowed.

At this time the Master, knowing the Empress Dowager's savings had grown ample, asked her to have the Bao'en Temple built. But because Japan had invaded Korea and the court was deliberating on sending troops to subdue it, the matter of rebuilding had to be suspended.
In the twenty-third year of the Wanli era
, the Master was fifty. In the second month of spring, the Master returned from the capital to Mount Lao, and in the third month he met with disaster and was cast into prison.

Previously, because the Shenzong emperor believed deeply in Daoism, he had long detested the eunuch envoys who were constantly running about on Buddhist business and spending money. Once, when the Empress Dowager sent a eunuch envoy to Mount Lao in the Eastern Sea, the inner court angered Shenzong over some accidental matter, and the Empress Dowager was also drawn in; the ministers all felt crisis lurking on every side. This gave the powerful courtiers opposed to the Empress Dowager their opening, and they used the old rumor of the Daoists' disturbance to strike at the Master and the Empress Dowager, and to have the sutra-delivering eunuch envoy removed. Therefore they dispatched the Dongchang
(a Ming-dynasty secret police agency)

runners, disguised as Daoists of Mount Lao, to strike the drum of petition and present a bill accusing Master Hanshan of embezzling the national treasury silver. The emperor read it and could not but fly into a rage, and issued an edict to arrest the Master and the envoy who had delivered the canon.

[The drum of petition] The drum hung outside the court hall; when the people wished to remonstrate or to seek redress for wrongs, they could strike the drum to reach the throne. [The Shenzong emperor believed deeply in Daoism] The Chronicle of Master Hanshan's Life says: “When the disaster of Mount Lao arose, the emperor (Ming Shenzong) had this to say: ‘The whole court is for the monks; I alone am for the Daoists.’”

When the Master heard this news, he gathered the assembly and said: “The Buddha's spirit of compassion that rescues from suffering is such that for the sake of a single sentient being he will not abandon even the three evil paths. This Eastern Sea is a border region, which has never heard the name of the Three Jewels
(the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Sangha-jewel)

. I have taught here for twelve years, and even three-year-old children know to recite the Buddha. As for those who have abandoned the false and turned to the right, and studied Buddhism and cultivated, they are in every village and household. Seeing the Dharma take root and sprout here, my vow is fulfilled; even in death there is nothing to regret! Only that I could not revive the Bao'en Temple — over that I feel some pain!”
When the Master bade everyone farewell and left Jimo city, the people of the city, old and young, all came to see him off with tears, and were all deeply anxious about the safety of his journey.
When the Master reached the capital, by imperial decree he was handed over to the Zhenfu commission
(a subordinate of the Ming Embroidered Uniform Guard, which ran the prison for detaining offenders under the emperor's edict)

. When he was brought up for torture and interrogation, the officials in charge had beforehand received the emperor's intent that the moneys the Empress Dowager had bestowed on the famous mountains and temples over the years, amounting to several hundreds of thousands, were all to be recovered. Under the torture of bitter punishment, the Master said: “I am ashamed to be a monk who cannot repay the state's kindness; now how could I, for the sake of sparing my own life, injure the emperor's great filial piety? If I wrong myself and confess falsely, though I comply with the emperor's intent, I would damage the moral order; this is by no means the sincere heart of a minister who loves his sovereign. How could I account for this to history? How could I face the pure and noble sages of the past?” With a sincere heart the Master resisted the false accusation, and admitted only to the more than seven hundred pieces of gold he had earlier given in relief; and he begged the emperor to examine the accounts of the inner treasury and the records of the earlier Shandong relief. After examination, besides the seven hundred pieces of gold given earlier in relief, there was truly not the slightest discrepancy. It was then that Shenzong understood, and mother and son became reconciled as before. But the emperor still, on the ground that the Master had privately built a temple, exiled the Master to Leizhou to serve as a soldier.

[Privately building a temple] As said earlier: “The Empress Dowager Li sent people to carry the canon to Mount Lao in the Eastern Sea. Because the Master had not known of it beforehand, when the canon arrived there was no place to house it. Seeing this, the local officials such as the provincial governors had to have it enshrined temporarily in the government offices. The Master, seeing that there was an imperial decree, had no choice but to go to the capital to give thanks. The Empress Dowager and the palace ladies each contributed silver to support the Master, having him build a temple at Mount Lao to house the canon, and the Empress Dowager named it the Haiyin Temple.” The Haiyin Temple that housed the canon was built with silver contributed by the Empress Dowager and the palace ladies, and named by the Empress Dowager — how is that “privately building a temple”? As the saying goes, when one wishes to fix a crime, how can one lack a pretext? [Leizhou] In the southwest of Guangdong province, located in the middle of the Leizhou Peninsula.

From the time the Master was imprisoned in the third month, temples inside and outside the capital all recited sutras and performed repentance rites for him; some monks even burned incense and pierced their arms holding mantras to aid the Master. The son of the Minister of War, the Grand Marshal Zheng Fanxi, held office in the Jinwu
(that is, the Imperial Guard, the emperor's bodyguard forces)

, and had never known the Master; yet he especially held a banquet for the court officials, begging them to rescue the Master, even to the point of weeping and crying, setting forth and defending the Master's injustice, and none of those present but grieved over it. From this one can see how, at that time, people's hearts protected the Buddha-Dharma. During the eight months in prison, only the attendant Fushan cared for the Master's food and drink.

Even at the very time when the Master's life hung in the balance, his single thought of joy did not diminish. He wrote: “Recently I have been framed because of spreading the Dharma, and the emperor flew into a rage (the Master was slandered on account of spreading the Dharma, the emperor raged, and he was arrested and cast into prison, tortured with severe punishments, his life or death unknown), like a bolt from a clear sky, at which those who heard stopped up their ears. From my arrest until my exile left the capital, over two hundred days, I passed through all manner of bitter things beyond words. From beginning to end, I looked within and found that a single thought of joy was not in the least diminished from usual, and those who saw it were all greatly astonished. Yet the sudden calamity of life or death — others were astonished for my sake; and when they saw that my joy was no less than usual, they were even more astonished. I am not astonished at the calamity of life or death that astonishes others, yet others are astonished that I am not astonished; perhaps there is some reason in it!” (The text is found in the Collection of Dream Wanderings, in the “Showing the Attendant Qi on the Boat Bound for Leiyang.”)
In the tenth month of winter, when he set off for the south, many high court officials came in plain dress, riding donkeys
(rather than in official robes on horseback or in sedan-chairs, to express their grief)
to the ferry to see me onto the boat. On the day of leaving the capital, Fushan and two or three other monks accompanied him.

In the eleventh month the Master reached Nanjing. By the bank of the Yangtze his old mother came to take her leave of him forever. The Master saw that as she talked with him in joy her voice was clear and bright, and there was not the least obstruction in her breast. So he asked her: “When you hear of your son’s passing from death to life, are you not grieved?” His old mother said: “Death and life are determined by karma. I do not grieve even over my own death and life, let alone yours. But people’s words differ, and I have no settled view on this matter, so I feel a little doubt.” Mother and son sat talking thus until daybreak. As they were about to part forever, his old mother charged him: “You should cherish yourself well with the great Way; do not worry on my account. Today I take my long farewell of you!” Having said this, she set off cheerfully without once turning her head. Watching his mother’s receding figure, the Master thought with feeling: “If only the fathers and mothers of the whole world were like this, would not the ties of birth and death be ended at once?” Thereupon he took up his brush and wrote the “Inscription on Mother and Son”:
The love of son and mother — a lodestone drawing iron; the wondrous nature, in itself, is perfect from the first.
I look upon my mother as fire born of wood: the wood is burned away; the fire had never any I.
Born, I do not cling; dying, I do not know — only then do I see this body of mine is a barren woman’s son.
[Barren woman’s son] The child of a barren woman: a metaphor for what does not exist, as when one speaks of a turtle’s hair or a rabbit’s horns. The Vimalakirti Sutra says:

“Chapter on the Perception of Living Beings” says, ‘Like the track of a bird in the sky, like a barren woman’s son.’ The line in the inscription, “only then do I see this body of mine is a barren woman’s son,” is a metaphor saying that this body of mine is an illusion. [Barren woman] A woman who cannot bear children.
Afterwards he set out, taking with him his nephew Kejiu, whose father and mother had both died.

Because Master Daguan had made a pact with the Master at Shijingshan, wishing to revive together the spirit of the school at Caoxi, and while the Master was in trouble Master Daguan was waiting at Tianchi Temple on Mount Kuang
(that is, Mount Lu in Jiangxi province)

. Hearing the news he was greatly shocked, and said: “Now that Master Han has met with disaster, our wish to go to Caoxi together can never be fulfilled!” So he first went to Caoxi, and then on to the capital to inform their friends, running everywhere to rescue him. When he had returned to Liaocheng in Shandong, he heard that Master Hanshan was about to leave prison, and so hurried straight to Jinling to wait for him. After Master Hanshan reached Nanjing, the two masters met in a hermitage by the bank of the Yangtze.

Master Daguan wished to do all he could to clear me of the injustice, but Master Hanshan said: “This matter is like a ruler commanding his minister, or a father commanding his son: one must obey. How much more since it is wrought by my own fixed karma — please do not trouble yourself about it further.” As they were parting, Master Daguan took hold of the Master’s arm and said: “When I heard at Tianchi Temple that you had met with disaster, I made a vow before the Buddha to recite the Lotus Sutra a hundred times. For your safety, this can only be accomplished by my vow and your tongue!” Hearing this, the Master thanked him again and again and took his leave. Master Daguan also gave him, as a parting gift, the essay he had written, “The Expulsion of the Guest.”
While in prison the Master read the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment and composed a “Chapter on the Four Marks”:

Bells and drums, bells and gongs, their sound knows no cease; sound on sound, day and night, they proclaim the unborn. Pitiful are those who wound their lives in drunken dreams; gazing at their forms in the mirror, their tears come down. (The mark of self)

[The unborn] The truth of nirvana, which has no birth or death, is therefore called “the unborn.” Hence one contemplates the principle of the unborn in order to shatter the afflictions of birth and death. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“All living beings, within the unborn, falsely perceive birth and death; therefore it is called revolving in birth and death.”
The Sutra of the King of Supreme Victory says:
“The unborn is real; birth is delusion. The foolish drift and drown in birth and death; the Tathagata embodies the real, having no delusion, and is named nirvana.”
Towering and steep
cuán wán
, high and craggy)

soars the Iron City, its knife-forest and sword-trees cold as ice. Who would have thought the fire would break out toward the mountain of ice? The mountain of ice burns away, and the fire is never born. (The mark of person)
The iron gate is shut fast, past finding
yao
, dark and dim)
, and hard to open; lock upon lock, bar upon bar — misery indeed. How strange that the long-night guest should moan and groan; who knows by what cause he came to be here. (The mark of living beings)

A single rod of blood shows no mercy at all; whatever it touches, it severs birth from death. Only when the pain has pierced your heart and stung your nose do you know that the king’s law keeps clear account. (The mark of a life-span)
When the Master came out of prison he passed through the markets of Chang’an, and composed four more poems:
Chang’an’s wind and moon are the same in every age; on purple paths and red dust the road never ends. Yet the place that calls to a man most intimately is a single cockcrow, and the fifth-watch bell.

The body, like empty space, is at ease of itself; not a speck of dust divides ten thousand fold mountains. Pitiful are the travelers under the bright blue sky, who stare with open eyes and sigh that the road is hard.
A squall and a sudden rainstorm sweep down at once; countless travelers cannot open their eyes. Then of a sudden the rain stops and the clouds scatter; the vast void was clear of dust from the first.

In the gandharva city in the sky, the wild-horse folk of the plain appear as a smoke-wrapped village before the eyes. But one must walk right into that city and look: the sounds and forms were never real at all.
[Gandharva city]
The city of the gandharvas, a city conjured by magic.

[Wild horses] A metaphor for illusion: the vapors that rise and shimmer over the fields look from afar like wild horses galloping through the sky, though in truth there are no wild horses. [The gandharva city in the sky, the wild-horse folk] People are like a mirage in the sky and like wild horses galloping through the air — they are illusion.
The savor of Chan and the savor of Dharma in these poems are well worth pondering.

blocks.text: 16. Exile to Leizhou

inline.s: In the twenty-fourth year of Wanli (

), the Master was fifty-one. In the first month the Master crossed the Wen River and paid a visit to Zou Jijian. The Grand Secretary Wang Xinghai of Luling came to the bank of the Wen River to pay his respects to the Master and asked him to write a commentary on the Lankavatara Sutra. In the second month the Master went up Dayu Ridge. At the top of the ridge he viewed the site where Huiming seized the robe and bowl, and wrote a poem in remembrance, in which are the lines “Turning over in my mind the traveler who walked by night so long ago, / How does he compare with the heart that crosses the ridge today?” Seeing that the travelers crossing the ridge suffered greatly, their bodies streaming with sweat, the Master gave instructions to a
devotee
(one who lives in a monastery but keeps his hair and practices)

, asking him to establish a tea hermitage at the head of the ridge. And seeing that the mountain road was steep and hard to walk, he urged people to repair it; within a few years it became a level highway.
When the Master reached Shaoyang he entered the mountain to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch. When he had drunk a mouthful of the water of Caoxi, his heart was moved and he chanted a poem:
A drop of Caoxi’s water, from its spiritual source, flows into the dark sea where the billows beat the sky.
How many fish and dragons have been transformed thereby? The single vein of the source is still as clear
(anciently the same as “ling,” meaning to wither or fade.)
as ever.
When the Master reached the ancestral temple of the Sixth Patriarch
(Nanhua Temple at Caoxi, also called Baolin Temple)
, he saw that it had fallen into utter decay, and could only take his leave with a desolate heart.
When he reached the Five Rams
(Guangzhou)

, the Master, wearing the prison garb of an exile, was received in audience by the General. The General himself untied his bonds for him and offered him a vegetarian meal, and that night he lodged at Haizhu Temple.
After the Master had settled there, Mr. Zhou Dingshi, Grand Counselor
(another name for a Vice Commissioner)

, who often lectured on the learning of Yangming, one day came with several dozen of his students to call on the Master. In the course of their talk Mr. Zhou raised the proposition from the Book of Changes, “To comprehend the Way of day and night is to know.” One of the old Daoist elders present offered his own understanding, saying: “Everyone has awareness: the awareness that deals with affairs by day is the same awareness that dreams by night — hence the saying, ‘To comprehend the Way of day and night is to know.’” Mr. Zhou said: “That is what everyone says, but in my heart I think it is not necessarily so.” He then asked the Master: “Old Chan Master, pray instruct us!” The Master asked: “From what classic does this saying come?” Mr. Zhou answered: “The Appended Phrases of the Book of Changes.” He then recited several lines of the Appended Phrases in succession. When the Master had heard them he said: “This is a sage pointing out to people the one point that is not subject to birth and death.” At these words Mr. Zhou struck the table and cried out in praise, saying: “It is the old Chan Master’s pointing that is truly intimate!” Everyone present was bewildered, and pressed him with questions.
