Mr. Zhou explained: “Birth and death are the Way of day and night; to comprehend day and night is to be no longer subject to day and night.” At this the whole assembly sighed in admiration.
[The learning of Yangming]

Yangming learning, also called Wang learning or the learning of mind, is a school of Confucianism developed by the great Ming Confucian Wang Shouren. Because Wang Shouren once built a chamber in the Yangming Cave of his native place, he was known to the world as Master Yangming, and so his teachings came to be called Yangming learning.
On the tenth day of the third month the Master arrived at Leizhou and lodged in an old temple west of the city.
On the first day of the fourth month the Master set to work on his commentary on the Lankavatara Sutra.
That year Leizhou suffered famine, and plague broke out on every side; for a whole year no rain fell, and the dead could not be counted. The place where the Master dwelt was like a charnel ground
(a place where the dead are cast out)

: corpses lay everywhere, and only because the Dharma-power protected him was he able to remain untroubled. The drought was so severe that even the well water dried up. The attendant Fushan, who followed the Master, could obtain only one jar of water at midnight, and that had to serve for a whole day’s use.

By the seventh month the dead lay strewn inside and outside the city. The Master urged people to gather up and bury them, and tens of thousands of corpses were buried. He also held a rite of deliverance for the local people. When the ceremony of the rite was finished, the heavens at once sent down a drenching rain, and three feet of water rose on the flat ground; from that time the pestilent air dispersed, and the people were saved.

In the first month of the following year the provincial capital also lost many people, and corpses lay exposed everywhere. The Master had several thousand gathered up and buried, and established a Universal Relief rite for seven days and nights, after which the provincial capital too grew peaceful. Formerly the people of Guangdong for the most part knew nothing of Buddhism; but since the Master’s teaching and transformation, many took refuge in the Three Jewels.

In the fourth month the Master finished writing the Lankavatara Notes. Because many of the scholars who had taken refuge with the Master had not yet entered into Buddhist principle, the Master also wrote for them the Direct Pointing to the Doctrine of the Mean, setting forth the meaning of the Buddha-Dharma.

When the Master first came to the Five Rams, the officials high and low, seeing that he was a monk under sentence, all looked on him with contempt. At that time the Governor-General (Viceroy) Grand Minister of War
Chen Wangru governed the army with severity, and the Master did not go to see him; yet Grand Minister Chen often sent people to wait upon the Master. In the ninth month of that year

), the Master and Ding Youwu went to call on him, and the gate-keeper replied that he would not receive them, so the Master could only turn back. That night Grand Minister Chen came in person to the Master’s boat, bringing tea and cakes, and they talked until the third watch. The Master’s extraordinary talents filled those present with astonishment and admiration. Afterwards Grand Minister Chen praised him warmly before his subordinates, saying: “Master Hanshan is the unicorn and phoenix among monks!” And he ordered the Three Offices (the Command Office, the Provincial Administration Office, and the Surveillance Office) to go and pay their respects to the Master. From that time on all Lingnan knew that the Master was a monk of very great virtue, and they likewise learned to revere the Three Jewels.

blocks.text: 17. Expounding the Dharma in Cap and Sash

inline.s: In the twenty-sixth year of Wanli (
), the Master was fifty-three. In the first month there came a censor named Fan Youxuan, who for raising the matter of
the appointment of an heir
(the establishment of an imperial prince as heir apparent)

had been banished to Leiyang. He came to the Five Rams to visit the Master, who was then proofreading the Lankavatara Notes. He asked the Master: “What is the scenery of Leiyang like?” The Master picked up the scroll of the sutra and said: “This is the scenery of Leiyang!” When Fan Youxuan heard this he marveled at the Master’s extraordinary breadth of mind, and at once raised funds on the Master’s behalf to print the Lankavatara Notes.
[The appointment of an heir] The establishment of an imperial prince as heir apparent.
Emperor Shenzong did not until the twenty-ninth year of Wanli (

), and then only under compulsion, establish his eldest son Zhu Changluo, who was already twenty by nominal age, as heir apparent. Before that, anyone who dared to propose the appointment of the eldest son Zhu Changluo as heir apparent was a thorn in Emperor Shenzong’s eye, and most were banished.

There was a Confucian scholar named Long Zhang who once heard the Master discourse on the Buddha-Dharma and was deeply astonished. Going home, he said to his friends Wang Anshun and Feng Changli: “A Chan master who has come from the north speaks a very wonderful Buddha-Dharma.” When the two heard this they came at once to seek instruction from the Master, who revealed to them the one step beyond of the Chan school. On hearing it they at once believed without a doubt and devoted themselves wholeheartedly to investigation. From that time, under the leadership of these three men, more and more people in the Five Rams came to take refuge with the Master.

The Master often recalled Master Daguan’s vow to recite the Lotus Sutra a hundred times, but as conditions had never allowed it, the vow remained unfulfilled. In the summer the Master built a meditation hut among the piled cliffs of the mountain. Following the example of Chan Master Dahui, who expounded the Dharma in cap and sash
(following the example of Chan Master Dahui, who when he had been struck from the monastic roll expounded the Dharma dressed as a Confucian scholar)

, he gathered the disciples who had formerly taken refuge with him, and while reciting the Lotus Sutra he expounded the Dharma for them. When he came to the “Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa” chapter, he suddenly awakened to the Buddha’s profound meaning: that this Saha world is, for every person, the Lotus Treasury world right before their eyes, and that the three transformations spoken of were simply a gradual showing of one part of it for the sake of those of lesser faculties. Thereupon he at once set to work and wrote a commentary, the Rhythmic Sections on the Lotus Sutra.

The Master’s disciple Ding Youwu was by nature impetuous and fierce, generous in spirit, but he knew only to revere monks and knew nothing of the Buddha-Dharma. When he was about to return home, the Master saw him off to his boat, and there applied the tongs and hammer once more, whereupon Ding Youwu suddenly had a great awakening. The Master gave him the name Layman Juefei, and wrote a “Inscription on Clarifying the Mind” to caution him:
The true nature, deep and still, is like settled water clear; let hate and love but strike it, and waves of affliction appear.
Stir it without cease, and the self-nature turns to mud; affliction and ignorance but breed more unawareness still.
Grasping at “me” and “that,” like mud poured into water; letting “that” stir “me,” like oil feeding fire.
“That” troubles my “true”; the trouble is born of me. If I do not give rise to it, the kalpa-fire turns to ice.
Therefore the man of the utmost lets the mark of self be emptied first. If the mark of self is empty, what can obstruct him then?
The work of forgetting the self lies in firm patience: the moment habit-energy stirs, at once and fiercely awaken.
In that very awakening one thought turns back the light; the traces swept away, just here and now is cool and bright.
Cool and still, wholly free and unconfined; serene and joyful, the spirit at peace — no thing can rival this.

In the spring of the following year the Lankavatara Notes came off the blocks. After the Master had expounded it once for his disciples, more than a hundred copies were printed and sent everywhere, to good teachers of the Buddhist world at home and abroad and to the protecting officials of the Dharma.

blocks.text: 18. Protecting the Country and Pacifying the People

inline.s: Guangdong’s customs were fond of killing. On the Zhongyuan Festival every household slaughtered livestock to sacrifice to their forebears. At that season the beasts piled up in the markets like mountains — truly a sight too cruel to bear. At this time the Master established an Ullambana Assembly and also lectured on the Commentary on the Ullambana Sutra, the Balance of Filial Piety, urging everyone to feed the monks, to release living creatures, and to sacrifice to their forebears with vegetarian food. Many people followed his advice. From that time on, whenever there was a funeral or memorial, a parent’s birthday, or a prayer to avert calamity
ráng

, or a repentance rite, they would release living creatures and keep a vegetarian fast; and later a Society for Releasing Living Creatures was established. Under the Master’s advocacy, the compassionate, world-saving spirit of the Buddha-Dharma gradually took root and sprouted here.
[Zhongyuan Festival]

The fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month. On this day Daoist temples hold vegetarian offerings, Buddhist monasteries hold Ullambana assemblies, and local custom also includes sacrifices to deceased kin.
[Ullambana Assembly]

A ceremony held on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month to deliver the spirits of ancestors, including such activities as feeding the monks, repentance rites, and the feeding of hungry ghosts.
In the twenty-eighth year of Wanli (
), the Master was fifty-five. The tax commissioners
(officials who collected monopoly taxes)

had just come forth from the court and behaved lawlessly among the people; and with Japanese pirates invading, everyone was anxious and fearful. Seeing that the situation was unfavorable for spreading the Dharma, the Master dismissed his disciples and shut himself away alone, hiding deep to avoid the disorder.

[The tax commissioners (officials who collected monopoly taxes) first came forth] In the middle and later years of Emperor Shenzong’s reign the finances were in difficulty, and so he sent eunuchs throughout the realm as mining supervisors and tax commissioners to fill the privy purse. Yet most of these mining supervisors and tax commissioners extorted the wealth of the people under false pretexts, running wild in every direction and throwing the realm into disorder. [The Japanese pirates’ invasion] At that time the Ming

government was corrupt, its coastal defenses neglected, and it had adopted a policy of closing the country to the outside. In Japan, moreover, wars were frequent, and some warriors and pirates joined forces with Ming merchants who had suffered from the closing of the country, and invaded China; so the Japanese pirates ran wild, plundering along great stretches of the coastal cities.

The region of the provincial capital suffered a shortage of grain because of the bad harvest, and rice was often shipped in from Fujian in white-cao boats. Just then local disorder broke out and grain was scarce, and the people feared only that the merchants would seize the chance to raise prices; they were deeply anxious about the matter.
[White-cao (
cáo

)] A seagoing vessel with a white-lacquered hull and a cargo hold. At that time seagoing freight vessels were of two kinds, the white-cao and the black-cao. The New Discourses of Guangdong says: “Those that cross the seas are called white-cao and black-cao; they are made of great iron-wood timbers joined together, shaped like a trough, and therefore called cao. The prow and stern are further shaped like a sea-dolphin (the right whale): the white ones have two black eyes, the black ones two white eyes; when a sea-dolphin sees them from afar, it takes them for its own kind and does not devour them.”
The son of the Governor
(Viceroy)

was about to set out on a journey, and his boat lay at the seaside, when it happened that several white-cao boats also moored beside the young lord’s vessel. The tax commissioners had long been scheming to strike down the General, and so they falsely claimed that the rice in these white-cao boats was a gift from the General to speed the young lord on his way; they gathered several thousand townspeople, who threw bricks and stones and smashed the young lord’s boat. Then they surrounded the general’s residence, pressing in with knives drawn, and the situation was extremely urgent. It happened that all the officials of the Three Offices, prefectures, and districts had gone to Duanzhou to present festival gifts, and there was not a single ranking official left in the provincial capital; if no one had come to the rescue, the danger would have been upon them in a breath.

[To fund his journey] Originally this meant a dowry (the property a bride’s family gives her at marriage); here it means to fund a journey, a euphemism for making a parting gift to one about to set out.

Unable to break the siege, the General sent his adjutant to the gate of the Master’s retreat to beg the Master to come to the rescue. The Master would not agree to go, saying: “I have no divine arts.” The adjutant knelt down weeping and said: “Even if the Master does not consider the safety of the commander, will he not consider the life and death of the people of this place?” At these words the Master felt a pang of alarm. He rose at once and went to the tax commissioners, where he reasoned with them calmly and opened their understanding. At a single word from the Master the tax commissioners indeed came to see the sense of it, and were willing to call the people to order and disperse the mob. Then the Master first went before the rioters and said: “What you are demanding today is nothing but cheap rice to eat; but if you commit a capital crime today, you will pay with your heads — and even if there were cheap rice, who would be left to eat it?” When the mob heard this they were all struck dumb, and in a moment the siege of the general’s residence was lifted. The elders of the city were deeply grateful to the Master.

At this time the officials of the Three Offices were dining at the Governor’s offices. Hearing that the townspeople had risen in disorder, they all laid down their bowls and chopsticks and hurried together to the provincial capital; finding that the mob had already dispersed, they breathed a sigh of relief.
The newly appointed Governor
(Viceroy)
Sir Dai
(Dai Yao)

, learning how the Master had pacified the rioters, was deeply grateful, and ordered the General to invite the Master to an interview. The General accompanied the Master to Sir Dai’s residence, where the Governor received him with the greatest courtesy and at once set out a vegetarian feast in his honor. When the Master took his leave, saying that he wished to go on to Caoxi, Sir Dai said that he wished to be a protector of the Dharma, and asked the Master to inform him at once if any matter should arise.
In the twenty-eighth year of Wanli (

), the Master was fifty-five. In the autumn the Surveillance Commissioner of Nan-Shao, Zhu Xingcun, repeatedly and earnestly invited the Master to go and set the ancestral temple of Caoxi in order. In the first month of the following spring the Master entered the mountain, and saw rogues from every quarter gathered at the temple gate: gambling dens, wineshops, butchers’ stalls — there was nothing that was not there. The place had been made utterly foul, and this accumulated abuse had lasted a hundred years. More lamentable still, graves had encroached upon the ancestral mountain, the monks’ property had in large part been seized, and wicked monks within the temple colluded with outside rogues to swindle away the temple’s lands. Not one of the monks in the temple dared to speak out; instead they abandoned the temple to live in country hermitages, and some even left altogether. Thus the temple gate grew emptier by the day, the rogues gathered by the day, and the harm done grew by the day. The Master could not keep from sighing: “This is a disease in the heart and vitals! If it is not removed, the Way-place of the Sixth Patriarch will in the end become a foxes’ den, and beyond all cure forever.”

So the Master went to Duanzhou and had audience with the Governor, Grand Minister of War Sir Dai, telling him in detail how the ancestral temple had been defiled and seized, and hoping that he would help to clear it up. Governor Dai at once ordered the local district to take charge, and within three days to drive out all the rogues, not leaving a single one, and to tear down the shops, not leaving a single tile. From that time the accumulated filth of the Caoxi temple gate was washed clean, and it recovered the purity of former days.

Afterwards Governor Dai kept the Master for a vegetarian meal, and in the course of their talk the Governor said: “The rank stench of the Sixth Patriarch’s Way-place — I have washed it clean for the Master. But at present the living beings of this region are in utter misery; what method of compassion has the great Bodhisattva to bring them relief?” The Master asked: “What do you mean?” The Governor said: “Along this coast there is a band of robbers who possess a thousand pearl-diving boats. Recently the imperial commissioners, by imperial decree, came to gather pearls, and this has further fed their power. When the pearl-gathering is over they will run wild upon the sea, plundering everywhere. That is the first. The second is the opening of mines in this region: the corvée levied by the court runs wild and lawless, digging up graves and destroying the property of the common people, so that the people suffer poison everywhere, more cruel than the plundering of the robbers. With these two harms, the people cannot live in peace. I ask the Master, how should it be dealt with?” The Master answered: “This matter is not easy; let us think of a way in time.”

The mining commissioner Li, sent by the court, had a rather believing heart. In the autumn of that year he came to Caoxi to offer incense, and stayed in the mountain several days. The Master expounded the Buddha-Dharma for him, and he was delighted to hear it. The Master urged him to be the chief benefactor who would spread gold to revive the ancestral temple, and he generously undertook it alone. The Master also spoke to him privately: “The opening of mines does great harm to the local people; this is probably not the Emperor’s own intent, is it? I beg you to set a time limit for the mining boats, and to punish any who overstay it. As soon as the mining is done, the corvée should be withdrawn as quickly as possible, so that it does no harm to the people. Can you do this?” When Commissioner Li heard it he agreed again and again. After he returned he enforced the restrictions with all his strength, and from that time the region was at peace.
[Protecting the Country and Pacifying the People]
Master Yinguang said:

“In the last years of the Ming, the royal order was not upheld and the great ministers had no authority. Those who held power were all ignorant, unlettered eunuchs. The wicked and malevolent used their power to work mischief; the well-meaning but timid had no wisdom to devise remedies. Thus the people were distressed and the country endangered, past all cure. Hanshan, Zibo, Lianchi, and Miaofeng all appeared in the world at this same time. Their secret support of the way of government and their hidden sheltering
(a variant of the graph meaning “to shelter”)

of the people’s livelihood were great indeed! Hanshan, for spreading the Dharma, was slandered and banished to guard Guangzhou. How deep and far-reaching was his saving of the people of Yue and his prolonging of the altars of state! Had Hanshan not been banished to Guangzhou, the people of Guangzhou would long since have taken desperate risks and become a grief to the nation. His withdrawal of the pearl-gathering boats, his quelling of the popular uprising, his pacifying of Qinzhou, and other great matters — all were settled with a single sitting’s words. Who but one who rides his vow and manifests birth to save the people from fire and water could do this?”
(from the Prefatory Commentary on the Chronicle of Master Hanshan)

Governor Dai was very grateful for the Master’s help, and wrote to thank him, saying: “Only today do I know how vast is the compassion of the Buddha and the Patriarchs!” For this reason his confidence in protecting the Dharma grew all the firmer. And because of their help the Master was able to spread the Dharma at Caoxi in peace. The Master opened up the ancestral temple, repaired the paths, chose worthy monks and gave them the precepts, and established a charity school to educate the novices. He also set up the treasury office and the rules of purity. He examined the land rents and redeemed the monks’ property. In the space of a single year, all that had fallen into ruin was restored.
The following year the Master rebuilt the ancestral hall, altered the paths, opened a spirit way, moved the monks’ quarters, expanded the meditation hall, and established new rules of purity.

blocks.text: 19. Daguan Enters Parinirvana

inline.s: In the autumn of the thirty-first year of Wanli (

), the Master was fifty-eight. From Caoxi the Master wrote to Master Daguan, asking him to come and revive the ancestral temple; but because of the “Case of the Demonic Book,” which shook the whole realm, Master Daguan was falsely accused of having a connection with the demonic book and was arrested and thrown into prison. Through repeated interrogations under torture he never once yielded. Later, although no evidence could be found, those in power still would not let him go, and condemned him to death. When Master Daguan heard this he said: “Since the law of the world has come to this, what use is it to remain long?” Thereupon he bathed, then lit an oil lamp, sat upright, and spoke a verse:
This smile of mine has always had another cause; who would have known the great earth cannot hold a speck of dust;
from now on I pack away these feet my mother bore: the iron post blooms, and waits for no spring.
Having said this, he passed away at once.

Master Daguan’s close attendant Cao Xuecheng, hearing that Master Daguan had already passed away, hurried to the spot. Seeing the Master sitting upright without moving, he stroked the Master’s back and said: “Master, you have gone well!” Master Daguan opened his eyes again, smiled, and took his leave. At this time he was only sixty-one years old. When court and countryside alike heard of an escape so free and at ease, there was no one who did not sigh in admiration.

[The Case of the Demonic Book] Emperor Shenzong’s empress, of the Wang clan, had no son, while Consort the Respectful had borne the eldest imperial son, Changluo, who by the rules of propriety should have been established as heir apparent; but the Emperor doted on the son of Consort Zheng, Changxun, and was unwilling to appoint an heir, so that the whole city was in an uproar. In the eleventh month of the thirty-first year of Wanli (

), someone wrote a piece entitled A Continuation of the Discussion of Anxiety and Danger, which was spread far and wide in the capital in the form of handbills, so that overnight it was everywhere, from the palace gates above to the streets and lanes below. The text said that Shenzong had been forced to establish Changluo as heir apparent and that the position of the heir was perilous, and it sharply criticized the chief grand secretary Shen Yiguan and the grand secretary Zhu Geng. When Emperor Shenzong learned of it he was greatly enraged, and ordered the Eastern Depot, the Embroidered-Uniform Guard, and the patrol offices of the five city districts to search and arrest at once, “to obtain without fail the name of the author of the book”; and from this the “Case of the Demonic Book” arose. Thereupon Shen Yiguan, of the Zhejiang faction, seized the chance to bring false charges against Guo Zhengyu, Shen Li, and other members of the Donglin faction. Master Daguan too was falsely accused of a connection with the demonic book, arrested and imprisoned, and after severe interrogation condemned to death.
When Master Hanshan heard the news of Master Daguan’s passing he wished to hurry to mourn him, but was never able to do so. More than ten years passed, until the forty-fourth year of Wanli (

), when the Master was seventy-one, and only then did he set out from Nanyue and travel several thousand li to mourn him and to conduct the cremation rites for Master Daguan. At the cremation ceremony the Master raised the torch and said:

The nature of fire is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true fire. Meeting on a narrow road, there is nowhere to hide. I reverently address the Venerable Zibo, the great monk Daguan: you came into the world by chance and fell into the dust of the world by mistake. With bare strength you stripped off the cloth shirt your mother bore you in; with shining light you revealed your original face. Shouldering the true Dharma, your shoulders were forged of pure steel. Saving people to the very end, your liver and heart were cast of pig iron. On the road of birth and death you came straight and went straight. At the gate of present affairs you left it half open, half shut. For more than sixty years, your breast held the pine wind and the moon in the water; one thousand seven hundred koans were your staff of rabbit horn and turtle hair. Yet let him have his final flourish of elegance as he may, he cannot help hiding his head and showing his tail. He has tossed down his stolen goods — who would have thought they would fall into the hands of the man of the Way Hanshan? Today, before the assembled hosts of gods and humans, I pick them up on the spot. Does the great assembly see them?” (He drew the sign ○ with the torch.) He also said:
“The staff parts the clouds on both paths; from the whole body pours forth the treasury of light;
take good care, all of you, to look well: only now will you believe there is no obstruction.”
After the cremation, the Master and Master Daguan’s disciples placed Master Daguan’s relics in a pagoda, and Master Hanshan also wrote a pagoda inscription. The inscription says:

After the Master was born he did not speak until he was five years old. A monk passing by the door stroked the top of his head and said to his father: ‘This child, if he leaves home, will be a teacher of gods and humans.’ Having said this, the monk suddenly vanished, and from that time the Master began to speak. In childhood he was already of a passionate, impetuous temper, and no woman dared come near him. At the age of seventeen he traveled north with a sword. Reaching the Chang Gate of Suzhou, he was caught in heavy rain. There he met the monk Mingjue of Huqiu. Seeing that the young Master was lofty and set apart from the common run, Mingjue was astonished, and so walked with him under the same umbrella and brought him back to the temple to eat and sleep. At night the Master heard the chanting of the Sutra of the Names of the Eighty-Eight Buddhas
(the Great Repentance Text of the Eighty-Eight Buddhas)
, and early the next morning
he untied the more than ten pieces of gold wrapped at his waist and asked to be shaved; he took Mingjue as his teacher.

One day the Master took leave of Master Mingjue and departed. Hearing a monk recite Zhang Zhuo's verse on seeing the Way, he came to the lines, “To cut off deluded thinking only aggravates the illness; to incline toward true thusness is likewise mistaken.” At this he was greatly perplexed. Wherever he went he would write these two lines upon the wall, until his doubt grew so intense that his face and head became swollen. One day, while taking a meal, he suddenly awakened, and the swelling of his face and head at once subsided. From then on he surpassed all the masters of the various quarters.

Passing Mount Kuang, he exhausted the profound meaning of the Dharma-characteristic school. One day he walked twenty li, his feet sore; the Master used a stone to rub the soles of his feet, until he could walk two hundred li a day, and only then stopped. He traveled to Mount Wutai and to the capital, where he called upon the elder Master Bianrong and stayed at the monastery. He called upon the many good and wise teachers, Xiaoyan, Xianli, and others.

He saw the Great Master Qian Run, who in his hall lectured on gong-an, taking the mouth and ear as the mind-seal and a handkerchief as the true transmission. The Master sighed and said, “Is the meaning of the patriarch's coming from the West no more than this?” Thereupon he listened no further. Turning south he reached Jiahe, where there was a scholar named Daokai, a native of Nanchang, who had left the Confucian path and gone forth as a monk, attending the Master as his attendant. In the prefectural city there was the Lengyan Monastery, the place where Master Changshui had composed his commentaries on the Surangama and other sutras, long since abandoned. The Master and the Grand Minister Lu Wutai, whose given name was Guangzu, being of like purpose, discussed restoring it, and built a meditation hall of five bays. On the day the work was completed, the Master pierced his arm with an awl, letting the blood fill a bowl, and wrote a couplet:
If one does not investigate the mind, sitting in meditation only increases the bitterness of karma;
If one can guard the thought, even scolding the Buddha still aids true practice.

The Master reflected that the volumes of the Great Treasury of Sutras were vast and heavy, so much so that in remote villages and out-of-the-way places there were people who never in their whole lives heard the name of the Dharma. He planned to carve the texts in folio form, to make them easy to circulate, so as to spread hearing and seeing everywhere, planting the diamond seed; and even if there were those who slandered, he would willingly bear the offense himself. Thus he promoted the folio editions and raised funds to carve and print them.

With the help of some lay patrons, the Master printed a great many single-volume editions of the Buddhist sutras in folio form. Because the folio editions were convenient to circulate and easy to page through, this produced an incalculable effect on the spread of Buddhism.
[Carving and printing folio editions to make them easy to circulate]

In ancient times the Tripitaka carved in our country was always bound in folded form, so the volumes were vast and numerous, bringing great inconvenience to circulation. Seeing this, the Master redesigned the carving of the Great Treasury of Sutras, changing it to the convenient thread-bound format. From then on people found it easy to read, and circulation flourished. At the same time, in the Supplementary Canon and the Further Supplementary Canon, the Master gathered a great many works outside the canonical collection, such as commentaries, repentance rites, and recorded sayings, greatly enriching the contents of the Great Treasury of Sutras, a contribution that cannot be overstated. Master Daguan pioneered the carving of the “folio canon,” broadening the circulation of the Dharma and aiding those who study and practice, so that it could be circulated by anyone anywhere, opening long the eyes of humans and gods. This had a vast and lasting effect on the propagation of the Dharma. What is called the “folio canon” is the printed edition of the Great Treasury of Sutras known to later generations as the Jingshan Canon, or the Jiaxing Canon.

The tomb inscription goes on to say: after the Master had carved the canon at Jiahe and everything had been arranged, he returned to Wumen. He learned that his ordination teacher, Master Mingjue, had returned to lay life and was famous as a physician. The Master then used a false name, claimed illness, and on a boat invited Mingjue to examine him. As soon as Mingjue saw the Master, he was greatly startled. The Master at once wept and urged him to shave his head and return to the monkhood. Mingjue, moved to shame and gratitude, put on the monk's robe again, and the Master still maintained the rites of a disciple toward him.
(From this one can see Master Daguan's utmost sincerity and gratitude toward his teacher.)
The tomb inscription also says: I
(Master Hanshan)

had been exiled south of the Ling five years, and because I had not yet put on the monk's robe again, Master Daguan would often sigh, “The Dharma gate has no one left! If I sit by and watch the banner of the Dharma be toppled, then where shall those who would carry on the Three Jewels direct their effort? If old Hanshan does not return, then it is one great debt I owe to the world; if the mine tax is not stopped, then it is one great debt I owe to saving the age; if the lamp of transmission is not continued, then it is one great debt I owe to the life of wisdom. If I am released from these three debts, I shall not walk again into Rajagrha
(a metaphor for the capital)

What Master Daguan constantly held in mind was Master Hanshan's restoration to the monastic order, the peace of the people, and the flourishing of the Dharma. Yet these three debts, during his own lifetime, were none of them brought to a perfect completion, and this responsibility was without question left to Master Hanshan.

blocks.text: 20. Reviving Caoxi

inline.s: As said earlier:
In the twenty-eighth year of the Wanli era (

), the Master was fifty-five. In autumn the Regional Inspector Zhu Xingcun of Nan-Shao earnestly urged the Master to go and restore the ancestral monastery of Caoxi. In the first month of the following spring the Master entered the mountain. He saw that rogues from all quarters had gathered at the monastery gate, gambling, opening wine shops and eateries, everything imaginable, and the grounds had been made filthy and foul. This corruption had already lasted a hundred years. What was more lamentable, graves had occupied the ancestral mountain, the monks' property had largely been seized, and evil monks in the monastery conspired with outside rogues to defraud the monastery of its property. None of the monks in the monastery dared to speak out; on the contrary, they abandoned the monastery to live in farm hamlets, or even left altogether. Thus the monastery gate grew emptier day by day, the rogues gathered ever more, and the harms multiplied. The Master could not refrain from sighing, “This is a sickness of the very heart and vitals; if it is not removed, the bodhimanda of the Sixth Patriarch will at last turn into a fox's den, forever beyond cure.”

So the Master went to Duanzhou to call upon the Governor-in-Chief, the Grand Marshal Sir Dai, and told him in detail how the ancestral monastery had been polluted and usurped, hoping he would help clear it up. Governor Dai at once ordered the district magistrate to sit in charge, and within three days to drive out all the rogues, not leaving a single one, and to tear down the shops, not leaving a single tile. From then on the accumulated filth of the Caoxi monastery gate was washed clean, and it returned to the purity of former days.
However, the halls and chambers of the monastery had collapsed,

the old institutions lay in ruins, and the monks were few and scattered. So the Master made the ancestral monastery his own concern, staking his body and life, and set about managing and restoring everything, in due order.

He chose promising young men from among the people and established free schools, hiring teachers to instruct them in deportment, so that in walking, sitting, standing, lying down, and all such conduct, they should accord with the precepts; and to study both the Confucian classics and the Buddhist scriptures. When they had come to a rather deep understanding of the Dharma and resolved to go forth, he had them shaved and ordained as monks. Then he established a meditation hall, so that they could follow the pure rules, receive the precepts, and chant and practice by day and night. The Master labored with careful nurturing for eight years and accomplished over a hundred monks.
In the thirtieth year of the Wanli era
) the Master

was fifty-seven. That year he rebuilt the halls and chambers, changed the paths, built monks' quarters, enlarged the meditation hall, created institutions, set up the storehouse offices, established pure rules, audited rents and taxes, redeemed the monks' property, and reclaimed what had been usurped. Thus the ancestral monastery of Caoxi rose again from ruin.
While clearing and examining the monastery's annual accounts
(account books)

, the Master found that there were debts, and the interest was very high. He asked the monk in charge, who replied, “The monastery's supplies are insufficient; we must rely on borrowing to get by.” The Master found this strange: “

There used to be incense-lamp estates and farmland; where has the rent and tax gone?” He at once gathered the assembly to audit the various estates. Each year, in total, the rent and tax amounted to more than four hundred taels, so how could they say the income did not cover expenses? The assembly said, “The various estates are each year collected in turn by the ten steward monks in charge; whatever they say they collected is what they remit.” After careful questioning, it came to light that the steward monks were colluding with the tenant farmers to cheat, so the rent and tax existed only in name but yielded nothing real, and therefore the monastery grew more destitute day by day. The Master then chose, from among the assembly, upright and capable men to serve as the ten steward monks. He had them take vows before the patriarch, pricking their flesh to write an oath in blood: “Not a single hair will I take for myself.” He also summoned the tenant farmers of all the estates, established rules, and fixed the time each year when they must come to the monastery to pay the rent and tax. He set up a storehouse office, appointing four overseers of the monastery to manage receipts and disbursements. All the monastery's expenses were governed by fixed rules; he wrote down regulations, omitting the smallest detail. When the accounts were thus calculated, the sum collected each year from all the estates exceeded all the monastery's expenditure, leaving a surplus. From then on, not only were the monastery's funds ample and its needs met, but they also escaped the karmic offense of going to hell for usurping the monastery's property.
In the
thirty-second year of the Wanli era

, the Master was fifty-nine. In the first month of spring, because of the case of Master Daguan, the court sent word to the censorial office, ordering the Master to return to his place of exile, so the Master left Caoxi for Leizhou.

After Master Daguan's death, Master Hanshan recalled that he had once said, “For the seven destinies and cause-and-effect of the Surangama Sutra, there is no commentary in the literature of the world to match it.” The Master had said at the time, “The Spring and Autumn Annals are precisely a book that sets forth cause and effect.” So in this year he resolved to write the Mind-Dharma of the Spring and Autumn Annals of Zuo, thereby bringing out the principle of cause and effect, exposing the corruption that results from neglecting cause and effect in politics, and advocating cause and effect as the foundation of the world.
In the thirty-third year of the Wanli era (

), the Master was sixty. In the third month of this year the Master crossed the Qiong Sea, seeking the Guanglang Hermitage and the White Dragon Spring, where Su Dongpo had once dwelt, and also seeking the traces of Chan Master Juefan, but he did not find them. That night he stayed at the Mingchang Pagoda, and wrote a preface to the Mind-Dharma of the Spring and Autumn Annals of Zuo.

The next day the Master visited Stone Mountain and wrote the Record of Marvels of the Qiong Sea and the Record of the Golden Chestnut Spring. That evening he climbed the prefectural walls and, seeing that the vitality of the city was poor, at once said to the local people, “The city of Qiong is about to have a calamity; you must flee quickly!” But everyone still thought the Master was deceiving them. When the Master packed his bags, preparing to leave the city, the scholars and officials of the city begged him to stay, but no matter what, he insisted on going.

The Master crossed the Qiong Sea, and a fortnight later a violent earthquake struck the city of Qiong. The old walls and gates on the east of the city sank down, the government offices in the city collapsed completely, and the Mingchang Pagoda toppled and crushed the very lodging where the Master had stayed. Many of those who knew the story believed the Master possessed spiritual powers.
In the thirty-fourth year of the Wanli era (

), the Master was sixty-one. The eldest grandson of Emperor Shenzong was born, and the court issued a great general amnesty: all those who had been sent into military exile and were aged or ill, and those who had been wrongly demoted, were permitted to set forth their case and be released. The Master was included in this case.
The next year

, the Master's monastic status was restored, and he returned to Caoxi. By this time the work of construction he had arranged was seven or eight parts in ten complete, and when it was built there remained a debt of a thousand taels for labor and materials. The Master begged alms from two palace envoys and repaid the loan. He also built the Changchun Hermitage at Green Gate in Wuyang, as a branch office of Caoxi, to make offerings on behalf of the Sixth Patriarch. Thus he often gave teachings to his disciples in the mountain.
In his youth the Master had read the Laozi

the Classic of the Way and Its Virtue, and because the text was ancient and the meaning deep, with phrases obscure and hard to grasp, he resolved to investigate its principle. Later, at the request of lay disciples, he undertook to comment on the Classic of the Way and Its Virtue. Thus the Master began to set down his ideas from the twentieth year of the Wanli era (

), and only put brush to paper when he had investigated completely; if a single character were not yet clear, he would never lightly let it pass. In this way, after fifteen years, only in this year did he complete the Commentary on the Classic of the Way and Its Virtue. The Master once said, “Whenever I wrote a commentary on a scripture, I would always gather my spirit and enter contemplation, embodying my mind to the Buddha-mind, and only when the wisdom within became lucid did I set it down on paper. If there were the slightest discursive thought, it would not be of use.” From this we see that the Master's writing all flowed from the mind of prajna.
In the thirty-sixth year of the Wanli era

, the Master was sixty-three. In the second month of spring, Feng Yuancheng was appointed to the Lingxi circuit and entered the mountain to call upon the Master. He lodged overnight at the monastery and dreamed that the Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara appeared to him; there was a spiritual response. The next morning he entered the hall to pay homage to the Buddha, and saw the main hall was decaying and about to fall. Startled, he asked the Master, “Why not restore it?” The Master said, “The work is vast and the expense great; my strength cannot reach it.” He asked again, “How much money is needed?” The Master told him the amount required. Feng said, “Do not worry; I will see to this.” On his return he told Governor Dai, and Governor Dai said, “Ah, is it so! Seeing a child fall into a well, one must hurry to rescue him; how much more when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are in such peril, and one is not moved at heart, such a person is not human.” Then he asked the cost, and Feng reported the amount the Master had named. Governor Dai said, “I fear it is more than this.” He at once ordered the Nan-Shao circuit to go survey and estimate, and invited the Master to consult. The Master went and saw Governor Dai, who magnanimously offered to bear all the expenses. The Master said to him, “If public funds are used, I fear it will be inconvenient. Better to follow the custom of the Buddhist order.” Governor Dai asked, “How shall it be managed?” The Master told him, “By going on alms-rounds. Please instruct the Lingxi circuit to set up twelve registers. The three commissions, circuits, and prefectures shall each set up one register, and the local officials and people may give as they wish, the sums then being gathered at the governor's office. In this way there is no toil and the funds are easily assembled.” Governor Dai took his advice, and in less than a month the sum raised reached a thousand taels. Then the Master went in person to western Yue and selected great timber, using iron-pear wood for the beams and pillars, in all worth more than three thousand taels, and transported it to Duanzhou, piling it on the bank of the Duan River, arranging for it to be shipped back by water.

In the beginning of the eleventh month of winter, the Yao and Zhuang barbarians of Annam broke through Qinzhou. The Master, using banners and jeweled canopies as his retinue, majestic as a heavenly being, entered their caves to preach and persuade them to submit. Then the bandits withdrew, peace was restored, and the lives of a million beings in Qinzhou were saved
(Master Yinguang states in his treatise:

“Such great matters as withdrawing the mining ships, settling the people's unrest, and making peace with Qinzhou were all settled by a single conversation. Who but one who came forth in fulfillment of a vow, to rescue the people from fire and water, could have done this?”

. Governor Dai then sent a memorial requesting the king's troops to punish the offense, in order to cover over the loss of Qinzhou. But since the Yao bandits had already withdrawn and the walls and city were safe and sound, after the court's review and decree, Governor Dai was merely dismissed from office, and escaped arrest and interrogation.
In the next year (

), in the second month, the Master was returning with timber from Duanzhou when he was blocked by a great wind at Lingyang Gorge. At this time the Master wandered about Duanxi and wrote the Record of a Dream-Wander to Duanxi. When the timber reached Meng River, the Master entered the mountain first, and was about to summon the monks to carry the timber, when unexpectedly a few wicked monks, incited by crafty merchants, came out to oppose the Master, spreading rumors that the Master had embezzled the monastery's funds, and rousing the assembly against him, so that the monastery was in an uproar. Seeing this, the Master sighed inwardly and said, “This is all because I have gravely transgressed the Buddha's teaching, grasping at appearances too much!”

Just as the assembly was in chaotic uproar, the Master sat alone in the hall, burning incense and reciting the Diamond Sutra. When he came to the Buddha's words “the four views, which are not the four views,” he suddenly had a great awakening, and at once set brush to paper to write Resolving Doubts on the Diamond Sutra. Thus after three days, when the draft was complete, the assembly had also grown calm.
[The four views, which are not the four views] The Diamond Sutra
original text:

“World-Honored One, the views of self, the views of persons, the views of sentient beings, and the views of a lifespan are not the views of self, the views of persons, the views of sentient beings, and the views of a lifespan; thus they are called the views of self, the views of persons, the views of sentient beings, and the views of a lifespan.”
(For the commentary, see
The Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
But these wicked monks did not give up, and lodged a complaint with the censorial office. The censorial office accepted their complaint and ordered the criminal tribunal
(the officials in charge of criminal matters)
to hear the case.

When the notice came down, the Master drifted out of the mountain and went to the censorial office to await the hearing. He lodged on a boat on the Lotus River, and waited a whole year without the case being tried, and the money he had on him ran out. At this time the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong, who was living at home on the Han
hán

River, invited the Master to come. The Master took a boat and set out, but on the way met a great wind; the boat broke and sank in the river, and the Master was rescued. Having with difficulty reached Sir Xiang's home, he once more fell gravely ill and nearly died, and Sir Xiang summoned physicians who did their utmost to save him. By the time he returned to the prefectural seat, he was lying ill awaiting the trial.
In the thirty-eighth year of the Wanli era
the Master
was sixty-five. This year he still lived on the boat awaiting the trial. In the seventh month of autumn, the Imperial Commissioner
(the official specially appointed to inspect and handle affairs of local government)

made his inspection tour and came to the prefecture to call upon the Master. When the officials hearing the case learned of this, they knew the case could be delayed no longer and could only begin the trial. The result of the trial was that the accusation was judged to be true, and the Master was found guilty of a transgression and was to be escorted out of the jurisdiction.

When the Imperial Commissioner learned of this, he strongly disapproved and rebutted, saying, “Master Hanshan has done great service for the Sixth Patriarch; all the work was personally planned by the Master, and all the funds were personally raised by the Master. Now the wicked monks have profited, and instead the Master is sentenced as guilty. Is this the gate of equality?” Thereupon he ordered the local circuit
(the local circuit and prefecture)
to investigate the case strictly. The circuit and prefecture
(the administrative head of the circuit-level local government)

at once set out, going in person into the Caoxi mountains, and examined the accusation of the wicked monks item by item. The result of the examination confirmed that the wicked monks had falsely accused the Master of misappropriating more than eight thousand taels of the monastery's funds, and that it was all a lie.

At the beginning, when the Master established the rules of the monastery storehouse office, he instituted numbered tickets. All receipts and disbursements of money and grain were recorded in writing by the overseers, and every sum received or spent had a numbered ticket as its voucher. At this time, the monks who had served in past years, relying on the numbered tickets, audited and calculated before the circuit and prefecture. The result was that the Master was untainted by a hair's worth. Only then did all, high and low, within and without, believe the Master was pure and without flaw, and the matter of the false accusation became clear to the whole world. The circuit and prefecture were furious and wished to deal severely with the wicked monks; had it not been for the Master's intercession, they could hardly have escaped with their lives.

Seeing the Master was so noble and pure, the circuit and prefecture urged him again and again to stay in the mountain, but the Master was already weary of it and declined with all his might. He handed over the meditation hall to his disciple Huaiyu, and drifted away for good. At the earnest request of the disciples at Wuyang, he took up residence at the Changchun Hermitage in Wuyang.
When the Master left Caoxi, he composed ten quatrains to give to his disciples, of which the following three are recorded:
The seed of merit's field must be planted deep, / Cause and effect as on a bright mirror's face. / A thousand times you've come to the treasure-mount; / This time you must not go back empty again.

Labor with diligence, no fear of toil, / Think of the stone once hung about the waist. / When one breath fails, ten thousand aeons pass; / Without planting virtue's root the suffering's hard to erase.
[The stone once hung about the waist] The Sixth Patriarch once hung a stone about his waist while husking rice. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The Patriarch
(the Fifth Patriarch)
secretly went to the husking shed, and seeing Huineng
(Huineng)
husking rice with a stone about his waist, said, “One who seeks the Way should forget the body for the Dharma; is this not so?””

[Husking rice with a stone about the waist] In ancient times, when husking a great quantity of rice, the principle of the lever was used, with the pestle on one end and a person treading on the other. Huineng tied a great stone about his waist to add weight to his body, so that the counterweight on the opposite side, at the pestle, could be heavier, thereby increasing the efficiency of husking the rice.
Do not let a lifetime pass lightly by, / Time flies like an arrow, a thing to startle. / Only fear that when the breath fails so soon, / When will you come again to the treasure-mount?
When the Master went to the southern mountain, he left ten quatrains for his disciples of Lingnan, of which the following three are recorded:
The matter is clear before your very self, / Do not go outward asking of fortune and fate. / But turn back the light where'er you touch, / And let no worldly toil entangle the true master.

[This matter] This affair. [Before your very self] Practicing it yourself (carrying it out personally). [Worldly toil] The labor of the mind in the dusty realms; another name for affliction. [The true master] The master of the house, meaning one's intrinsic nature.

The great Way never was apart from the true root, / Most often division makes near kin and far. / You must see through the face born of your mother, / Only then are you one who truly discerns amid the dust.
For the Dharma, who would shrink from the long road
(the endless distance)
, / How can one call the miasmic sea the very end of the sky? / Let but a single drop of the water of Caoxi / Water the flower of five leaves come from the West
(the coming of the patriarch Bodhidharma from the West)

[The flower of five leaves] After the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, the Chan school branched into the five schools of Caodong, Linji, Yunmen, Weiyang, and Fayan, and so is called one flower with five leaves.

blocks.text: 21. The Journey to the East

inline.s: In the thirty-ninth year of the Wanli era (

), the Master was sixty-six. The Master was recuperating from illness at Dinghu Mountain in Duanzhou. There were many Confucian scholars who came to seek his instruction, and the Master wrote a Resolving Doubts on the Great Learning.

The next year the Master moved to the Changchun Hermitage at Wuyang, where he explained to his disciples the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana, the Verse on the Eight Consciousnesses, the Treatise on the Gateway of the Hundred Dharmas, and others. And because his Staccato Notes on the Lotus Sutra were so interconnected in meaning and structure that scholars could hardly grasp them, he also wrote the Sectional Notes on the Lotus Sutra.
In the fortieth year of the Wanli era (

), the Master was sixty-seven. The Master held the summer retreat at the Changchun Hermitage and explained the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment to his disciples. The exposition had barely reached half when suddenly a severe back abscess broke out, as large as a rice bowl; the several physicians who were called could not cure it, and his life hung by a thread. The great general of Wuyang was preparing to arrange the Master's last affairs. Just then a local physician named Liang Xingshan arrived, as if summoned by a spirit. As soon as he saw the Master's back abscess he said, “This is a beehive abscess, already very dangerous; if delayed any longer it will be beyond saving!” He at once went up the mountain to gather herbs, pounded and applied them, and there was an immediate effect; by winter he had completely recovered. After the abscess healed, the Master wrote an article to thank
(see
the Dream-Wander Collection, Preface Presented to the Good Physician Liang Xingshan

. The abscess the Master now had was the same as when he first learned to sit in meditation forty-eight years earlier, both being karmic debts from past lives. Though it had often broken out during these forty-eight years, it had always stopped after prayer, and this time was to be the final repayment of that karmic debt.

[Summer retreat] Also called abiding, meaning that during the three months of summer the monks may not go out at will, in order to devote themselves to sitting in meditation and cultivating the Dharma.
The next year

, the Master left the Changchun Hermitage for Hengyang, where he gave the precepts to the monks at the Great Virtue Monastery. The layman Feng Yuancheng built the Tanhua Hermitage for the Master, as a place for spreading the Dharma. At this time the Empress Dowager passed away, and the Master established a repaying-kindness bodhimanda here, and, facing the tablet of the Empress Dowager, shaved his head, gave thanks for the imperial favor, and put on the monk's robe again.
[Putting on the monk's robe again] The Master's monastic status was restored in
, and it was not until

, when the Empress Dowager passed away and he built the repaying-kindness bodhimanda, that he faced the tablet of the Empress Dowager, shaved his head, gave thanks for the imperial favor, and put on the monk's robe again. The depth of his gratitude is beyond words.

When the Master was at the Eastern Sea he had resolved to write a General Discussion of the Surangama, but because he had no leisure he had not begun it. In the fifth month of this year he set to work, and in fifty days the draft was finished. Just then his accomplished disciples Wuxin and Zhuanyu came to visit, and the Master composed verses to give them:
The verse Sending the Abbot Wuxinrong Back to Jingkou says:
In the empty mountain I thought to keep me to the end of years, / Who would have thought you'd go east and board the Dharma-boat?
Wait till above the sea gate the lonely moon arises, / And for this old monk round off the tale of the word.
The verse Asking After the Illness of Zhuanyu Heng says:
The four greats have long been seen as bubbles and shadows; / Where can the demon of illness find a place to hide?
The ancients had their own method of serene ease, / It lies only in the single thought of the unborn.
In the forty-third year of the Wanli era (

), the Master was seventy. In the spring of this year the Master explained the General Discussion of the Surangama to the assembly. In the fourth month the Master composed the General Discussion of the Lotus Sutra, because neither the Staccato Notes nor the Sectional Notes on the Lotus Sutra had fully threaded together the whole text; so he wrote this general discussion to make up for their omissions. Then the Master went on to explain the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana and to write the Annotated Summary of the Awakening of Faith.

The next year was the twelfth anniversary of Master Daguan's death, and the Master could not forget the bond of their friendship in the Dharma and had long wished to go in person to mourn him. In the fourth month the Master left Hudong, and at the Dragon Boat Festival came to Wuchang to pay homage to the great Buddha. He visited Mount Jiufeng and paid homage to the pagoda of Chan Master Wunian. In the sixth month he reached Xunyang, visited the Donglin Monastery, and wrote poems of remembrance of antiquity. He climbed Mount Lu to pay homage to the pagoda of Chan Master Chekong. In summer he sought relief from the heat at Jinzhu Ping, where he wrote the Commentary on the Zhao Treatise. The secluded beauty of Mount Lu made the Master wish to retire here. So he toured all the scenic spots of the mountain, spreading the Dharma with conditions along the way. In the seventh month he visited the Guizong Monastery
(located at the foot of Mount Lu in Jiangxi)
, climbed Golden Wheel Peak, paid homage to the relic pagoda, and left some poems here as well.
At this time a monk made a gift to the Master of the Wuru Temple
(located below the Wuru Peak south of Mount Lu)
, and the Master, seeing that it was very secluded and quiet, was quite pleased; later the disciples built a hermitage there.
In the eighth month the Master went to Huangmei
(today's Huangmei County in Hubei Province)

to pay homage to the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin and the Fifth Patriarch Hongren of the Chan school. He entered Purple Cloud Mountain, passed through Tongcheng, visited Mount Fu, climbed Mount Jiuhua, reached Jinsha, crossed Liang Creek, reached Mount Hui, passed through Wujiang, and all along the way met old friends and spoke of the Dharma, until at last he arrived at the Jizhao Hermitage on Mount Jing.

At Mount Jing, together with many of Master Daguan's disciples, the Master commemorated Master Daguan. The Master wrote a memorial, set it alight in cremation, and then placed Master Daguan's relics on Manjusri Terrace. His disciple Fakai built a pagoda, and the Master composed a pagoda inscription to be engraved before it.

That year the Master spent the New Year at Mount Jing, and opened the hall to expound the Essentials of Investigating Chan to the assembly. Because Fakai asked about the meaning of the Dharma-characteristic school, the Master wrote a Treatise on Worldly Characteristics. Around this time the Master also wrote a Song of the Plank-Carrying Fellow, together with its preface, which is quoted below:

The Dharma cave of Mount Jing, ever since Dahui revived the way of Linji, has continued the life of wisdom, and in each generation there have been those to carry it on. In recent times the Chan gate has fallen silent, its echo long gone. Lately, a throng of those practicing investigation has filled the mountain. Among them there are even some who, in a single glimpse
(seeing their nature)

, have had the reality appear before them and attained great freedom. What a pity they sit on the pure ground and will not let it go, taking it as something extraordinary, not knowing it has instead become a hindrance to the Dharma; in the teaching it is called the obstacle of what is known. Therefore the ancients said: “Even if you have done
(supposing you did so)

‘the bright moon in the cold pool, the bell in the still night, responding to the striker without loss, touching the waves without scattering’, this is still an affair on the shore of birth and death.” That is to say, it is easy to set foot among the brambles, but hard to turn your body beneath the moonlit curtain. People cling to the pole-top, still and sunk in dead water. Even this is not permitted to them, let alone those who, having not yet glimpsed, have casually attained a flash of lightning samadhi and take it as attainment, playing with the shadow of consciousness. This is taking a little as enough in the practice of Chan, the common sickness of all ages. Fearing it may fall into worldly discourse and mislead many, when someone asked for instruction, he laughingly wrote the Song of the Plank-Carrying Fellow to show him.

[Carrying-Board Man] A term of the Chan forest. Originally it meant a laborer who shoulders a plank: because he can see only what lies ahead and nothing to either side, the Chan gate uses him to picture one whose views are one-sided and cannot penetrate the whole. In this article it means those who practice Chan and are content with a little, who think that once they have reached “returning to the One” they have arrived at the ultimate, and so mistake the conjured city for the treasure ground. This clinging to “returning to the One” is like carrying a plank on the shoulders: one sees a single side and knows nothing of the whole. Therefore the song says:
“Pity him who sits upon the ground of dazzling white
(stalled in the state of returning to the One)
, unwilling to let it go, taking it for something wonderful, never knowing that it has instead become a dharma-obstruction.” “I urge you, do not carry
(do not cling to the state of “returning to the One”)

[Conjured City] A phantom city. It comes from the parable of the conjured city in the Lotus Sutra. The parable says: the place where all living beings attain buddhahood is the treasure ground, yet the road to that treasure ground is steep, perilous, and far. The Buddha, fearing that travelers would grow weary and turn back, conjured a city midway so that they might rest a while, gather their strength, and then press straight on to the treasure ground. The Buddha wished to bring all living beings to the fruit of buddhahood, but because beings are timid and weak and cannot bear the burden, he first taught the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle, so that having attained that nirvāṇa they might rest a while, and from there give rise to the greater resolve and advance toward the true treasure ground of the Greater Vehicle's nirvāṇa, the fruit of buddhahood. (For the full annotation see
“Notes on the Song of the Carrying-Board Man”
The song runs:
Carrying-board man, carrying-board man, how have you let it cheat you so?
You think only of lightening your shoulder, and never heed the stumble at your feet.
Though you carry it all the way to the time before your birth, it has long since blocked off half of you.
This plank, a cangue on your neck, makes all your flesh and bone belong to it.
If you do not fling it off at once, for a hundred thousand kalpas it will be your true foe.
Sitting, it wearies you; walking, it wearies you. The obstruction is plain to see, so why do you not know it?
Only because at the outset you mistook the false for the true, does a pure house and quiet door breed goblins and sprites.
With open eyes you see it, with closed eyes you see it: by broad daylight, lightning flashes from the empty sky.
A gandharva city shows its shadow in the void; the foolish child takes it for a heavenly palace.
To be light, you must put it down. A stinking dead toad, what price can it fetch?
Black beans offered to buy new eyes; a fish's eye must be told from the true pearl.
There is a road, and the best of all to walk, broad and level as the beam of a balance.
Only do not linger among the flowers and willows by the way, and you are sure to enter the imperial capital in years to come.
Give up body and life as you would the great earth; ox, horse, camel, donkey, you need not flee from them.
If you can really cast it over Mount Sumeru at one throw, the forest of swords and mountain of knives are a child's game.
If you cherish it, it will harm you; most burdens come of fretting to keep it.
One morning, when the lapis lazuli bottle is smashed, the great earth and its rivers and mountains are all ground to dust.
I urge you, do not carry it. The sweat on a skull dries on the spot.
Dividing the body, scattering shadows through a hundred thousand million worlds, from today he no longer enters the gate of death.

Reading the “Song of the Carrying-Board Man,” one finds in those vivid words, so deep in principle, a clear view of the scenery along the road of Chan and of the news of arriving home; it is truly a guide for real practice in the Chan gate.

blocks.text: 22. A Bodhisattva Appears in the World

inline.s: In the forty-fifth year of Wanli (

), the Master was seventy-two. In the first month he preached the precepts for the assembly at Jingshan, and when that was done he took leave of the Jingshan assembly and went to Mount Yunqi to mourn Master Yunqi. By then more than a thousand of Master Yunqi's disciples had long been waiting in the mountain. In the meditation hall the Master gave voice to the hidden practice of Master Yunqi during his lifetime, and as the disciples listened, some let fall tears and broke into sobs. They then asked the Master to write the “Pagoda Inscription for Master Yunqi Lianchi Hong”
(see
“Annotations on the Pagoda Inscription for Master Lianchi”
for the full text

As the Master came out of the mountain, Dharma Master Xuanjin, the layman Tan Mengxun, and many Confucian scholars and gentry entreated him to preach the great bodhisattva precepts at Jingci Monastery. At this time the Master wrote a “Record of the Hall of the Mirror of the Source”
(“Record of the Hall of the Mirror of the Source at Jingci Monastery, West Lake”)

Word of the Master's presence in Hangzhou drew many famous and virtuous men from all over the country. They gathered at West Lake, each setting forth his own views and raising objections, and the Master answered them one by one. The atmosphere was fervent; it was a dharma assembly of unequaled splendor among the assemblies of the Southeast.

Here Dharma Master Xuanjin and the layman Tan Mengxun gathered the scattered pieces the Master had written during his earlier travels into the Eastern Journey Collection and had it printed for the world.

By now the Master's practice had ripened to full roundness. Though he taught the Dharma everywhere, he had no need to carry a fly whisk or a staff with him. His face was clear and glossy as jade, and his body exceedingly strong; even walking in the fiercest heat, he showed not the least sweat. When he washed morning and evening, the water in the basin remained clear and unstirred. When he sat, it was always in the full cross-legged posture, and he needed no help from his hands. Closing his eyes he entered samādhi, opening them he rose from it; by day or by lamplight, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, it was always so. Day or night, in all four postures, as soon as he heard another request a Dharma phrase, he opened his eyes and their light was like lightning. There was not the least residue in his eye sockets, nor did he need to wipe them with his hand. When he mounted the seat to teach, his eloquence was unobstructed; once he opened his mouth it was thousands of words, and he never swallowed a single one, while his voice was like a great bell, shaking all outside the hall. When he took up his brush to write instructional phrases, he did not rise from his seat, and at a stroke there were thousands of words, the brush never pausing. Ordinarily, his left hand was forever turning a recitation-bead string, while his right hand held a folding fan with a white bamboo frame; winter or summer it was always in his hand, raised but never waved, folded but never opened. Whenever some great matter of directing gods and men in the three realms arose, one blow on his desk and nothing failed to respond.

The manifestations of the Master's power of the Way and his spiritual penetrations were beyond counting. Once, while he was at the Hall of the Mirror of the Source, he had just ascended the seat to teach when he saw two monks supporting a third up the steps, and the monk they supported was raving without pause. The two monks begged the Master, saying: “This brother of ours has kept the Great Compassion Mantra for five years and has always behaved properly; we do not know why he has been possessed and come to this. Please, Master, cure him!” The Master said: “This illness can be cured!” He ordered an attendant to find three monks in the hall who kept the Ucchuṣma Vajra Spirit Mantra. First the Master himself held the spirit mantra in his seat, then he told the three monks to transmit the spirit mantra to the raving monk. At first the man was unconscious of anything; the Master struck the desk with his fan in awesome might, and as soon as he raised a phrase and gave it to him, the raving monk could repeat it after him. When the phrases had been transmitted one by one in this way, the raving monk woke as from a dream and at once returned to normal.

On another day a monk came to bow to him. Before the bow was finished, the Master struck his fan and shouted at him: “Murdering thief, what do you want with me?!” The guest-prefect monk heard and came hurrying, and the bowing monk went off without a word. The whole assembly stared in astonishment, unable to understand. The next day this monk was arrested by the authorities, and only then did the assembly understand the Master's marvelous working of spiritual penetration.

The Master's spiritual feats are too many to name one by one. Once more, when the Master was in the meditation hall of Jinming Monastery in Jiaxing, he was discoursing on the Buddha Dharma with friends of the Way one evening, when suddenly a man with a club in his hand came shouting outside the hall door. Someone who knew him said he was a yamen runner named Qian in the grain office, and everyone took him for drunk and wanted to drive him off. But not only would he not go, he shouted the louder, and mixed Buddhist terms into his voice: “Today a living bodhisattva has come down; it is time I were saved! Do not you stand in my way.” The others found this strange and went to tell the Master. The Master said: “Let him come in.” The moment the man entered he joined his palms and bowed, with the full dignity of a son of the Buddha. The assembly watched him in wonder as he knelt on both knees and said: “Your disciple Zhong Riren kept a long fast in his lifetime and practiced the Pure Land for eight years. Today is the seventh-day period of my death, and I have borrowed the body of the runner Qian to beg the Master to save me. I do not wish to go to the underworld; I want to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. I beg the bodhisattva in his compassion to guide me.” With that he fell to the ground weeping, sobbing without cease. The Master had six elders of the assembly who devoted themselves to the Pure Land stand in attendance; he himself twirled the recitation beads, gave him a string of beads, and told him to recite the Buddha's name a thousand times. The body possessed by the spirit could follow along in the recitation, and the whole hall was hushed and silent. When the recitation ended, the Master in turn expounded the text of the Mengshan Food-Bestowal Rite, and when he came to the line, “One should contemplate the nature of the dharma realm: all is made by mind alone,” he raised his fan, struck the desk, and cried out: “Be freed at once!” The man answered: “Freed indeed!” Thus three calls and three answers in succession, with the speed of thought. Afterwards the possessed body rose and stood, with the full dignity of a son of the Buddha, and thanked the Master for attaining rebirth in the Pure Land. He bowed again to the assembly on either side, east and west, and said: “Strive each of you; let us meet at the Dragon Flower Assembly!” At that time the assembly was still gathered in the meditation hall and had not dispersed; some were weeping, some sighing, some secretly laughing to themselves, and some even whispering criticism, while the Master remained unmoved and utterly at ease. He followed the crowd as they escorted the Master to the riverbank to board his boat (the Master was lodging on the boat), and in gratitude he bowed to the Master. Then he returned as before to the door of the meditation hall, said a few words of thanks to old Master Qian for the loan of his body and for attaining deliverance, and suddenly fell to the ground and woke, and was the same runner Qian as before. At this a man nearby who knew the matter said: “Zhong Riren is the father of the scholar Zhong across the river, and in his lifetime he practiced the Pure Land with great devotion; this response was indeed only fitting.” The Master's newly converted lay disciple Fu Zheng was standing by and said: “That scholar Zhong is my society friend Zhong Shengfu.” Thereupon he went with several dozen good men and women to call at his house. When they arrived, they learned that Zhong Riren had been dead for thirty-five days, the full seventh-day period, and that the runner Qian, having come to press for grain, had arrived before his spirit tablet, and Zhong Riren had seized the moment when he was drunk to borrow his body and gain deliverance.

A few days later there was a layman, Xu Taiwei, who had long believed in the Buddha. Having seen the Master's spiritual responses, he invited the Master to his house, set up a spirit tablet for his father, and begged the Master to preach the Dharma. In that one discourse the Master pointed out at every turn the hidden deeds of his father's life, and all who heard were overawed by the Master's astonishing power of the Way.

In only a few days people ran to tell one another that a living bodhisattva had appeared in the world. Men and women, old and young, all held a devout wish to see the Master once. Just then the Master was at the East Pagoda, and in a moment the people came surging in; thousands upon thousands filled the whole space from the mountain gate to the abbot's quarters, and the cries of those who wanted to see the Master rose wave upon wave. Then the Master and a few attendants went to a second-story window of the East Pagoda and bowed in compassion to the crowd. The moment the people saw the Master, the crowd bowed and rose like rising smoke and cloud. From the Master's virtue and spiritual penetration they saw the greatness of Buddhism, and the devotion and joy in their hearts passed all words; they bowed on until after nightfall, and only then did they gradually disperse.

The next day the tide of people coming to bow and make offerings to the Master still surged without cease. The Master felt that this could not go on, and on the third day he crossed the river to Songling.

[Editors' Note] The original text of the deeds above is found in the Chronicle of Master Hanshan with Annotation, and was seen with his own eyes by Fu Zheng, the author of that chronicle and a disciple of Master Hanshan. The Chronicle with Annotation says:
“Zheng
(Fu Zheng)
wherever he went
(the Master's)
power of the Way and spiritual penetration reached, witnessed a hundred kinds with his own eyes, and briefly recorded the chief of them.”

blocks.text: 23. Pointing the Way to the Pure Land

inline.s: In the forty-sixth year of Wanli (

), the Master was seventy-three. That year he began building the Buddha hall and the meditation hall at Wuru Monastery. Following the fine rule of Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, who recited the Buddha's name at the six periods of the day, the Master burned incense in place of the water clock, and he charged his disciples to make a finely wrought image of the Three Saints of the West in the Buddha hall.

[Wuru Monastery] It stands below Five Wuru Peaks on the southern side of Mount Lu and is also called Wuru Cloister; it was first built in the Song dynasty. When Master Hanshan came here from Caoxi he took a liking to the mountains and waters of the place and enlarged and rebuilt the monastery. After the expansion Wuru Monastery's fame rose swiftly, its incense offerings flourished as never before, and pilgrims and visitors came in an unbroken stream. The monastery housed portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs of Buddhism, the masterwork of the Xin'an painter Ding Yunpeng, with a record composed by the Jingling-school poet Tan Yuanchun.

The following year, when the halls were finished, the Master began in the first month to recite the Avataṃsaka Sutra, and during this time he also expounded for the assembly the General Commentary on the Lotus Sutra. In summer he further expounded for the assembly the Śūraṅgama Sutra, the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, the Diamond Sutra, the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Consciousness-Only Treatise, and others.
