On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, when the sutra-lecture assembly was completed, the Master sealed himself in retreat for quiet practice and turned away all outside involvements. In his quiet room the Master burned incense in place of the water clock and recited the Buddha's name at the six periods
(twelve hours)
, with his mind fixed wholly on the Pure Land.

[Burning incense in place of the water clock, reciting the Buddha's name at the six periods, with the mind fixed wholly on the Pure Land] In his letter “Reply to the Grand Historian Qian Shouzhi” Master Hanshan wrote:
“Now within the retreat
(within the sealed retreat)
all Chan talk and Buddha Dharma is put up on a high shelf, and I simply keep to my dullness
(simply reciting the Buddha's name with one mind; “keeping to my dullness” here means no longer investigating Chan or studying the teachings)
I follow in particular Master Yuan[gong], with the lotus clock of the six periods
(the “lotus clock” is the lotus water clock: Huiyao, a disciple of Master Huiyuan, told the time at the Mount Lu way-place with a lotus made into a clepsydra)
, and with incense in place of the flower
(in place of the lotus clock I burn incense to tell the time)
. For several months now,
body and mind have of themselves reached the Land of Ultimate Bliss
Dream-Journey Collection

Before long the Master reflected that the Huayan school was in danger of being lost, because the text of Qingliang's commentary and subcommentary is vast and its meaning profuse, and the resolve of students does not reach so far, so that most dared not go deep into it. The Master therefore took only the essential purport of the commentary and set his brush to writing the Essentials of the Avataṃsaka Sutra, which played a part in the revival of the Huayan school.
In the forty-eighth year of Wanli (

), the Master was seventy-five. In the spring of that year his attendant Guangyi asked the Master to compose the Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Direct Explanation of the Awakening of Faith, and the Commentary on the Inner Seven Chapters of Zhuangzi.

In summer the Master's feet became diseased and walking was difficult. In autumn many laymen came up the mountain to ask about the Way; the Master taught them the Buddha Dharma from his sickbed, and also wrote more than seventy short biographies of the patriarchs of successive generations, each with a verse of praise appended, and had them circulated in the world.

It was already eight years since the Master had left Caoxi for Mount Lu, and those disciples who remained at Caoxi missed him day and night. They often sent representatives to Mount Lu to inquire after him and to ask him to return to Caoxi, but the Master would not consent. Later many lay disciples of Caoxi also came to invite the Master, and with illness as his excuse he politely declined their sincere offers.

In the summer of the following year the assembled disciples asked the Master to expound his Notes on the Śūraṅgama Sutra. In the tenth month the Master's disciple, the provincial graduate Liu Qixiang, and others again asked the Master to go to Caoxi, and again he declined on the grounds of illness.
In the second year of Tianqi (

), the Master was seventy-seven. That year he completed the Essentials of the Avataṃsaka Sutra. He also expounded for the assembly the Śūraṅgama Sutra, the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, and the Treatises of Sengzhao. At this time Wu, the prefect of Caoxi, the prefect of Shaoyang, and many other disciples asked the Master a third time to go to Caoxi, and since he could not bring himself to refuse, he decided to make the journey. That winter the Master left Mount Lu, crossed Lake Peng, and on the eighth day of the twelfth month reached the south of the passes, entering Caoxi on the fifteenth. There, at the request of the assembly, the Master began to write his chronological autobiography.
In the third year of Tianqi (

), the Master was seventy-eight. In spring the prefect of Shaoyang and other laymen came into the mountain to ask the Master to preach, and disciples such as those of the Fasheng community of Wuyang also came to Caoxi. Though the Master was already advanced in years, his bodhisattva compassion and his giving of Dharma knew no weariness: in the meditation hall he first preached the great precepts for the assembly, then expounded the Awakening of Faith, the Consciousness-Only Treatise, and the Śūraṅgama Sutra.

In the eighth month the Master sent an attendant to thank Prefect Wu for the sincerity of his protection of the Dharma. As the attendant was about to set out, the Master charged him, saying: “In a buddha-patriarch's spreading of the Dharma, what matters is the season and the causal conditions. When conditions conflict with the season, to whom shall the teaching be entrusted? Once this one period's work is done, I shall be going home!” The assembly heard this in bewilderment, and took it that the Master meant to return to Mount Lu.

On the Double Ninth Festival the Master wrote out the “Poems of Mountain Dwelling” for his attendant Shenguang. In the postscript he said: “Though this old man is lazy with brush and inkstone, I fear that if a single breath does not come again I shall leave another debt for a future life. If you look at these only as poetry and calligraphy, then you do me great wrong!”

On the first day of the tenth month his disciple Tongjiong came from Mount Lu to pay his respects to the Master, and the Master asked after all the resident assembly of Wuru Monastery and the elders of the various monasteries in the mountain, greatly pleased at heart. Then his disciple Jingtai asked the Master to write a “Self-Eulogy” setting out the gist of his life.

On the third day of the tenth month the Junior Minister (vice-president of the Ministry of Personnel) Xiao Xuanpu came into the mountain to visit the Master. The Master talked with him for three days and nights, and when the Junior Minister asked for the essentials of the Dharma, the Master wrote out two Dharma phrases and three poems and gave them to him.

On the sixth day the Junior Minister came out of the mountain, and the Master charged him, saying: “You are the hope of the altars of soil and grain and of the common people; take good care of yourself on the road ahead!” The Junior Minister made an appointment with the Master to meet again, and the Master said: “This mountain monk is old, and the four elements are about to leave me. The time for you and me to meet again will be at the Dragon Flower Assembly!”
[Dragon Flower Assembly]

Bodhisattva Bodhisattva Maitreya now dwells in the Inner Court of the Tuṣita Heaven, and in the future he will descend into the human world and attain buddhahood; under the dragon flower tree in the Dragon Flower Garden he will hold a dharma assembly to save gods and men universally, and this is called the “Dragon Flower Assembly.”
On the eighth day the Master showed a slight illness, and the assembled disciples all came to inquire after him. The Master said to them: “This old man is weary, it is not illness!”

On the ninth day his disciples brought the Master medicine, and the Master said: “I am about to go; what use is medicine to me!” When his attendant Guangyi heard this, his face changed greatly, and he said: “Should the Master pass away
(a euphemism for death)

, what charge have you to leave us?” The Master rebuked him, saying: “You have attended this old man for many years; how can you hold such a view?” Then he said to the assembly: “You should bear in mind that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence swift; recite the Buddha's name in earnest!” Guangyi asked again: “If the Master will not leave a single word, how shall we follow it in practice?” The Master said: “What the golden mouth proclaimed has already become old paper; what use are my words!” And so he left not a single word.

On the twelfth day of the tenth month, which was the Master's birthday, monks and lay disciples gathered in clouds at Caoxi. The prefect of Shaoyang came into the mountain and presented a purple silk Chan robe to wish the Master long life, and the two sat facing one another in talk for a whole day. In the evening, after the prefect had gone out, the Master called his attendant to bring water for a bath. The next morning the Master put on the purple silk robe the prefect had given and went to take his leave of him. When the prefect came again to the Master's couch, the Master said to him: “This mountain monk is going. Many thanks for the great protector's abundant kindness of heart!” The prefect said: “The Master's dharma body knows no illness; this unworthy one
(my humble self-designation)
who guards the soil of this place is its host, and everything rests with this unworthy one.” The Master heard this, smiled, joined his palms, and gave thanks.

At noon the prefect took his leave and went down the mountain, and the Master called his attendant to bring pure water to rinse his mouth, saying: “Today I cut off the trailing vines.” He then called for hot water to bathe and change his robes. After that he gathered the assembly around him to recite the Buddha's name. When the sound of the recitation ceased, the Master said to the assembly: “Do not be alarmed. Follow the Buddha's rule: you may not wear hemp and mourning, and you may not weep. You must recite the Buddha's name with one mind!”
At the hour of Shen
(three to five in the afternoon)

, the eye of gods and men, the guide of the three realms, sat upright and passed away. That night a ray of white light lit up the sky, the birds in the mountain gave forth mournful cries, and the sound of the monks' and lay disciples' grief shook the valleys.
After the Master's parinirvāṇa his face remained as clean and glossy as jade, his lips as red and moist as ever, his hands and feet as soft as ever, just as in his usual samādhi.

[Editors' Note] In his later years Master Hanshan sealed himself in retreat at Five Wuru Peaks on Mount Lu to recite the Buddha's name, and in the his “Self-Preface to the Chronicle” in the Dream-Journey Collection
Self-Preface to the Chronicle he wrote:
“In the forty-seventh year, the year jiwei, I was seventy-four.
At the full moon of the eighth month
(the fifteenth day of the eighth month)
I sealed myself in retreat and shut out conditions, following Master Yuan
(Master Huiyuan, first patriarch of the Pure Land school)
and at the six periods
(twelve hours)
burning incense in place of the water clock,
with my mind fixed wholly on the Pure Land work
In the letter “Reply to the Grand Historian Qian Shouzhi” he wrote:
“Now within the retreat
(within the sealed retreat)
all Chan talk and Buddha Dharma is put up on a high shelf, and I simply keep to my dullness
(simply reciting the Buddha's name with one mind; “keeping to my dullness” here means no longer investigating Chan or studying the teachings)
I follow in particular Master Yuan[gong], with the lotus clock of the six periods
(the “lotus clock” is the lotus water clock: Huiyao, a disciple of Master Huiyuan, told the time at the Mount Lu way-place with a lotus made into a clepsydra)
, and with incense in place of the flower
(in place of the lotus clock I burn incense to tell the time)
. For several months now,
body and mind have of themselves reached the Land of Ultimate Bliss
(Dream-Journey Collection)
Master Hanshan entered parinirvāṇa on the thirteenth day of the tenth month in the third year of Tianqi (
), at the age of seventy-eight. It is recorded in the Chronicle of Master Hanshan with Annotation:
On the twelfth day, the Master's birthday
(his date of birth)

, monks and lay disciples gathered in clouds. The prefect of Shaoyang, Lord Zhang Sanxing, came into the mountain and presented a purple silk Chan robe to wish the Master long life, and they sat talking together the whole day. When evening came, Lord Zhang went out. That night he called three times for water to bathe.

Early the next morning he at once called for the Chan robe Lord Zhang had given, put it on, and took leave of Lord Zhang. When Lord Zhang came again to his couch, the Master said: ‘This mountain monk is going. Many thanks for the great protector's abundant kindness of heart.’ Lord Zhang said: ‘The Master's dharma body knows no illness; this unworthy one
(a humble self-designation, meaning “without talent”)
who guards the soil of this place is its host, and everything rests with this unworthy one.’ The Master smiled, joined his palms, and gave thanks.
At noon

, Lord Zhang took his leave, and he at once called his attendant to bring pure water to rinse his mouth, saying: ‘Today I cut off the trailing vines.’ He still called for hot water to bathe and change his robes, and
the assembly gathered around him to recite the Buddha's name
. He charged them, saying: ‘You must not be alarmed. Follow the Buddha's rule: you may not wear hemp and mourning, and you may not weep.
Recite the Buddha's name with one mind
Right at the hour of Shen
(three in the afternoon)

the Master sat upright and passed away. That night a ray of white light lit up the sky, the flocks of birds cried mournfully, and the monks' and lay disciples' grief shook the valleys. When he had passed away he sat upright for three days, his face white, his lips red, his hands and feet soft and pliant, as though he had entered samādhi.
This shows that Master Hanshan recited the Buddha's name and was reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Master Hanshan not only recited the Buddha's name himself and sought rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, but also firmly held that every dharma door should point the way home to the Pure Land. In the “Preface Pointing the Way to the Pure Land” in the Dream-Journey Collection
the Pure Land, the Master wrote:
“The
Pure Land

is the one door that covers all three capacities alike; the sudden and the gradual enter it together, and no capacity is left unembraced. This is what is called transcending the three realms sideways;
it is the supreme dharma door
Of all the patriarchs from of old, of all who have awakened to mind, there has never been one who did not take this as his home
, as Nāgārjuna
(Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna)
and Aśvaghoṣa
(Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa)
praised and proclaimed it with all their might
.” “For one of the highest capacity in the Chan school,
there is none who does not return to the Pure Land
Five days before his entry into quiescence he admonished his attendant, saying:
“You should bear in mind that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence swift;
recite the Buddha's name in earnest
(Chronicle of Master Hanshan with Annotation)
The Master's disciples sent word to the prefect, and the prefect at once dispatched officials to condole and to seal the reliquary for the Master.

At this time the Junior Minister Xiao Xuanpu had been parted from the Master only five days and was still at Xiongzhou. Hearing the news of the Master's passing, he grieved the whole day. When he also heard the circumstances of the Master's death, he was greatly cheered and said: “The Master is one of the holy ranks; had he not penetrated the barrier of birth and death through and through, how could he have had such freedom!” He at once composed a mourning address and sent it, and also donated two hundred taels and wrote a letter charging the prefects of Nan and Shao to build a shadow hall for the Master.

When the disciples at Wuru Monastery on Mount Lu heard the news of the Master's passing, the disciple Fushan and others set out at once for Caoxi. On the twenty-first day of the first month they bore the Master's reliquary back to Wuru, and on the twenty-eighth day of the second month they reached Fayun Monastery at Five Wuru Peaks in Mount Kuang.

blocks.text: 24. Diamond Indestructibility

inline.s: After the disciples had escorted the Master's physical body to Mount Lu, because the climate of Mount Lu is damp and overcast his attendant Fushan built a pagoda court and installed the Master's bodily reliquary in offering above the pagoda.

Eleven years later, fierce tigers wrought havoc on Mount Lu, and Fayun Monastery at Five Wuru Peaks was in danger. Fushan, fearing for the safety of the pagoda site, reverently brought out the Master's bodily reliquary. Seeing that half of the protecting reliquary had been eaten away by insects and ants, he dared not proceed with burial and sealed it in the pagoda as before.

Nine years after that, the disciples of Lingnan, Chen Zongbo and Liu Qixiang and others, entrusted by the Buddhist circles of Caoxi, went to Mount Lu to welcome the Master home to Caoxi. When the Master's physical body had been escorted as far as Meiling, they happened to meet the newly appointed commander of Guangdong
(another name for the chief military commander)
Song Zhaoming, who ordered his soldiers to carry the reliquary by cart and escorted it in person to Caoxi.

Only a few months after taking up his post, Song Zhaoming came again to Caoxi. At this time the disciples guarding the reliquary, Guangcheng and Cili, saw that the reliquary chamber had cracked, and on their own bored a small hole in the crack to peep inside. They saw the Master's physical body sitting upright as in life, and wanted to open the chamber, yet their hearts wavered. When Song Zhaoming learned of it he drew his sword and split the crack open. They saw the Master sitting cross-legged and upright, as dignified as in life; his nails and hair were still growing, the color of his skin was still fresh and red, and his clothes and shoes were like new. Then a gust of wind came, and the clothing suddenly broke apart like scattering cloud and flying stars, dancing away on the wind; the local people gathered the pieces up as tokens of auspiciousness.
Just then a monk suddenly appeared and asked to use an Indian
(ancient Indian)
method to protect the Master's physical body. With the assembly's consent he smeared the Master's body with sandalwood powder from Hainan, like lacquer. This done, the monk went off of himself.

During the Master's lifetime a devout maiden of Caoxi had vowed to embroider a robe of a thousand buddhas as an offering to the Master. Fearing that her breath was impure, she covered her mouth with yellow silk as she worked. When the robe of a thousand buddhas was finished, the Master had already entered the reliquary, and the robe was kept in the storehouse of Baolin. Now this robe was brought out again and draped over the Master's physical body; though twenty years had passed, its radiance dazzled the eye, as if newly made. The disciples installed the Master's physical body in the old pagoda court for offerings, naming it Hanshan Monastery, about half a li from Nanhua Monastery, where the physical body of the Sixth Patriarch rests.

[Editors' Note] The Chronicle of Master Hanshan with Annotation says: the deeds above were written down from personal witness by Guangcheng and Ciren. Guangcheng was abbot of Fayun Monastery and Ciren abbot of Qixia Monastery; they were the Dharma kin who attended in person on the two journeys to Caoxi, first to welcome the reliquary and then to escort it back. Guangcheng was a disciple personally transmitted by Master Hanshan, and Ciren was Guangcheng's disciple. The Chronicle with Annotation records:
“Master Xuzhong, whose name was Guangyi, at the Baolin assembly
(the Chan session presided over by Master Hanshan in the Baolin Meditation Hall of Nanhua Monastery at Caoxi)
personally realized nirvāṇa.
Master Xuzhong had a disciple Ciren, styled Jianru, who was abbot of Qixia.”

Following the custom of making offerings to the Sixth Patriarch, the disciples each morning used a bowl of hot fragrant water to steam the Master's face until it broke into sweat, then wiped it dry with a towel, and afterward made food offerings just as in his lifetime. Once a year they also bathed the body.

Every year in the second and eighth months Buddhist disciples from all over the country came up the mountain in companies to pay homage to Master Hanshan's physical body. With hearts full of reverence, they bowed and made vows before the Master, drawing from him the spiritual strength to seek the Buddha Way above and transform living beings below. More than four hundred years later, the Master still sits there upright in his adamantine body, firm and indestructible. Who says the Master has passed away? Does the Master not still watch over the human world with those compassionate eyes and benefit all living beings?
Master Yinguang praised him, saying:
Master Hanshan, a great manifestation of spiritual power. His merit in spreading the Dharma was deep, yet the jealous slandered him.
He was banished to guard Guangzhou, thereby warding off calamity. Fortunately there was a great official who looked on him with special regard.
He spread the Dharma at Caoxi, renewing the severed life of wisdom. Speaking the Dharma in accord with occasion, great abuses dissolved.
Protecting the country and comforting the people, his merit rose to the rank of an honored counselor. After his passing, his body remained, unrotted and unchanged.
Guangdong and Jiangxi contended, and he was carried back to the banks of Caoxi. The Sixth and Seventh Ancestors are proclaimed in the proverbs of the time.
He added luster to the sun of Buddha, serving as a moat and rampart for the Dharma. His writings are vast and broad, bright as sun and moon.
(In the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Inscription on the Six-Verse Handscroll of Master Hanshan)
[The Sixth and Seventh Ancestors
The Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan says:

'Every year the pilgrims of Caoxi, in the second and eighth months, people from the whole province enter the mountain to pay homage; and after offering incense to the Sixth Ancestor, they say they will offer incense to the Seventh Ancestor — hence the title 'the Seventh Ancestor of Caoxi.'

blocks.text: 25. Returning by the Power of His Vow

inline.s: Master Yinguang said:
'Hanshan's former vow was not yet fulfilled, so again he manifested birth as Jieliu
(Master Xingce)
. He denounced those who cultivate the blessings of the human and heavenly realms, saying they are truly the peers of the icchantika and candala
(they are precisely the class of the icchantika and candala)

. The mind of Buddha and of my own self is originally no different; Buddha is already accomplished while I have not yet cultivated. If one would have mind and Buddha both without difference, one should seek it through recollecting and reciting the Buddha.'
(From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · the Tenth Patriarch of the Qing, Master Xingce of Puren Monastery, Yushan)

[Icchantika] The brief form of e-icchantika, meaning one who does not believe in cause and effect, commits the five heinous offences and the ten evil acts, cuts off all roots of good, and falls into the avici hell. [Candala (
zhān
)] The brief form of candala; here it denotes evil people.
[Those who cultivate the blessings of the human and heavenly realms]

In the later Essay on Urging the Arousal of True Faith, Master Xingce taught: without real faith, although one recites the Buddha's name and observes a pure diet, releases lives and cultivates merit, still one is only a good person of this world, who at the end of life is reborn in a good place and there enjoys bliss. While enjoying that bliss he then creates evil karma; and having created evil karma, he must fall into evil paths. Seen with right eyes, compared with the classes of the icchantika and candala, he is only a single step short.
Master Xingce
, the tenth patriarch of the Pure Land school)
was a native of Yixing, Jiangsu, of lay surname Jiang, styled Jieliu.
His father Jiang
Quanchang was versed in both Confucianism and Buddhism,
and was
Master Hanshan's
intimate
bosom friend.
Five years after
Master Hanshan passed away,
Jiang
Quanchang dreamed
that he saw Master Hanshan, leaning on his
monk's staff,
walk
into the
inner
chamber, and thereby Xingce was born; because of this
he gave him the
name Menghan. When he grew up and his parents died one after another, he roused the resolve to leave the world. At twenty-three
years of age
he went to the Ruo
ruò
hermitage of Li'an Monastery in Wulin to take refuge under Master Wengong. He sat long without lying down
not lying on a bed at night
for five years, and suddenly penetrated the very source of the Dharma.

After Master Wengong passed away, Master Xingce at Baoen Monastery met a fellow practitioner, Master Ying of Xi'an Hermitage, who urged him to cultivate the pure karma. Later he met Master Qiaoshi of Qiantang, who guided him to read the doctrine of the Tiantai school. He then entered a pure chamber together with Qiaoshi and practiced the Lotus samadhi. The wisdom of his past lives thereupon became suddenly clear, and he completely awakened to the essence of the Tiantai teaching.
In the second year of Kangxi

, he built a thatched hut on a small islet in the Western Creek of Fahua Mountain in Hangzhou, and there devoted himself solely to the Pure Land practice, and so named the place where he dwelt 'Fu-Lian Hermitage'
(fu
fū
, a flower calyx)
. In the ninth year of Kangxi
, he dwelt at Puren Monastery on Yushan, and advocated establishing a Pure Land Lotus Society, and those who followed gathered from all sides.
The master
wrote
an
Essay on Urging the Arousal of True Faith:
The samadhi of Buddha-recitation has a long and distant origin.
Though it is said to be
of high merit and easy to advance in, yet practitioners in the last age seldom
obtain
any
efficacious
response;
this
is all because their faith and vows are not single-minded,
for they have not
been able
to take faith and vows
as the guide for practice, nor to make rebirth in the Pure Land the essential matter.

[Guiding practice by faith and vows] Let faith and vows direct one's practice, and moreover be carried out in practice. [Taking rebirth in the Pure Land as the essential matter] For one who recites the Buddha's name, rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss should be regarded as the foremost great matter.
Now,
having
already
widely invited good companions to cultivate together the pure cause, if one does not
carefully
examine
whether
the
faith
mind
that has been aroused is true
how can one know
the
essential
path
to escape suffering
All the fellow practitioners who join this
dharma assembly
must certainly
all
possess
true faith.
If
one has
no true faith,
then though
one
recites the Buddha's name
and observes a pure diet
, releases lives and cultivates merit,
still he is
only a good person of this world,
who at death
is reborn in a good place
and
enjoys bliss. In enjoying that bliss he then creates
evil
karma; and having created
evil
karma, he must fall into
evil paths.
Seen with right eyes,
compared
with the icchantika
and the candala
class,
he is only
one step short
and nothing more
Such
faith, how can it be true? What is called
true faith
is:
First, one must believe that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are in three respects without difference. I am an unaccomplished Buddha,
Amitābha Buddha
is an accomplished Buddha;
the awakened nature of each
the two is without difference. Though I
am
bewildered and upside down,
yet
my awakened nature has never
been
lost.
Though I have
turned
through the
wheel for countless eons,
yet
my awakened nature has never been
moved
Therefore it is said:
'In a single thought, turning back the light, one is the same as what was originally gained
Second, one must believe that I am a Buddha in principle
and a Buddha in name,
while Amitābha Buddha
is the ultimate Buddha.
Though the
nature is
without a second,
yet
the
stages
are as
far apart
as heaven and the deep.
If one does not single-mindedly recollect that Buddha and seek rebirth in his land, one will surely drift along with karma and undergo immeasurable suffering. What is called
the Dharma-body flowing through the five destinies
(gods, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals)
is not to be called Buddha,
but
is called a sentient being.

[Buddha in principle, Buddha in name] These are the first two of the six stages of Buddhahood. [Six stages of Buddhahood] The six stages that mark the course of a common being's practice up to Buddhahood:
First

, the Buddha in principle (the noumenal Buddha): all sentient beings, though they revolve in the six destinies and abide daily amid the dust of afflictions, turning their back on the awakened essence, yet the merit of Buddhahood is still fully present, so it is called 'the Buddha in principle.' Second, the Buddha in name: whether from a good teacher or from the scriptures, one hears that the very mind inherently possesses the unborn, undying Buddhahood, and through the name comprehends it, suddenly awakening, so it is called 'the Buddha in name.' Third, the Buddha in contemplation and practice: not only does one understand the name, but further one contemplates and practices according to the teaching; the mind's contemplation is clear, and the principle and wisdom correspond, so it is called 'the Buddha in contemplation and practice.'
(Here 'principle' is the object of contemplation, and 'wisdom' is the wisdom that contemplates; for 'correspond' means

mutually fitting — that is, the realm and the wisdom are in accord, and words and deeds are consistent.) Fourth, the Buddha in near-resemblance: the practitioner at this stage, in contemplation, contemplates more and more clearly, and in stillness becomes more and more still; though not truly awakened and realized, yet he is near the principle, as though truly realized, so it is called 'the Buddha in near-resemblance.' Fifth, the Buddha in partial realization: this is after the ten stages of faith, when one breaks a portion of ignorance and realizes a portion of the three virtues, entering the first abiding stage and realizing the Dharma-body; from here one becomes a Dharma-body great being, and from the first abiding stage on, breaking ignorance and realizing the three virtues stage by stage up to equal enlightenment, passing through forty-one stages and breaking forty-one portions, so it is called 'the Buddha in partial realization.' Sixth, the Buddha in ultimate realization: from equal enlightenment one breaks the final portion of ignorance, and then delusion is exhausted and the true is pure, completely realizing the Tathāgata nature inherent in this very body and entering the stage of wondrous enlightenment to become a Buddha, so it is called 'the Buddha in ultimate realization.' [Three virtues] First, the virtue of the Dharma-body; second, the virtue of prajna; third, the virtue of liberation.
Third, one must believe that though I
have
heavy obstructions and deep karma and have long dwelt in the realm of suffering, yet I am
a sentient being within the heart of
Amitābha Buddha.
Amitābha Buddha
though
he
is adorned with ten thousand virtues and far away beyond ten thousand
trillion

Buddha-lands, is the Buddha within my heart. Since the mind-nature is without a second, naturally the spiritual response and the path commune with each other, like a magnet drawing iron, beyond doubt. What is called
recollecting and reciting the Buddha, now and hereafter one will surely see the Buddha, never far from the Buddha
is this.
[Spiritual response and the path in mutual communion] The response of sentient beings and the response of Amitābha Buddha commune with each other.
One who is possessed of the above true faith
and
vow
mind

, though a single hair's worth of goodness or a mote of merit, may all be dedicated to the West and adorn the Pure Land. How much more so observing a pure diet and holding precepts, releasing lives and giving alms, reciting the Mahayana, and making offerings to the Three Jewels — all these good practices, how could they not fill the provisions for the Pure Land
Only because the point of faith is not true do they fall into the cause of the conditioned
(the outflows)

. Therefore, in the present practice there is no other essential method than adding these three kinds of true faith throughout the two six-hour periods of the day; then all the goodness done is not in vain.
Cause of the conditioned (outflows)
] The karmic cause that brings the retribution of the three realms (the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm). [In vain (tang juan)] Cast aside in vain.
The master further
put forth the effort of a
Buddha-recitation
retreat of seven days,
and
composed a piece to show the assembly:

In these seven days of holding the name and reciting the Buddha, what is prized is a single-minded, unconfused state, unbroken and unmingled, not the swiftness and multitude of the recitation. One should be neither too slow nor too urgent, holding the name closely and closely, so that the Buddha-name in the heart is clear, distinctly perceived. Whether dressing or eating, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the one great name flows on continuously and unbroken, like the breath itself, neither scattered nor drowsy. Reciting the name with such single-minded diligence may be called the one who is able to practice the reliance-on-matter with single-minded vigor.

[What is called the one who is able to practice the reliance-on-matter with single-minded vigor] There is the Buddha-recitation of the matter and of the principle. The matter-recitation is to recite Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the principle-recitation is to probe one's own nature or to contemplate truly the reality of all dharmas. The matter-path is earnest toward rebirth; the principle-path aims at seeing the nature. The one-mind of matter and the one-mind of principle are also called the undivided mind of matter and the undivided mind of principle. Master Ouyi says:
'The one-mind of matter is distinctly clear, neither drowsy nor scattered; the one-mind of principle is the silent accord with the unborn and the clear penetration of one's own nature.'

(From the Collected Writings of the Master of Lingfeng, Occasional Talks in the Brahma Chamber) [Contemplating truly the reality of all dharmas] This is the Buddha-recitation of reality. [Four kinds of Buddha-recitation] First, holding the name: calling
the

Buddha-name. Second, contemplating an image: contemplating the Buddha's statue or picture. Third, contemplating the visualization: contemplate according to the Contemplation Sutra of Amitāyus. Fourth, Buddha-recitation of reality: contemplate truly the reality of all dharmas, which reality is precisely the Buddha's Dharma-body, and use the Dharma of 'ultimately empty, nothing existing' to recite the Buddha. (Concerning the reality of all dharmas, see
The Reality of All Dharmas

If one is a genuine seeker of the Way, one can directly probe that all dharmas are one and the same, and that there is no difference among them. That is to say, sentient beings and the buddhas are non-dual, oneself and others are non-dual, the retributions of the environment and of the body are non-dual, the pure and the defiled are non-dual, pleasure and suffering are non-dual, delight and aversion are non-dual, taking and rejecting are non-dual, enlightenment and affliction are non-dual, and birth-and-death and nirvana are non-dual. All of these two-fold dharmas are in reality of one and the same mark, equally pure.
[Probing that all dharmas are one and the same, with no difference among them] This is probing the reality of all dharmas, and is the Buddha-recitation of reality. The Buddha-Store Sutra says:
'What is called the reality of all dharmas? That is, all dharmas are, in the ultimate, empty, existing as nothing. With this Dharma of 'ultimately empty, nothing existing' one recites the Buddha.'
Again it says:

'To see nothing existing is called reciting the Buddha.' 'In such a Dharma, even a small thought cannot be obtained; this is called reciting the Buddha. Shariputra, this Dharma of reciting the Buddha cuts off the path of speech, goes beyond all thoughts, and cannot be thought of; this is called reciting the Buddha.'
(For details see
The Buddha-Store Sutra, Selected Annotations

) [The two retributions] The retribution of the environment and the retribution of the body. The lands, houses, implements, and so on of the world, as that on which the body relies, are called the 'retribution of the environment'; the body of a sentient being, made up of the five skandhas in temporary combination, as the recompense of past karma, is called the 'retribution of the body.'
One need not forcibly arrange anything to do; one simply probes truly by oneself:
All dharmas are thus, with no second mark.

When the probing reaches its utmost, it suddenly accords with one's own fundamental mind, and one realizes the undivided mind of principle. Then one knows that dressing and eating are always samadhi; laughing and scolding are none other than Buddha-work; and the one-mind and the scattered mind are in the end but idle talk. Throughout the two six-hour periods, if one perceives
qù
that not a hair's breadth of a different mark is obtainable, then though one be mindful with utmost sincerity
and

call the name, it is the same as open scolding and reviling; and though one be diligent in cultivation, it is likewise an ascetic practice in a dream. Only when one is thus enlightened is he a genuine seeker of the Way, one who holds the name with single-minded vigor.

[All dharmas are thus] All dharmas are one and the same, with no difference. [Thus] The meaning of 'one and the same.' In Buddhism, the true, unchanging nature of all dharmas can hardly be described in words, so the word 'thus' is borrowed to represent it. The nature is the reality; the reality is the 'thus.' Because the true face of all dharmas is entirely the same, it is called 'thus.' [Fundamental mind] The original state of the mind. (For details see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha
The former kind of undivided mind
(the undivided mind of matter)
seems hard but is easy;
the
latter kind of undivided mind
(the undivided mind of principle)

seems easy but is hard. As long as one is able to attain the undivided mind of matter, one will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. He who also attains the undivided mind of principle is reborn in the highest grade of the highest rebirth.

However, these two kinds of undivided mind are both things that ordinary people can do; anyone who has a mind can cultivate and learn them. The monks and laypeople together in this hall must not regard the undivided mind of principle as unattainably high, and so be content to dwell in a lowly state. Each should diligently spur on body and mind: nearer, within these seven days; farther, throughout a whole life, always holding this faith, always cultivating this practice. Even if one cannot realize the realm of accord with one's own fundamental mind, still the cause of rebirth is very superior, and the grade of transformation within the lotus bud will surely not be in the middle or lower.
If, after these seven days, one turns a deaf ear to the above instruction, and the familiar place
(that is, attachment to the emotions)
after all never becomes unfamiliar, and the unfamiliar place
(that is, reciting the Buddha)

remains hard to make familiar, and the ignorance and karmic habits entangle and interweave, vainly expecting to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss through the merit of this single vigorous seven-day retreat — while in these seven days one has not even
reached

the state of the undivided mind of matter — this is precisely the 'few roots of goodness, blessings, and conditions.' How can rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss be hoped for? So that Śākyamuni Buddha's
golden-worded sincere utterance

in the Amitabha Sutra is instead suspected to be deceptive. Whose fault is this after all? Pure practitioners of the Buddha-retreat, may you each examine this and, being admonished by this instruction, take care to spur yourselves.

[The familiar after all never becomes unfamiliar, the unfamiliar remaining hard to make familiar] In practice, one must 'turn the unfamiliar to the familiar, and the familiar to the unfamiliar.' For a reciter of the Buddha, the unfamiliar recitation turns familiar, and the familiar attachment turns unfamiliar. [The golden-worded sincere utterance] The Buddha taught in the Amitabha Sutra:

'If there are good men or good women who, having heard of Amitābha Buddha, hold his name, for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, with a single-minded, undistracted mind — then at the end of that person's life, Amitābha Buddha together with the holy assembly appears before him. When that person dies, his mind is not inverted, and he is instantly reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.'

Master Miaofeng's Dharma name was Fudeng, and his lay surname was Xu; he was a descendant of Xu Juju, a famous man of the Spring and Autumn period. In the nineteenth year of Jiajing of the Ming dynasty (C.E.

) he was born in a poor family in Pingyang Prefecture of Shanxi (present-day Linfen, Shanxi). At seven he met a year of famine and both his parents died of illness and hunger. At that time the family was so poor that even a thin coffin could not be bought; with the help of neighbors and relatives, two torn mats were used to wrap the bodies and the parents were buried carelessly.

After this Miaofeng became an orphan with no one to raise him, and every day he herded sheep for the villagers, barely keeping himself alive. In this way he grew to twelve, and really could not go on; he heard there was a Buddhist monastery nearby where one could shave the head and become a monk, cultivating and observing a pure diet. This too was a way out for a poor boy, and so he ran off and left the home life.

In the middle of the Ming dynasty, Buddhism was in decline, and many monasteries had in fact nothing of precepts and practice to speak of; monastics too were ranked in grades, the rich like landlords and merchants, the poor like hired laborers and tenant farmers, and oppression, exploitation, and discrimination were common. Unfortunately Miaofeng entered just such a pit of fire: poor, ugly, young, and weak, he was bullied everywhere. Not to speak of receiving precepts and studying the Dharma and practicing, even coarse food and tattered clothes could not be assured. Miaofeng muddled along painfully for five years and, seeing himself at seventeen, with nothing accomplished and growing more and more difficult, he simply ran away, taking a broken gourd as a beggar's bowl and wandering the rivers and lakes.

Wandering from Pingyang to Puzhou (present-day Yongji city), he stopped running about. By day he begged in Puzhou city, and by night slept in the Wenchang Pavilion. The old monk Langgong of Wenchang Pavilion was a true practitioner with a mind of compassion, and treated Miaofeng well, often looking after him. Gradually, Miaofeng's fate took a turn for the better.

blocks.text: The Favor of the Prince of Shanyin

inline.s: In Puzhou city there dwelt a prince of the imperial clan of the Ming, the Prince of Shanyin, whose surname was Zhu and name Junshan. His ancestor was the thirteenth son of the founding emperor Taizu, Zhu Gui, the Prince of Dai, enfeoffed at Datong; after several generations the clan multiplied, and since life in Datong was difficult a few branches moved to southern Shanxi. The Prince of Shanyin, Zhu Junshan, was such a collateral minor prince, an ordinary noble. The history records of him: 'In the twentieth year of Wanli (

), when the Western Xia was unruly, the Prince of Shanyin, Junshan, submitted eight chapters of poems, which carried the intent of remonstrance. Since the Dai lineage dwelt at the frontier and its branches had passed through calamity again and again, his words were all deeply concerned and far-sighted, beyond even what the court officials of the middle kingdom could reach.' We can see that he was an enlightened noble with a sense of concern, and had literary talent and believed in Buddhism. Because of his favorable regard, the life of Master Miaofeng was changed.

One day the Prince of Shanyin saw Miaofeng in the Wenchang Pavilion, and saw that this young man, though he was extremely ugly and every feature apparent, had a focused spirit and solid bones — a makable talent — so he hinted to Master Langgong to look after Miaofeng. After a while a great earthquake struck southern Shanxi, and Puzhou was in ruins; Miaofeng too was crushed under a collapsed house, and Langgong dug him out, finding that his skin and flesh were unharmed. As the saying goes: 'He who survives a great disaster is destined for future fortune.' The Prince of Shanyin therefore regarded Miaofeng even more favorably, judging that he would surely become a great vessel, and so deliberately nurtured him.

The Prince of Shanyin said to Miaofeng: 'You have escaped a great disaster; why not earnestly reflect on the great matter of birth and death and begin your practice early?' Miaofeng was now twenty-one, and hearing this wished to travel far to seek learning. The Prince of Shanyin thought Miaofeng's foundation in Buddhism too thin, and that he could not learn much by going out, so he had him go to the Qiyan Monastery on Zhongtiao Mountain nearby to practice in 'seclusion.' Qiyan Monastery had been the place where the eminent monk Tanyan of the Northern Dynasties first rose to prominence, and by then it had fallen into ruin; the Prince of Shanyin helped Miaofeng repair a few rooms to dwell in.

So-called 'seclusion' means to shut the door and not come out, concentrating energy on practice, while the needs of life are cared for by a 'guardian.' Miaofeng asked a nearby Dharma master about the practice method of the 'Realm of Dharmas' contemplation, and began the long 'seclusion.' This method requires one to practice always standing, not allowed to sit or sleep for several years, and is extremely hard. Miaofeng persisted for three years, then suddenly had some awakening, and joyfully wrote four lines of verse on paper, entrusting someone to deliver them to the Prince of Shanyin for his verification. The Prince of Shanyin read them, wondered exceedingly, and judged that Miaofeng truly had spiritual faculties and far-seeing insight. But on reflection he thought that Miaofeng was still too young, and that if he were not subjected to checks and tempering, he might in time become an arrogant, vain, word-deceiving wild monk. The Prince had a flash of inspiration, made someone find an old shoe, cut off the smelly sole, put it in an envelope, and added a sheet of paper writing: 'This smelly shoe-sole, I seal and send to you; not for any other thing, but only to strike that mouth that makes verse!' and sent it back to Miaofeng. When Miaofeng saw it he immediately understood the Prince's deep intent, and before the Buddha earnestly bowed several times, and taking a thread, tied the smelly shoe-sole and hung it about his neck as a 'motto,' continuing his hard practice, and from then on never uttered rash opinions. After another three years the 'seclusion' came to an end, and he came out to pay respects to the Prince of Shanyin, carrying himself with the dignity of an eminent monk in his movements and speech.

The Prince of Shanyin continued to encourage Miaofeng: 'Though your practice now has some foundation, you have not yet heard true Dharma, and if you are not careful you may in time fall into wrong views. Now there is an eminent monk in Jieshan preaching the Shurangama Sutra; I will provide a bit of travel money, and you should go listen.' Miaofeng was twenty-seven that year, went to Jieshan to hear the sutra, and received the full precepts, gaining greatly. After returning to Puzhou, the Prince of Shanyin again said: 'You may now be counted a qualified monk, but beyond the mountain there are mountains and beyond the sky there is a sky; if your steps never leave the monastery gate, you are still like a frog at the bottom of a well with no knowledge. There are many eminent Dharma masters of the South; go and travel and visit them, and broaden your horizons. When you return, tell me all about it in detail — consider it a hard journey taken on my behalf.'

The Prince of Shanyin personally prepared the implements and travel money for Miaofeng's wandering pilgrimage, and took off the woolen clothes and stockings he himself wore, and over them sewed a layer of humble torn cloth, and gave them to Miaofeng to keep warm on the road.
Miaofeng then traveled alone, wandering among the clouds and waters, visiting the eminent masters of the South to seek their instruction, and made a pilgrimage to Putuo Mountain of the South Sea.

blocks.text: The Friendship with Master Hanshan

inline.s: The wandering pilgrimage of a monastic is very hard work. When one chanced upon a temple one would lodge and take a pure meal; when not, one ate and slept in the open. Miaofeng came down from Putuo Mountain, crossed the sea back to Ningbo, and unfortunately contracted the epidemic rife there, lying ill in an inn. Alone, with no one to look after him. At night he wanted a sip of water, but though he called for a long time the inn servant did not answer. Half dead with thirst, he remembered there was a little water in the washbasin, and forcing his sick body, he scooped a few mouthfuls with his hand. The bathwater entered his mouth, and it tasted utterly sweet. In the morning he rose, and looking in the light, saw the basin actually held filthy, stinking water; at once sickened and disgusted, he vomited for a long time.

But in the life of a monastic all things require awakening to Buddhist principle. When Miaofeng had finished vomiting, he suddenly thought: last night when he was terribly thirsty the water was sweet, but in the morning, when the light was plain, the water turned out to be dirty — it seems 'purity and defilement come from the mind'! He understood this principle at once, immediately no longer felt the nausea and vomiting, his heart was relieved, and his illness soon healed, though he was left covered in yellow swellings and itching sores.

Next he wandered to Nanjing and lodged temporarily at Tianjie Monastery. The monks of the monastery, seeing that he was ugly and dirty, assigned him a duty of cleaning the latrines, what in the monastery (that is, the temple) is called the 'clean-head.' Through this connection he made the acquaintance of Master Hanshan Deqing, later called one of the four great masters of the late Ming.

The meeting of the two was very interesting. Hanshan was younger than Miaofeng, but he came from Baoen Monastery, a great monastery of the nation, and was a disciple of a distinguished house, an emerging talent. Moreover his talent overflowed and his bearing was elegant, so his fame was already on high at the time. Master Wuji lectured on the Lotus Sutra at Tianjie Monastery, and Hanshan served as a co-lecturer, comparable to a 'teaching assistant' — a post that drew much attention. Yet Hanshan was not content with preaching the sutra; in secret he often sought out extraordinary people, wishing to probe the 'one final stroke upward.' Every morning when he went to the latrine, he found that this latrine of Tianjie Monastery was very clean, yet he never saw anyone sweeping it, and thinking it strange, he pondered that there must be a person of worth. So he deliberately spied for several days, and found that the 'clean-head' who cleaned the latrine was a sick practitioner with yellow swellings, who every night lit a lamp and worked, and by the early hours when the monks rose to use the latrine, his work was already done. So Hanshan concluded that this sick practitioner with yellow swellings was a person of worth, and resolved to befriend him.

After a few days the latrine suddenly was not clean. Hanshan asked about it, and learned that the 'clean-head' had fallen ill, so he went to see him, and by this he became acquainted with Master Miaofeng. The conversation when the two met was also quite interesting. Miaofeng said: 'The sickness of the body I can still bear; it is the sickness of craving that is hard to cure.' Hanshan asked him why; Miaofeng said: 'When I see others eating steamed buns, my heart cannot put it down.' Hanshan knew Miaofeng had gone hungry too long — an outside sick monk, not valued in the monastery, hungry and no one looking after him — so he found some pastries and gave them to Miaofeng, who ate them very happily, and by this the two established a sincere friendship.

Miaofeng had heard Hanshan lecture on the scriptures and greatly admired his learning. Hanshan, for his part, greatly admired Miaofeng's practice, and said he wished to wander and visit [teachers] together with Miaofeng. But after Miaofeng recovered from illness, feeling that his own great matter was not yet settled and fearing that Hanshan would be a burden to him, he slipped away quietly.

Miaofeng returned to Puzhou, went to pay his respects to the Prince of Shanyin, recounted his experience of wandering and visiting [teachers], and spoke of Hanshan's talent and character. Afterwards he hid deep in Mount Zhongtiao and practiced austerities with fierce diligence, for three years in a row not cutting his hair or beard even once. The Prince of Shanyin increasingly believed in Buddhism, built a temple, and invited Miaofeng out of the deep mountains to serve as its abbot, and entrusted him to go to Beijing once and print a set of the Great Treasury of Scriptures to bring back. Miaofeng had no time to shave off his hair and beard, and catching a ride with an official who was going to the capital, he hurried to Beijing. Here he met Hanshan for the second time, and the meeting was again full of drama.

At this time Hanshan was seeking an opportunity in Beijing to rebuild Bao'en Temple, and was not doing very well. When Miaofeng came to see him, he falsely said that he was a salt merchant. They faced each other; his hair and beard were disheveled, his two eyes shone brightly, and he asked Hanshan: “Do you still recognize me?” Hanshan stared at him for a long while, and at last recognized from those bright eyes the formerly jaundiced, swollen sickly ascetic of Tianjie Temple. Now the jaundice and swelling had completely subsided, but much hair and beard had grown, so that he was quite different from before — he really did look like a salt merchant. Miaofeng said with feeling: “I have changed my head and face!” Hanshan laughed and said: “Your original face is still there.”

The next day they met again, sharing a couch and conversing through the night, as close as brothers. Hanshan once again said he wished to follow Miaofeng in practice, and Miaofeng said modestly: “I am willing to be your vanguard to drive away the dogs.”

Hanshan's friend, the Minister of War Wang Boyu, also thought very highly of Miaofeng, and urged Hanshan to take Miaofeng as a good friend and practice together. Hanshan was by nature a man of high gifts and proud spirit, and later hesitated somewhat, unwilling to follow at another's heels. Wang Boyu admonished and urged him again and again, and finally, after Miaofeng had set out, Hanshan followed after him, and the two returned to Puzhou together.

The following year, Hanshan helped Miaofeng bury his parents, and the two went together to Mount Wutai to live in seclusion and practice. Miaofeng had begun practice earlier than Hanshan and had more experience, and in the course of practice he often gave Hanshan guidance and confirmation.

blocks.text: The Great Buddhist Ceremony at Mount Wutai

inline.s: After several years of secluded practice on Mount Wutai, both Miaofeng and Hanshan had made considerable progress. In order to repay the kindness of his parents in raising him, Hanshan resolved to write out a copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra in his own blood. Miaofeng also actively responded, vowing to write out a copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood from his tongue. The two men's ascetic practice and filial heart moved the Emperor Shenzong of the Ming and the Empress Dowager Cisheng, who specially sent people to bestow the gold and paper for writing the sutras.

After several years of writing the sutras, the merit was completed, and Miaofeng and Hanshan decided to hold an “Unobstructed Assembly” in commemoration and celebration. This was a large-scale Buddhist activity, with complex ceremonies, many participants, much time spent, and much money and grain consumed. The two divided the tasks: Miaofeng would go down the mountain to beg for money and grain, while Hanshan would prepare the other matters on the mountain. At this time, because Emperor Shenzong had had no heir since his marriage, the imperial household sent people separately to Mount Wutai and Mount Wudang to make both Buddhist and Daoist prayers. Hanshan had a strong political awareness, and thought this was an opportunity for a monk, a subject outside the court, to do his utmost loyalty for the state, and so decided to change his long-prepared “Unobstructed Assembly” into an assembly to pray for an heir.

In this matter, Miaofeng and Hanshan had a disagreement, and the eunuch sent by the court also felt that Hanshan was flattering and attaching himself to the imperial house, climbing the dragon and clinging to the phoenix. Hanshan argued his case with sound reasoning, and in the end Miaofeng and all the other parties agreed with Hanshan's approach. So the Unobstructed Assembly was changed into an assembly for praying for an heir, and it was held very successfully. This matter had a great influence on the later lives of both Miaofeng and Hanshan. For it happened that ten months after the assembly was held, a young palace maid bore a son for Emperor Shenzong, who was the later Emperor Guangzong. The Empress Dowager was endlessly grateful to these eminent monks, and in turn did much to benefit Buddhism. And so, in some popular sayings, people went so far as to call Hanshan, Miaofeng, and the others the “maternal uncles of the state.”

After the assembly ended, both Hanshan and Miaofeng gained great fame, known throughout the world. The two felt that under such great fame they could not long remain, so they quietly left Mount Wutai. This pair of Dharma-brothers from then on parted ways, and never met again. At parting, Miaofeng, being affectionate, gave his little disciple, the novice Dezong, to Hanshan to attend to his daily needs.

Hanshan went into seclusion on Mount Lao in Shandong. Later, because he built Haiyin Temple, he fell into dispute with the Daoists, and became entangled in a dispute within the palace; he was sued, forced to return to lay life, and banished to Lingnan. Thereupon he spread Buddhism in the south, wrote books and established his teachings, revived the ancestral courts of the Chan school, and finally became a famous monk of a generation.

Miaofeng, for his part, went into seclusion on Mount Luya in Shanxi. In later years, with the support of the imperial house, the nobility, officials, and the broad mass of Buddhists, good deeds followed one after another and his Dharma-fortunes flourished; over several decades he built many grand projects.

blocks.text: The “Lu Ban” of the Buddhist Order

inline.s: In his early years, Master Miaofeng chiefly manifested himself as a diligent practitioner, a true eminent monk. But in his later years his outstanding talent in architectural engineering and the like was displayed one after another, so that one could hardly take it all in. Perhaps because in his youth he had been poor and able to do humble work, having learned some craftsman's skills, later, when he investigated Chan and awakened to the Way, his wisdom burst forth, and he mastered the “craftsmanship” among the “five sciences” of which Buddhism speaks, turning from an ordinary talent into a genius.

Not long after Miaofeng went into seclusion on Mount Luya, the grateful Empress Dowager Cisheng sent people to find him, allocated special funds to build Huayan Temple on Mount Luya for Miaofeng to dwell in, and later built a seven-story iron pagoda on the mountaintop. This was the beginning of Miaofeng's work in construction.

Soon after, Wangu Temple in Puzhou also needed rebuilding. The local official Wang Jianchuan provided the funds and invited Miaofeng to oversee the project. Wangu Temple was a place Miaofeng had visited in the past, so naturally he could not decline; he returned to Wangu Temple and worked for three years, completing the project, with the pagoda and halls newly renovated. Next, Sanyuan in Shaanxi wanted to build the Wei River bridge, and the local official Li Kuoan invited Miaofeng to supervise; it took two years to complete.

Having finished the projects in his native place and in Shaanxi, Miaofeng returned to live on Mount Luya. Passing through Ninghua on the way, he saw a stone cliff of a thousand fathoms, as level as the palm of a hand — the very best place to build a Buddhist grotto. Miaofeng, who had just been doing construction for a few years, was full of enthusiasm; he raised funds and began work, completing the exquisite stone-carved structure the “Cave of Ten Thousand Buddhas,” which to this day remains a local historical monument and tourist attraction.

Before long, Xuanhua Prefecture (present-day Zhangjiakou, Hebei) wanted to build a bridge over the Yellow River, and invited Master Miaofeng by reputation to oversee the project. This project had considerable difficulty — the water was broad and the sand deep — but Miaofeng personally surveyed and designed it, and in the end built a twenty-three-arch bridge, and succeeded as well.

According to historical records, throughout his life, apart from chanting scriptures, worshiping the Buddha, sitting in meditation, begging alms, and wandering, Miaofeng devoted all his heart and strength to building Buddhist temples, constructing bridges, and opening roads. In the capital, Shanxi, Hebei, Shaanxi, Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou, Hubei, Henan, Anhui, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang — everywhere there are traces of his feet. In every place he set foot, there is a building of his. “Of the great merits he performed, none can be fully recounted” (see the Dream Travels Collection) — truly he was a master builder of the samgha.

After this, Master Miaofeng also had cast the three great bronze halls of the three great Buddhist holy mountains — Emei, Baohua, and Wutai — and so on. Because he wandered in all directions and built in every place, his merit was known throughout the realm. Therefore in the thirty-third year of Wanli (

), when Miaofeng delivered the third bronze hall to Xiantong Temple on Mount Wutai for installation, the Wanli Emperor issued an edict commanding him to expand Xiantong Temple, with all the expenses funded from the imperial treasury. Miaofeng acted in accordance with the edict, and the emperor funded the temple's repair; for a time it was a great stir, and the work was vigorously undertaken, and in only two years the project was completed. The newly expanded Xiantong Temple became the largest, most extensive, most highly regulated, and most magnificent great temple complex on Mount Wutai, the holy land of the Buddha-land. The Xiantong Temple we see today — “six stories front and back, with encircling pavilions towering one above another, in grand and splendid scale” — was built by the hand of Miaofeng in those years.

After the great Xiantong Temple was rebuilt, the Wanli Emperor abandoned the name “Xiantong,” and personally bestowed the name “Great Protectorate of the State, Holy Light Yongming (Everlasting Light) Temple,” and enfeoffed Miaofeng as “State-Protecting Chan Master,” to be abbot of Yongming Temple and to manage Mount Wutai in general. During the period when Miaofeng was abbot of Yongming Temple and managed the Buddhist affairs of the whole of Mount Wutai, he laid stone courses and paved roads, erected bridges, and built temples along the way, across several hundred li of high mountains and steep ridges from Fuping in Hebei to Taihuai township on Mount Wutai; the works were extremely vast. History relates: “He set bridges over the streams, built and opened temples, and paved in stone a great road of over a hundred li.” (See the Record of the Cool and Clear Mountain.) The Puji Bridge of Fuping, the Huiji Temple of Longquan Pass, the famous Ciyou Yuanming Temple and within it the Longzang Pavilion, the Tathagata Hall, the bell and drum towers, the two corridors of “monks' cells,” the thirty-six-foot [image of] the receiving Buddha — the Amitabha image, the tall and open heavenly-king hall of the mountain gate — all were created at this time, all products of Miaofeng's original genius. This huge series of construction works opened up a clear route for the imperial household and high officials of the capital to make pilgrimages to Mount Wutai, and for the scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants of Hebei and the northeastern provinces who believed in Buddhism.
In the thirty-sixth year of Wanli (

), the eleventh prince of the Jin domain, Prince Jinmu Zhu Minchun, invited Miaofeng to the provincial capital Taiyuan Prefecture's Great Tower Temple to build halls, enlarge its scale, and also serve as its abbot. The Great Tower Temple of Taiyuan Prefecture was the “Yongming Temple” built by the local gentry, including Fu Shan's grandfather Fu Lin. That year Miaofeng was already

years old, approaching the age of seventy. Yet, heedless of his advanced age and failing strength, he gladly accepted Prince Jinmu's invitation and went in person to the Great Tower Yongming Temple in Taiyuan, where he managed the great project of rebuilding and expanding the temple. Before long, since the “Yongming Temple” of Taiyuan shared its name with the “Holy Light Yongming Temple” that the emperor had ordered built on Mount Wutai, Miaofeng changed the character “Ming” (Light) to “Zuo” (Blessed), taking its meaning from the line “eternally bestow blessed posterity” in the Book of Songs, and changed Yongming Temple to Yongzuo Temple. At the beginning of the work, Miaofeng discovered that the great tower built by the original temple was tilted toward the north, and so, with the funding of the mother of the Prince of Jin, he added a new tower to the northwest of the old one, achieving the wonder of “two towers standing together.” From then on, the customary name of the Great Tower Temple was replaced by “Twin-Tower Temple,” and its original name was lost in the dust of history, unknown to people.

In the design of the Yongzuo Temple rebuilt by Miaofeng, it was far beyond the scale of today; it was to be much grander and more magnificent. But Miaofeng, already advanced in years, in four years of unremitting toil by day and night, at last fell ill from overwork, like a guttering candle in his waning years. When the tower work was completed and the temple had only finished the Great Hero Hall, the Three Sages Pavilion, the meditation quarters, and the guest lodgings, he returned to the “Holy Light Yongming Temple” on Mount Wutai despite illness, and passed into nirvana three months later. In the remaining years, he devoted himself to temple construction and to bridge and road building; of what he built, for the most part it still remains in the world today, and some still benefits the people. To call him a famous architect of the Ming dynasty is by no means extravagant praise. The Yongzuo Temple and the Buddha's relic tower he built finally became a great sight of Taiyuan, the emblem of Taiyuan for nearly four hundred years, and at present are honored as a national cultural protection unit. Moreover, according to local records, when he built the temple and the tower, “he planned to build a great bridge over the Fen River, with stone almost reaching the height of the mountain.” Sadly, heaven did not grant him life enough, and this long-cherished wish was left unfulfilled.
